Key points
• Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) develops when your body doesn’t have enough insulin to allow blood
sugar into your cells for use as energy.
• DKA is most common among people with type 1 diabetes.
• DKA is serious and can be life-threatening.


Overview
DKA is a serious complication of diabetes that can be life-threatening. DKA is most common among
people with type 1 diabetes . People with type 2 diabetes can also develop DKA.
DKA develops when your body doesn't have enough insulin to allow blood sugar into your cells for
use as energy. Instead, your liver breaks down fat for fuel, a process that produces acids called
ketones. When too many ketones are produced too fast, they can build up to dangerous levels in
your body.
Read on to learn more about DKA, how you can prevent DKA, and how to treat it if needed.


Signs and symptoms
DKA usually develops slowly. Early symptoms include:
• Being very thirsty.
• Urinating a lot more than usual.
If untreated, more severe symptoms can appear quickly, such as:
• Fast, deep breathing.
• Dry skin and mouth.
• Flushed face.
• Fruity-smelling breath.
• Headache.
• Muscle stiffness or aches.
• Being very tired.
• Nausea and vomiting.

title: CDC: Diabetic Ketoacidosis
text:
• Stomach pain.
Sometimes DKA is the first noticeable sign of diabetes in people who haven't yet been diagnosed.


Causes
Very high blood sugar and low insulin levels lead to DKA. The two most common causes are:
• Illness. You may not be able to eat or drink as much as usual, which can make blood sugar hard
to manage.
• Missing insulin shots, a clogged insulin pump, or the wrong insulin dose.
Other causes of DKA include:
• Heart attack or stroke.
• Physical injury, such as from a car accident.
• Alcohol or drug use.
• Certain medicines, such as some diuretics (water pills) and corticosteroids (used to treat
inflammation in the body).


Prevention
DKA is a serious condition, but you can take steps to help prevent it:
• Check your blood sugar often, especially if you're sick.
• Keep your blood sugar levels in your target range as much as possible.
• Take medicines as prescribed, even if you feel fine.
• Talk to your doctor about how to adjust your insulin based on what you eat, how active you are, or
if you're sick.
If you're at risk for type 1 diabetes, you can also prevent DKA through early treatment. Even people
who don't get treatment to prevent type 1 diabetes can monitor for signs and symptoms of DKA to
avoid an emergency situation.
If you're concerned about DKA or have questions about how to manage your diabetes , talk to your
diabetes care team. Ask them for a referral to diabetes self-management education and support
(DSMES) for individual guidance. DSMES services are a vital tool to help you manage and live well
with diabetes while protecting your health.


Testing


Test for ketones
If you have diabetes and you're sick or your blood sugar is 250 mg/dL or above, you'll need to
check your blood sugar every 4 to 6 hours and check your urine for ketones. Ketone test kits are
affordable and widely available over the counter to check your ketones at home. You should also
test for ketones if you have any of the symptoms of DKA. Elevated ketones are a sign of DKA. This
is a medical emergency that needs to be treated immediately .
Go to the emergency room or call 911 right away if you're having any of these signs:
• Your blood sugar stays at 300 mg/dL or above.

title: CDC: Diabetic Ketoacidosis
text:
• Your breath smells fruity.
• You are vomiting and can't keep food or drinks down.
• You're having trouble breathing.
• You have multiple signs and symptoms of DKA.


High ketones? Call 911
High ketones can be an early sign of DKA, which is a medical emergency. Call 911 or go to the
emergency room right away.


Treatment
If you have DKA, you'll be treated in the emergency room or admitted to the hospital. Your
treatment will likely include:
• Replacing fluids you lost through frequent urination and to help dilute excess sugar in your blood.
• Replacing electrolytes (minerals in your body). Too little insulin can lower electrolytes.
• Receiving insulin . Insulin reverses the conditions that cause DKA.
• Taking medicines for any underlying illness that caused DKA, such as antibiotics for an infection.

Insulin for Injection | Insulin Switching | Insulin Mixes | Insulin Pumps
This guide explains how to store and use insulin during an emergency, when your usual supply may
not be available. Always follow your doctor's instructions when possible.


Insulin Storage and Effectiveness
During a disaster, you may receive insulin from a different manufacturer than what you normally
use. You may also not have access to a refrigerator. Here is what you need to know about storing
insulin safely.


Insulin for Injection
According to the product labels from all three U.S. insulin manufacturers, it is recommended that
insulin be stored in a refrigerator at approximately 36°F to 46°F. Unopened and stored in this
manner, these products maintain effectiveness until the expiration date on the package.
Insulin products contained in vials or cartridges supplied by the manufacturers (opened or
unopened) may be left unrefrigerated at a temperature between 59°F and 86°F for up to 28 days
and continue to work. However, an insulin product that has been diluted or removed from the
manufacturer’s original vial should be thrown away within two weeks.


Extreme Temperatures
Extreme temperatures make insulin less effective. The longer insulin is exposed to extreme heat or
cold, the less effective it becomes. Over time, this can make it harder to control your blood sugar.
Under emergency conditions, you might still need to use insulin that has been stored above 86°F.
You should try to keep insulin as cool as possible. If you are using ice, avoid freezing the insulin. Do
not use insulin that has been frozen. Keep insulin away from direct heat and out of direct sunlight.
Once you have access to properly stored insulin, throw away any vials that were exposed to
extreme temperatures and replace them as soon as possible. If patients or healthcare providers
have specific questions about the suitability of their insulin, they may call the manufacturer at the
following numbers:

Note : Manufacturer contact numbers are subject to change. Patients and healthcare providers
should verify current contact information using the product's package insert or by visiting the
manufacturer's official website.


Special Storage: Once-Weekly Insulin (Awiqli)
Awiqli (insulin icodec) is only available as a prefilled pen. It has a longer unrefrigerated storage
window than other insulin products. Unopened Awiqli FlexTouch pens stored in a refrigerator (36°F
to 46°F) may be kept until the expiration date. Once removed from the refrigerator, or when in use,
Awiqli pens may be stored at room temperature below 86°F for up to 12 weeks. The total combined
time at room temperature, whether opened or unopened, must not exceed 12 weeks. Do not freeze
Awiqli; do not use if it has been frozen.
Note : The in-use pen may also be stored in a refrigerator (36°F to 46°F) for up to 12 weeks — the
12-week limit applies regardless of whether storage is at room temperature or refrigerated.


Special Storage: Insulin Pumps
Insulin in the pump’s infusion set (such as the reservoir, tubing, catheters) should be thrown away
after 48 hours. Unless your pump device’s instructions are different. For example, NovoLog, Kirsty,
and Humalog U-100 specify up to 6–7 days in the reservoir; Fiasp PumpCart specifies 4 days.
Always follow the specific product's prescribing information and your pump device's instructions for
use.
If the pump insulin is exposed to temperatures above 98.6°F, throw it away.


Switching Insulin
Always switch insulin under a doctor’s care, with close monitoring of your blood sugar. If you cannot
reach a doctor during an emergency, follow the guidance below — but monitor your blood sugar
closely and see a doctor as soon as you can.


Short-acting (regular insulin) and Rapid-acting Insulins
In an emergency, you can switch one brand of regular insulin (such as Humulin R or Novolin R) for
another brand of regular insulin, or for a rapid-acting insulin (such as Apidra, Fiasp, Humalog, or
NovoLog), and vice versa. Use the same number of units.
Inject regular insulins approximately 30 minutes before the start of each meal. Rapid-acting insulins
begin working more rapidly than regular insulin and are to be injected no more than 15 minutes
before the start of each meal to avoid dangerously low blood sugar levels.

title: FDA: Information Regarding Insulin Storage and Switching Between Products in an Emergency
text:
Intermediate and Long-acting Insulins
In an emergency, you can switch one brand of intermediate-acting insulin (such as, Humulin N,
Novolin N) for another intermediate-acting insulin on a unit-per-unit basis. You can also switch
 intermediate-acting insulins for long-acting insulins (e.g., Lantus, Toujeo, Tresiba) on a total
unit-per-day basis, or vice versa.
Important :
• If you switch from a once-daily long-acting insulin (e.g., Lantus, Toujeo, Tresiba) to an
intermediate-acting insulin, keep your total daily dose the same but split it into two equal injections.
Give half in the morning with breakfast and half in the evening with dinner to avoid a dangerously
low blood sugar.
• If you switch from an intermediate-acting to a once-daily long-acting insulin, add up the total
amount of intermediate-acting insulin units for one day, and give it as a single long-acting insulin
dose once a day.
Close monitoring of blood sugar and adjustment of your insulin dose may be needed in the
transition.


Once-weekly Long-acting Insulin
If you use the once-weekly long-acting insulin, Awiqli (insulin icodec) and need to switch to a
once-daily long-acting or intermediate-acting insulin in an emergency, base your dose on your total
weekly dose.
When switching from a once-daily long-acting insulin to insulin icodec, give the first insulin icodec
dose on the day after your last daily long-acting insulin dose. For Week 1, multiply your previous
total daily dose by 7, then by 1.5, and round to the nearest 10 units.
Important: Because insulin icodec stays active for about one week, its blood sugar-lowering effect
continues for several days after the last dose. If you switch from Awiqli to a basal (background)
long-acting insulin, switching should be done under close medical supervision with increased blood
sugar monitoring to avoid low blood sugar (hypoglycemia).
Note : Insulin icodec must not be used in an insulin pump, mixed with other insulins, or drawn from
the pen into a syringe.


Insulin Mixes
Switching between types of insulin should be done with a doctor’s guidance and close blood sugar
monitoring.


What is an Insulin Mix?
Insulin mixes combine two types of insulin, intermediate- and short/rapid-acting, in one dose. The
first number shows how much intermediate insulin is in the mix and the second number shows how
much short/rapid-acting insulin. For example, each dose of a 70/30 mix contains 70%
intermediate-acting insulin and 30% short/rapid-acting insulin.


Switching from Your Insulin Mix: Substitution or Replacement
If you use a pre-mixed insulin (e.g., Humulin 70/30, Humalog Mix 75/25, Novolin 70/30, NovoLog
Mix 70/30), here are your options in an emergency:

title: FDA: Information Regarding Insulin Storage and Switching Between Products in an Emergency
text:
• In an emergency, you can switch one insulin mix for another on a unit-per-unit basis.
• Insulin mixes with rapid-acting insulin analog (e.g., Humalog Mix, Novolog Mix) should be injected
closer (within 15 minutes) to the start of the meal compared to mixes containing regular insulin
(e.g., Humulin 70/30).
• If an insulin mix is not available, patients should follow this two-step process:
• Step one: replace an intermediate-acting part of the mix (about 70% of the total units for each
dose) with an intermediate-acting or a long-acting insulin on a unit-per-unit basis.
• With an intermediate-acting insulin :
• Give 70% of total units for each dose
• With a long-acting insulin :
• Add up the total insulin units given in one day
• Give 70% as one daily dose
• Step two: if regular or rapid-acting insulins are also available, use them before major meals. The
dose should be about 30% of your total of pre-mixed insulin for that meal, in addition to the
intermediate- or long-acting.
Note : Inject longer and shorter acting insulins separately unless your doctor tells you otherwise.


Insulin Pumps
If your pump supplies are not available or your pump is not working properly, you may need to
switch to injected insulin. This should be done with a doctor's guidance and close blood sugar
monitoring whenever possible.


Using a Different Insulin in Your Insulin Pump
I n an emergency, you may be able to swap one rapid-acting insulin (such as Apidra, Fiasp,
Humalog, Novolog) for another on a unit-per-unit basis . Check your pump’s instructions to make
sure the available insulins are compatible with your devices.
Note : Not all rapid-acting insulins are approved for pump use. Merilog (insulin aspart-szjj) is not
currently labeled for insulin pump use. Humalog U-200 and Lyumjev U-200 must NOT be used in
insulin pumps. Always check the specific insulin product labeling before use in a pump.


Switching from an Insulin Pump to Injected Insulin
If you must switch from your pump to injected insulin, use the following guidance:
• Replace your pump’s total 24-hour basal (background) dose with insulin on a unit-per-unit basis.
• For intermediate-acting insulin, split the 24-hour basal (background) dose into two equal injections
per day. For example, if your 24-hour basal (background) dose is 24 units, inject 12 units twice
daily.
• For long-acting insulin, give the full 24-hour basal (background) dose as one injection per day.
• If regular or rapid-acting insulin is also available, use it with each meal. Match your pump’s bolus
(mealtime) dose on a unit-per-unit basis.
• For example, if your pump gives a bolus (mealtime) of 5 units to cover breakfast, inject 5 units of
regular or rapid-acting insulin to cover that meal

Introduction
   ATP 4-02.11 provides discussion on casualty response and first aid procedures for nonmedical personnel in
   environments from home station to combat situations. This publication is meant to be used by trainers and
   individuals being trained based on common first aid tasks. These tasks are meant to reinforce and maintain
   proficiency in the correct procedures for providing first aid throughout a Service member’s time in Service.
   ATP 4-02.11 is designed to facilitate training and first aid competencies by bridging first aid training across
   the spectrum of assignments from initial military training to permanent duty station and deployment. ATP 4-
   02.11 introduces Tactical Combat Casualty Care (TCCC) with first aid tasks and procedures associated with
   combat situations. Training scenarios can be completed by combining individual and multiple first aid tasks
   with collective tasks.
   ATP 4-02.11 consists of three parts, 20 chapters, and two appendixes.

title: U.S. Army: Casualty Response, Tactical Combat Casualty Care, and First Aid (ATP 4-02.11)
text:
PART ONE
                                                        289B




                                     CASUALTY RESPONSE
                                     29B




Casualty response is of paramount importance to military units and leaders in winning our
Nations’s wars and providing a critical role in ensuring the welfare and effectiveness of the
armed forces. In the unpredictable and high-stakes environment of warfare, casualties are
an unfortunate reality. Whether it is injuries sustained on the battlefield or the loss of fellow
Service members, casualty response encompasses the immediate and long-term actions
taken to mitigate the impact of these incidents. Effective casualty response saves lives but
also boosts the morale of troops, enhances unit cohesion, allows leaders to maintain
operational readiness, and win our Nations’s wars.

                                                               Chapter 1
                                            Casualty Response

CASUALTY RESPONSE OVERVIEW
195B




          1-1. Casualty response is the immediate and organized care, evacuation and reporting of those injured
          or killed in action. Casualty response is a leader driven system designed to synchronize the planning,
          rehearsal, and execution of individual and collective tasks required to complete the mission while improving
          casualty outcomes. Due to the nature of military operations both at home and in combat, nonmedical Service
          members must sometimes rely on themselves and other Service members to render first aid until medical
          assistance arrives. Self-aid, buddy aid, and combat lifesaver (CLS) support is normally the first care a casualty
          receives in an operational setting and is provided until medically trained personnel (combat medic, corpsman,
          or medical technician) arrive to begin treatment.
          1-2. First responder care includes self-aid, buddy aid, CLS tasks, and Tactical Combat Casualty Care
          (TCCC). Care provided by first responders is not limited to Service members but is provided to all those
          requiring initial treatment, stabilization, and when necessary, movement to higher roles of care for further
          treatment.
          1-3. First responder care varies by Service, with the core training focused on TCCC. The application of TCCC
          occurs anywhere in the pre-hospital setting and can be tailored by the Joint Trauma System (JTS) to support
          Service-specific mission requirements. The TCCC training has four individual tiers or sets of responsibilities
          (see table 1-1 on page 2):
               • Self-aid or buddy aid.
               • Combat lifesaver.
               • Combat medic or corpsman.
               • Combat paramedic and provider.
          1-4. Department of Defense Instruction (DODI) 1322.24, directs standardized combat casualty care training
          for all Service members and Department of Defense (DOD)-expeditionary civilians. According to DODI
          1322.24, all Service members will be trained and proficient in basic lifesaving TCCC skills. The TCCC skills
          replace legacy military first aid skills. This evidence-based approach to combat casualty care reflects the
          lessons of nearly two decades of war and has the potential to reduce preventable prehospital trauma-related
          deaths.

title: U.S. Army: Casualty Response, Tactical Combat Casualty Care, and First Aid (ATP 4-02.11)
text:
Casualty Response



          1-5. The JTS established the standard of care for TCCC or prehospital medicine in the operational
          environment for the DOD. The JTS is part of the Defense Health Agency (also known as DHA) providing
          clinical practice guidelines (CPG)s and performance improvement for all levels of military trauma care. The
          Committee on Tactical Combat Casualty Care (CoTCCC) also supports the JTS. The committee is composed
          of representatives from the Army and Air Force and are responsible for developing CPGs for the delivery of
          TCCC in the operational environment.

TERMINOLOGY
196B




          1-6. A thorough understanding of the fundamentals of casualty response can save a life, prevent permanent
          disability, or reduce long periods of hospitalization. Knowledge of key terms used in Army and joint doctrine
          helps Service members better understand and appreciate the role they play in providing first aid in tactical
          and nontactical environments. Knowledge of the fundamentals of casualty response and key terminology also
          helps Service members understand when and how to provide first aid in all settings.
          1-7. A casualty is any person who is lost to the organization by having been declared dead, duty status –
          whereabouts unknown, excused absence-whereabouts unknown, missing, ill, or injured. (Joint Publication
          [JP] 4-02). The casualty classification is given to a Service member prior to treatment by medical personnel.
          A Service member who is wounded and conducts self-aid or is given treatment by a CLS is still classified as
          a casualty. That Service member is then moved to a casualty collection point (CCP) where medical personnel
          conduct triage and treatment of that casualty. Once treated by medical personnel, the Service member is now
          classified as a patient and enters the roles of medical care. Once a casualty is deceased, they become human
          remains and should be separated from the patient flow. The requirements for handling human remains are
          different and specifically explained in ATP 4-46. Service specific procedures should be followed when
          providing aid, evacuation, and reporting of combat casualties.
          1-8. A casualty collection point is a location that may or may not be staffed, where casualties are assembled
          for evacuation to a medical treatment facility with medical personnel (ATP 4-02.2). The CCPs are normally
          predesignated along the axis of advance or evacuation routes. Forward of the Role 1 battalion aid station
          (BAS), the combat medic or corpsman, CLS, and Service members take casualties to the CCPs. A battalion
          aid station is the forward-most medically staffed treatment location organic to the maneuver battalion (ATP
          4-02.4). These points facilitate acquisition of casualties by supporting ambulance teams and reducing
          evacuation time. When used by the BAS, CCPs help preserve BAS mobility, preclude carrying casualties
          forward, and reduce evacuation time to the sustainment area.
          1-9. Casualty evacuation is the unregulated movement of casualties aboard any vehicle. Also called
          CASEVAC (JP 4-02). The Army defines casualty evacuation as the movement of casualties aboard
          nonmedical vehicles or aircraft without en route medical care (ATP 4-02.13). If a casualty is moved to a
          medical treatment facility (MTF) in a nonmedical vehicle without en route care provided by a medically
          trained Service member (such as a combat medic or corpsman) then the TCCC should be continually
          performed while the casualty is being transported. Casualties transported in this manner do not normally
          receive en route medical care. If the casualty is acquired by a dedicated medical vehicle with a medically
          trained crew, the role of first aid ceases, and the casualty becomes the responsibility of the Military Health
          System chain and is then referred to as a patient.
          1-10. The core principles of casualty response include self-aid or buddy aid (first responder care), medical
          treatment (provided by combat medics, corpsmen, or medical technicians), and leader responsibilities (such
          as security, scene control, establishing a CCP, monitoring personnel, managing casualty movement, fulfilling
          reporting requirements, and coordinating evacuation). These principles must be thoroughly rehearsed and
          executed to maximize survivability in any operational environment. While these principles remain constant,
          the specific conditions in which they are applied can vary widely and are relevant to both military operations
          and civilian incident responses. This adaptability ensures that the response strategies are effective in different
          settings and enhances the overall efficacy of emergency management.
          1-11. Joint Publication 4-02 defines combat lifesaver as a Nonmedical Department of Defense person who
          has received additional trauma training and equipment, providing enhanced medical treatment beyond self-
          aid or buddy aid. (JP 4-02). The United States (U.S.) Army defines a combat lifesaver as a Soldier trained
          and equipped to provide enhanced first aid as a secondary mission, known as CLS. Enhanced first aid
          is the measures which require an additional level of training above self-aid and buddy aid. The CLS provides

title: U.S. Army: Casualty Response, Tactical Combat Casualty Care, and First Aid (ATP 4-02.11)
text:
Chapter 1



    this level of enhanced first aid and treats the most common causes of death on the battlefield, which are
    massive hemorrhage, airway and/or respiratory problems. The CLS also taught the skills to prevent
    complications and treat others associated but not life-threatening injuries. A minimum of one individual per
    squad, crew, team, or equivalent-sized unit should be trained. The primary duty of this individual does not
    change. The additional duty of a CLS is to provide enhanced first aid for injuries based on their training
    before the combat medic or corpsman arrives.
    1-12. First aid is the immediate lifesaving measures performed on casualties or military working
    animals. Every Service member is trained to be proficient in a variety of specific first aid procedures on
    injured personnel. This training enables the Service member or a buddy to apply immediate first aid measures
    to alleviate a life-threatening situation on an injured person. Select Soldiers are trained to perform first aid
    on military working animals. For additional information on first aid for military working animals refer to the
    deployed medicine website.
    1-13. A first responder is anyone who provides initial and immediate treatment to self or others. (JP 4-02)
    First responders play a crucial role in casualty response by providing immediate aid, including hemorrhage
    control and airway management, and improving the chances of survival for wounded personnel in the
    operational environment.
    1-14. Medical evacuation is the timely and effective movement of the wounded, injured, or ill to and between
    medical treatment facilities on dedicated and properly marked medical platforms with en route care provided
    by medical personnel. Also called MEDEVAC (ATP 4-02.2).
    1-15. A medical treatment facility is a facility established for the purpose of furnishing medical and/or dental
    care to eligible individuals. Also called MTF (JP 4-02). The Army defines a medical treatment facility as any
    facility established for the purpose of providing medical treatment (FM 4-02). This includes battalion aid
    stations, Role 2 facilities, dispensaries, clinics, and hospitals.
    1-16. Medical treatment is the care and management of wounded, injured, or ill Service members by
    medically trained, certified or credentialed personnel. It may include emergency medical treatment (EMT),
    advanced trauma management, and resuscitative and surgical intervention.
    1-17. Joint services define a patient as a sick, injured, wounded, or other person receiving medical care,
    dental care, or other medical treatment (JP 4-02). The U.S. Army defines a patient as a wounded, ill and
    injured Soldier who receives medical care or treatment from medically trained personnel (ATP 4-02.10).
    Once the casualty has entered the medical continuum of care (combat medic, corpsman, evacuation crew, or
    MTF), the role of first aid in the care of the casualty ceases and the casualty becomes the responsibility of
    the Military Health System. Once the casualty has entered the Military Health System they are referred to as
    a patient.
    1-18. Tactical Combat Casualty Care is the deliberate integration of tactics and medicine to treat casualties
    during combat. Also called TCCC (JP 4-02). The unit standard operating procedure (SOP) and operation
    order should address TCCC procedures and casualty evacuation (CASEVAC) in detail to include aid for
    chemical casualties with particular emphasis on lifesaving tasks. The SOP should cover the duties and
    responsibilities of essential personnel, the evacuation of chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear
    (CBRN) contaminated casualties (on routes separate from non-contaminated casualties), and priority for
    operating essential weapons and positions. The SOP should specify preferred and alternate methods of
    evacuation, and the SOP should make provisions for retrieving and safeguarding the weapons, ammunition,
    and equipment of casualties. Slightly wounded personnel are treated at the appropriate role of care and
    returned to duty as soon as possible. CASEVAC and medical evacuation (MEDEVAC) should be rehearsed
    like other critical parts of an operation.
    1-19. Triage is the system of sorting and prioritizing casualties based on the tactical situation, mission, and
    available resources (FM 4-02). Casualties are sorted and categorized in one of the treatment categories
    (immediate [I], delayed [D], minimal [M], and expectant [E]) prior to being taken to the treatment areas. This
    sorting occurs at the triage point and is called the "IDME" or the "DIME." See paragraph 3-87 on page 38
    for additional information on the triaging of casualties.

title: U.S. Army: Casualty Response, Tactical Combat Casualty Care, and First Aid (ATP 4-02.11)
text:
Casualty Response



CASUALTY COLLECTION POINT OPERATIONS
197B




          1-20. When designating a CCP, the unit commander determines if medical personnel will be at the CCP. This
          decision is based upon the assessment of risk versus the availability of personnel. Medical personnel may not
          be available to staff these points, and CLS and ambulatory patients may be required to perform self-aid,
          buddy aid, or CLS support. The CCPs should be identified on watercraft, operational overlays, and planned
          by phase for operations. The CCP planning considerations include site security, proximity to the landing zone
          (LZ), cover and concealment, and access to evacuation routes. Leaders should provide guidance on aid and
          litter teams, distribution of casualty equipment, and proper avoidance of choke points. Medical personnel are
          responsible for activity inside the CCP, and the supported unit leaders are responsible for activity outside the
          CCP.
          1-21. It is essential for units to meticulously plan the movement of casualties from the point of injury (POI)
          to supporting Role 3 MTF. Medical staff and unit leaders must be well-versed in the flow of casualties,
          extending their understanding at least two levels above their own. This encompasses knowledge of medical
          regulating, casualty tracking, and hospitalization protocols. For instance, platoon leaders and their medics
          should clearly know the path a casualty takes once they depart from the company CCP and BAS. Similarly,
          company leaders and senior medics should be familiar with the trajectory of a casualty beyond the BAS and
          through the Role 2 MTF.
          1-22. Moreover, it is vital to consider potential changes in the designated Role 3 MTF, which may occur
          when crossing a phase line or when the capacity of a facility is reached. Medical personnel must stay informed
          about these variables and regularly update themselves on their current status. This will ensure that the casualty
          care and evacuation chain remain efficient and responsive to dynamic operational conditions.
          1-23. Leaders must be able to answer the following questions to establish the tactical casualty flow:
              • Where are the casualties being evacuated to?
              • Will ground, air, or water assets conduct evacuation to the CCP?
              • How will evacuation be conducted to the CCP?
              • What are the distances and times of travel?
              • Will expected casualties be able to make it that far? If not, what parts of the plan need to be
                  corrected?
              • Who will evacuate the casualties (CASEVAC or MEDEVAC)?
              • Are medical assets positioned to ensure continuity of care?
SITE SELECTION
25B




          1-24. The CCP layout (see figure 1-1 on page 6) site is addressed during the planning phase of the military
          decision-making process, or troop leading procedures (commonly known as TLPs). Tactical battle plans will
          vary depending on the type and number of units incorporated in the plan. Mission variables are always a
          factor for CCP site selection during operations.

text:
Chapter 1




                  Figure 1-1. Casualty collection point layout in an open area or field
    1-25. The location of the CCP will depend on the unit location, the tactical situation, and the number of
    casualties to be evacuated. The unit first sergeant determines the location of the company CCP, or the platoon
    sergeant for the platoon CCP with guidance from the respective combat medics. Battle drills and the tactical
    SOP should be established on how casualties will be moved from the POI to the CCP.
    1-26. The company CCP should be in a covered and concealed position in the company trains area while the
    platoon CCP should be located at the platoon’s rear. The CCP should be:
         • Away from natural or enemy choke points.
         • Covered and concealed.
         • Expandable if casualty load increases.
         • In a building or on a hardstand (exclusive CCP building limits confusion).
         • In an area with good drainage.
         • Inside the perimeter and allow for passive security.
         • Near lines of patient drift, or natural routes along which wounded Soldiers may be expected to go
             back for medical care from a combat position.
         • Near and have access to evacuation routes (foot, vehicle, and aircraft).
         • Near templated areas of expected high casualties.
         • Next to objective choke points.
         • Reasonably close to the fight.
         • Trafficable to evacuation assets.

            Note. “Lines of Drift” are paths of least resistance that offer the greatest ease while considering
            obstacles and modes of transit to the objective.

    1-27. Establishing a CCP in a building (see figure 1-2 on page 7) may be the only choice when conducting
    operations in urban areas. After the unit ensures that the building is cleared and secured, leaders—
        • Determine the structural, environmental, medical, and CBRN hazards prior to receiving casualties.
        • Determine location of control point and triage.
        • Minimize congestion.
        • Remove or relocate furniture or obstructions.

             •    Consider rigid litter or non-rigid pole-less litter for movement.
             •    Use largest rooms possible.
             •    Separate treatment categories by room. If triage categories are separated by walls, it is more difficult
                  to monitor all the casualties.

                                Figure 1-2. Casualty collection point in a building
CASUALTY COLLECTION POINT SITE SELECTION
26B




         1-28. The CCP site selection is addressed during troop leading procedures and the CCP SOP should be
         rehearsed. The CCP should be established with:
             • A day and night marking system.
             • A triage point for entry into and exit from the CCP to track casualties and control access.
             • Properly marked evacuation categories for day and night (non-tactical or tactical) operations.
             • A killed in action (KIA) area away from the other casualties.
             • A medical resupply area.
             • A helicopter landing zone (commonly known as HLZ).
         1-29. The first sergeant or platoon sergeant is responsible for casualty flow and everything outside the CCP.
         They—
             • Provide for CCP structure and organization (color coded per tactical SOP for both day and night).
             • Maintain command and control and situational awareness.
             • Control aid and litter teams.
             • Ensure security is established and maintained.
             • Remove, collect, identify, organize, and maintain casualty equipment outside of the treatment area.
             • Track casualties and equipment into and out of CCP.
             • Establish accountability and send reports to higher.
             • Move casualties through CCP entrance and exit control point.
         1-30. Medical personnel are responsible for operations inside the CCP. Medical personnel assigned to the
         CCP include the:
             • Triage officer or noncommissioned officer who sorts and organizes the casualties into appropriate
                 treatment categories.

text:
Chapter 1



               •    Medics, corpsman, or medical technicians who organize medical equipment and supplies.
               •    Medical personnel, CLS, and aid and litter teams who assist with treatment and packaging of
                    casualties.
           1-31. Once triaged, casualties categorized as "Minimal" should ideally stay with their assigned unit or assist
           with security at the CCP, if possible. Deceased personnel are designated as KIA. Their remains should stay
           with the assigned unit until mortuary affairs personnel arrive, or until the remains are transferred to a morgue.
           The mortuary affairs SOP should clearly outline the handling of the remains, considering theater-specific
           requirements, environmental factors, and the religious beliefs of the Service member.
           1-32. It is also important to note that the remains of deceased personnel should not be moved with patients
           on MEDEVAC ambulances. This practice helps maintain the dignity of the deceased and ensures the focus
           remains on providing urgent care to the living casualties during MEDEVAC.

CASUALTY RESPONSE FOR UNITED STATES ARMY UNITS
198B




           1-33. The treatment and evacuation of casualties are difficult tasks for an organization to execute due to the
           operating distance away from its higher headquarters. Units should allocate adequate assets to the platoon to
           assist in casualty treatment and evacuation. Platoon medics evaluate and treat sick and injured Soldiers and
           assist the unit in the evacuation of casualties.
CASUALTY CARE
27B




           1-34. When casualties occur, the platoon must provide aid to those wounded in action. Combat medics, who
           are assisted by nonmedical personnel, provide EMT to alleviate potentially life-threatening injuries and to
           ensure maximum survivability. This support is commonly provided by enlisted personnel and includes first
           aid (self-aid or buddy aid), enhanced first aid by the CLS, and EMT by the platoon medic.

Wounded in action
295B




           1-35. The ability of fellow Soldiers to provide aid to wounded comrades is heavily influenced by the tactical
           situation. Minimizing casualties is more achievable when Soldiers concentrate on defeating or neutralizing
           the enemy responsible for causing the injuries.
           1-36. During combat, it is crucial to move casualties to a covered and concealed position where first aid can
           be administered safely. Once the immediate threat subsides, squad leaders should coordinate the evacuation
           of the wounded to the platoon CCP, typically located to the rear of the platoon's position. At the CCP, the
           platoon medic will perform triage, stabilize the injured, and initiate their transfer to more comprehensive
           medical facilities. For detailed operations at the CCP, refer to paragraph 1-20 on page 4.
           1-37. Before evacuating casualties to the CCP or further, leaders must ensure that:
               • The casualty's personal protective equipment, such as protective masks, accompanies them.
               • All vital operational, sensitive items, and equipment are removed from the casualty.
               • Medical documentation and identification tags are securely attached to each casualty to streamline
                   medical treatment and tracking processes.
           1-38. Additionally, the removal of equipment should include items like automated network control devices,
           global positioning systems, maps, position-locating devices, and laser pointers. Each unit should have an
           SOP for managing the weapons and ammunition of its wounded personnel, ensuring these measures are
           systematically applied, and adhere to safety and operational security standards.

Killed in Action
296B




           1-39. The platoon leader designates a location for the collection of KIAs. Personal effects remain with the
           human remains. While treating the human remains with dignity and respect, squad leaders remove, and
           safeguard all equipment, and government issued items until they can turn the equipment over to the platoon
           sergeant. The platoon sergeant turns over the human remains to the first sergeant. The platoon should not
           transport human remains on the same vehicle as wounded Soldiers. The human remains are normally
           transported to the rear on empty resupply trucks but are dependent on unit SOP.

title: U.S. Army: Casualty Response, Tactical Combat Casualty Care, and First Aid (ATP 4-02.11)
text:
Casualty Response



          1-40. Commanders and first sergeants establish command procedures to ensure the Soldier’s next of kin are
          properly notified in accordance with (IAW) ATP 4-46/MCRP 3-40G.3/NTTP 4-06/AFTTP 3-2.51. The
          potential for unofficial communications exists with the KIA and casualty operations. The use of cell phones
          and computers in proximity to the area of operation enables many Soldiers to contact their home station
          regarding the casualty. This kind of communication is unofficial and unacceptable. The next of kin for
          Soldiers wounded in action or KIA should not receive notification through unofficial means. Therefore, the
          use of cell phones and computers in proximity to the area of operation should be subject to a communication
          blackout until the next of kin is notified by a casualty notification officer. No internet or phone calls home
          should be permitted during the communication blackout.
EVACUATION CONSIDERATIONS
28B




          1-41. Conducting CASEVAC is a fundamental unit responsibility and a key aspect of sustainment operations.
          To effectively execute CASEVAC, unit leaders should consider the following points to optimize their
          planning and response:
              • Know the Evacuation Platform:
                  ▪ Determine if a medical provider is onboard.
                  ▪ Check for the presence of necessary monitoring equipment.
                  ▪ Ascertain the capacity of the platform regarding how many ambulatory and littler casualties it
                       can evacuate.
              • Understand Platform Specifications:
                  ▪ Large Platforms: Evacuate multiple casualties, with routine cases loaded first, followed by
                       priority, and critical (urgent) cases last, ensuring they are first off at the destination.
                  ▪ Small Platforms: Prioritize evacuation of critical (urgent) and priority cases first, with routine
                       cases evacuated as space allows.
                  ▪ Verify that all securement devices are functional and appropriate for the type of litter and
                       evacuation platform being used.
              • Packaging Requirements for the Evacuation Platform:
                  ▪ Identify the types of litters available.
                  ▪ Determine if the litter is stirrup-based verses non-stirrup-based pole-less and is compatible with
                       the evacuation platform.
                  ▪ Ensure there is enough equipment to prevent hypothermia and keep the casualty warm and dry.
              • Secure the Casualties and Determine the Loading Sequence on the Evacuation Platform:
                  ▪ Implement procedures for tying down or securing litters to the vehicle, ensuring safety during
                       transportation.
                  ▪ Ensure a clear and prioritized loading sequence to streamline the evacuation process.
                  ▪ Plan and coordinate the movement of casualties to the evacuation platform efficiently.
          1-42. By addressing these areas and integrating enhancements such as leading in conducting CASEVAC and
          ensuring all litters are securely tied down, leaders can improve the efficiency and safety of evacuation
          operations, ultimately enhancing casualty care during critical situations.

Medical Evacuation
297B




          1-43. A MEDEVAC may be provided by dedicated air or ground ambulances. The MEDEVAC includes the
          provision of en route medical care, whereas CASEVAC may not provide medical care during movement. For
          more information on MEDEVAC refer to ATP 4-02.2. If dedicated MEDEVAC platforms (ground and air)
          are available, casualties should be evacuated on these conveyances to ensure they receive proper en route
          medical care. If both MEDEVAC and CASEVAC are used, the most seriously injured should be evacuated
          on MEDEVAC platforms while the less seriously injured are moved by CASEVAC.
          1-44. When possible, medical platoon ambulances provide evacuation and en route care from POI or the
          platoon or company’s CCP to the BAS. The ambulance team supporting the company works in coordination
          with the senior combat medic supporting the platoons. In mass casualty situations, nonmedical vehicles may
          be used to assist in CASEVAC as directed by the company commander or leader. However, plans for use of
          nonmedical vehicles to perform CASEVAC should be included in the unit SOP and briefed at the sustainment
          and combines arms rehearsals.

title: U.S. Army: Casualty Response, Tactical Combat Casualty Care, and First Aid (ATP 4-02.11)
text:
Chapter 1



            1-45. Ground MEDEVAC is the primary means of evacuation during large-scale combat operations due to
            the operational environment and the greater availability of ground ambulances. Aeromedical evacuation is
            the preferred method of evacuation due to the greater speed and range of air ambulances. Mission variables
            should be considered before executing aeromedical evacuation. When selecting a site for a LZ, the LZ should
            be relatively flat and free of hazards such as power lines. Loose debris should be removed to avoid objects
            being sucked into engines or causing injury due to the rotor wash. The platoon provides local security of the
            LZ until the evacuation is complete.
            1-46. The senior military person present determines whether to request evacuation. The decision to request
            MEDEVAC is based on the advice of the senior medical person at the scene, the patient’s condition, the
            tactical situation, and availability of a dedicated medical platform. Casualties will be picked up as soon as
            possible, consistent with available resources and pending missions. The following are evacuation priority
            categories of precedence and criteria used in their assignment:
                 • Priority I – Urgent is assigned to emergency cases being evacuated as soon as possible and within a
                      maximum of one hour to save life, limb, or eyesight; to prevent complications of serious illness; or
                      to avoid permanent disability.
                 • Priority IA – Urgent Surgical is assigned to patients that should be evacuated as soon as possible
                      and within a maximum of one hour who must receive far forward surgical intervention to save life,
                      limb, or eyesight and stabilize for further evacuation.
                 • Priority II – Priority is assigned to sick and wounded personnel requiring prompt medical care. The
                      precedence is used when the individual should be evacuated within four hours or if the medical
                      condition could deteriorate to such a degree that the casualty becomes urgent, or whose requirements
                      for special treatment is not available locally; the individual will suffer unnecessary pain or disability.
                 • Priority III – Routine is assigned to sick and wounded personnel requiring evacuation, but condition
                      is not expected to deteriorate significantly. The sick and wounded in this category should be
                      evacuated within 24 hours.
                 • Priority IV – Convenience is assigned to patients for whom evacuation by medical vehicle is a matter
                      of medical convenience rather than necessity.

                  Note. The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) Standardization Agreement (STANAG)
                  3204 has deleted the category of Priority IV - CONVENIENCE. There is a requirement for it in
                  an operational environment and is still included in the United States Army evacuation priorities.


Medical Evacuation Request
298B




            1-47. Immediately following an attack and upon learning of a casualty within the platoon, the vehicle
            commander, squad or section leader, and platoon sergeant will start to prepare an evacuation request. There
            is no difference between a ground or air evacuation request. Units transmit a 9-line MEDEVAC request,
            report number M030 IAW FM 6-99 to the command post. Units use Graphic Training Aid 08-01-004,
            MEDEVAC Request Card, for the correct reporting lines and brevity codes for United States Forces. Units
            use this report to request evacuation of sick and wounded personnel. This report is like the NATO
            MEDEVAC request (9-liner MEDEVAC) IAW STANAG 2020 and STANAG 2627. The NATO 9-liner
            MEDEVAC request is used only when specifically directed in the orders process.
            1-48. Along with the standard 9-line MEDEVAC request format, the higher role of care may require a
            mechanism of injury, injury type, signs and symptoms, and treatments (MIST) report, which should be
            provided by the platoon medic or CLS on-site. The Department of Defense (DD) Form 1380 (Tactical
            Combat Casualty Care (TCCC) Card), when complete, is the MIST report. For more information on

            various multimodal patient movement (MMPM) or CASEVAC assets are employed to conduct the
            evacuation mission, with MMPM being the preferred method of evacuation.

Casualty Response



Casualty Evacuation
29B




         1-50. Service members may have to be available to perform or assist in an extraction, rescue, and evacuation
         of casualties. There are multiple extrication devices, tactical situations, environmental situations, and
         maneuvers to accomplish appropriate movement for a casualty. For detailed information on casualty
         movement, refer to ATP 4-02.13.


                                                      WARNING
                      Casualties transported in this manner may not receive proper en
                      route medical care or be transported to the appropriate MTF to
                      address the patient’s medical condition.
                      If the casualty’s medical condition deteriorates during transport,
                      or the casualty is not transported to the appropriate MTF, an
                      adverse impact on the casualty’s prognosis and long-term
                      disability or death may result.


         1-51. CASEVAC is the responsibility of the unit to transport less severely injured casualties when
         MEDEVAC resources are limited. The planning of CASEVAC is synchronized with existing medical support
         plans to ensure a streamlined process. This involves organizing, preparing, coordinating, and practicing the
         evacuation procedures in advance to guarantee efficiency. The plan ensures that teams trained in first aid are
         adept at handling stretchers, working around medical posts, and correctly assessing triage categories.
         Whenever possible, non-medical vehicles, aircraft, and watercraft used for transporting casualties should be
         supported by CLS or medical staff to provide necessary care during transport.
         1-52. Sufficient space may not be available to permit a caregiver to accompany or assess the casualties. Refer
         to ATP 4-02.13 for more information. The type of en route monitoring and medical care or first aid provided
         is limited by the following factors:
              • Skill level of the individual providing care. The combat medic is qualified to provide EMT, while
                   the CLS is trained to provide enhanced first aid. The combat medic can provide emergency medical
                   interventions, whereas the CLS can only monitor the casualty and ensure the basic lifesaving first
                   aid tasks are accomplished.
              • Medical equipment available.
              • Number of casualties being transported.
              • Accessibility of casualties. If a nonstandard evacuation vehicle is loaded with the maximum number
                   of casualties, the combat medic or CLS may not be able to attend to the casualties while the vehicle
                   is moving. If the condition of a casualty deteriorates and emergency measures are required, the
                   vehicle may need to be stopped for the combat medic or CLS to provide additional care.
MULTIMODAL PATIENT MOVEMENT
29B




         1-53. When medical personnel provide care during the transport of casualties on non-medical platforms, it's
         called MMPM. MMPM involves moving casualties efficiently and providing care en route using available
         transportation methods, as outlined in JP 4-02. MMPM platforms can include maritime, land, or air vehicles,
         and they may serve as the primary or secondary mode of transportation between care facilities. However,
         utilizing these platforms means accepting increased risks for both patients and transport teams due to their
         combatant status. To ensure safe patient movement, MMPM platforms may carry standardized medical kits,
         emphasizing the importance of thorough planning and preparation.
UNIT REPORTING
30B




         1-54. A casualty report is filled out when a casualty occurs, or as soon as the tactical situation permits. The
         casualty report is usually completed by the Soldier’s squad leader and turned into the platoon sergeant, who
         forwards it to the first sergeant. The report should include a brief description of how the casualty occurred
         (including the place, time, and activity being performed) and who or what inflicted the wound is included. If

            1-55. As casualties occur, the nearest observer informs the platoon sergeant who then informs the first

            a radio voice). The first sergeant submits a personnel status report to the Battalion S-1 section. This report

Medical and Personnel Accounting
30B




            1-56. When a Soldier becomes a casualty, the platoon combat medic or senior combat medic records the
            medical treatment the Soldier receives on the DD Form 1380. The BAS and the Role 2 read the Soldier’s DD
            Form 1380, when they treat the Soldier. The Battalion S-1 should electronically receive a notification
            message to update the Soldier’s patient tracking status. In turn, this message should be forwarded to the
            Soldier’s company. In this manner, the casualty’s location can be determined, and the Soldier can be properly
            accounted for by their unit.

Personnel Reports
301B




            1-57. Units employ personnel reports to inform the command group about casualties and to initiate requests
            for replacement personnel. Typically, a request for replacements is made immediately following a casualty
            report. This systematic approach ensures that the command group remains fully informed about personnel
            status and can quickly respond to the need for additional forces to maintain operational effectiveness. The
            prompt communication of these details is crucial for strategic planning and the swift adaptation to evolving
            battlefield conditions.

Personnel Battle Loss Report
302B




            1-58. Units transmit a Casualty Report (known as CASREP), report number C001, also known as the
            personnel battle loss report, IAW FM 6-99 to the command post as casualties occur. This report is like the
            NATO notification of casualty (stage 1) (NOTICAS1) IAW STANAG 2020. The unit completes a DA Form
            1156 (Casualty Feeder Card) with witness statements and submits the entire packet to the first sergeant. The
            personnel battle loss report is an interim report to update information sent in the last personnel daily summary
            report.
            1-59. The DA Form 1156 is used to report those Soldiers who have been killed and recovered or those who
            have been wounded. This form is also used to report Soldiers who are KIA, missing, captured, or not
            recovered. The Soldier with the most knowledge of the incident should complete the witness statement. This
            information is used to inform the Soldier’s next of kin, and to provide a statistical base for analysis of friendly
            or enemy tactics. For more information on the Army casualty program refer to Army Regulation (AR) 638-8.
            1-60. Once the casualty’s medical condition has stabilized, the company commander may write a letter to
            the Soldier’s next of kin. During lulls in the battle, the platoon forwards casualty information to the company
            headquarters. The first sergeant ensures a completed DA Form 1156 is forwarded to the Battalion S-1, who
            then enters the data into the defense casualty information processing system.
CASUALTY RESPONSE REHEARSALS
31B




            1-61. During the troop leading procedures, the organization rehearses the CCP plan per unit SOP. Unit
            leaders and planners include the leaders from the medical platoon in the military decision-making process,
            orders production and in CCP rehearsals. This ensures the evacuation plans mutually support the unit’s
            mission and the medical tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) are understood. Some areas to concentrate
            on when conducting a casualty response rehearsal are:
                • Alerting aid and litter teams, and conduct:
                     ▪ Alert and movement.
                     ▪ Evacuation equipment preparation.

DUTIES AND RESPONSIBILITIES
32B

          requirements through the company and ensuring sustainment operations are properly executed when support
          elements arrive in the platoon area. The platoon sergeant is normally in charge of these functions, with

                  Note. The duties and responsibilities of leaders and platoon members must be executed even in

Medical Planners

          1-64. During the planning phase, battalion medical personnel and planners play a critical role by:

              • Collaborating with unit leaders to coordinate various aspects, including:

304B




          1-66. The platoon leader is responsible for their platoon’s execution of the sustainment plan at platoon level.

text:
Chapter 1



     1-67. The platoon leader, assisted by the platoon sergeant, is responsible for developing their sustainment
     plan. This starts with checking their current Class VIII supplies in order to find out exactly what is available.
     Knowing what they have on hand helps them accurately estimate their support needs. It’s crucial for the
     commander to be aware of these supplies so they can prepare for treating expected casualties and identify
     critical supplies. This verification is key not only to confirm the sustainment plan's accuracy but also to ensure
     that the platoon’s support requests are made as early as possible. Based on this inventory and their maneuver
     plans, the platoon leader can then create and submit their sustainment execution plan and support requests.
     1-68. The sustainment plan should address key operational considerations, including:
         • Types of support: Determine the specific medical support needed based on operational requirements
             and tactical factors.
         • Quantities: Assess the quantities of support required, including potential needs for Class VIII
             resupply or adjustments to preconfigured Class VIII packages.
         • Threat assessment: Analyze the composition, disposition, and capabilities of the expected enemy
             threat, considering factors such as anticipated contact locations, expected casualties, and the impact
             of enemy special weapons capabilities.
         • Terrain and weather: Evaluate how terrain and weather conditions will impact the sustainment plan,
             including considerations for securing maintenance areas and CCPs, determining CASEVAC routes,
             and planning for contaminated personnel and equipment evacuation.
         • Time and location: Identify when and where sustainment support will be needed, including—
             selecting optimal locations for CCPs, enemy prisoner of war collection points, and determining
             travel times to medical treatment facilities.
         • Requirements: Define support requirements by element and type, including prioritization of medical
             support and emergency resupply.
         • Risk assessment: Assess whether lulls in the battle will provide opportunities for support elements
             to conduct resupply operations safely.
         • Resupply techniques: Select the most suitable resupply technique based on information gathered
             during the sustainment planning process.
     1-69. During the planning phase, unit leaders undertake various crucial tasks to ensure effective medical
     support:
         • Allocate aid and litter teams and CASEVAC equipment to facilitate timely response to casualties.
         • Conduct rehearsals for casualty responses to ensure readiness and effectiveness in handling medical
              emergencies.
         • Perform precombat inspections of medics, platoon casualty response kits, and CLS bags to verify
              equipment and readiness. Casualty response kits are unit dependent tailored to their specific mission
              that would include appropriate litters, litter straps, panel markers, hypothermia prevention kits or
              extra medical supplies.
         • Establish an accountability and reporting plan to track medical resources and casualties accurately.
         • Determine the CASEVAC plan for each phase of the operation, including CCP, helicopter landing
              zone, and ambulance exchange point locations.
         • Organize the gathering and distribution of casualty equipment and sensitive items as needed
              throughout the operation.
         • Establish accountability procedures and submit reports to higher commands as required.
         • Rehearse the proper management of KIA remains to ensure respect and dignity in handling.
         • Identify and ensure the security of CCPs, HLZs, and ambulance exchange point locations to prevent
              disruptions to medical operations.
         • Determine the task organization and distribution of medical personnel to optimize their effectiveness
              and coverage.
         • Prepare evacuation requests and establish CASEVAC link-up points to facilitate smooth patient
              transfers.
         • Assist medics with EMT augmentation and provide guidance in directing aid and litter teams to
              maximize medical support capabilities

Casualty Response



Platoon Sergeant
305B




          1-70. The platoon sergeant holds a pivotal role as the primary sustainment planner, coordinator, and operator
          within the platoon, reporting directly to the platoon leader. They execute logistical plans, relying on
          established SOPs from both the platoon and company. Working closely with the platoon leader and squad
          leaders during mission preparations, the platoon sergeant determines specific support requirements aligned
          with the tactical plan and ensures their proper arrangement. Additionally, the platoon sergeant:
              • Coordinates human resources support with the company first sergeant, covering personnel
                   accountability reports, casualty reports, replacement operations, and other administrative tasks.
              • Supervises the evacuation of casualties, unprivileged enemy belligerents, and damaged equipment.
              • Oversee the collection, initial identification, and evacuation of human remains to the mortuary
                   affairs collection point.
          1-71. As the second-in-charge, the platoon sergeant primarily follows instructions from the platoon leader.
          However, they typically establish and operate the unit's CCP, which involves directing aid teams and
          managing the CASEVAC process during operations. They also maintain the platoon's strength level
          information by consolidating casualty reports and orienting replacements.
          1-72. In the event of wounded soldiers requiring evacuation, the platoon leader or platoon sergeant can take
          various actions:
              • Coordinate ground evacuation with the nearest company.
              • Request attachment of a dedicated ambulance from the company or battalion for operations forward
                    of the larger element.
              • Use organic platoon assets for evacuating wounded soldiers.
              • Coordinate for Army aeromedical evacuation and aerial CASEVAC through the company or
                    battalion channels.

Squad Leader
306B




          1-73. It is the squad leaders’ responsibility to ensure casualties receive immediate TCCC and then
          immediately notify the platoon leader or platoon sergeant of all casualties. The use of CLS is critical. As a
          minimum, one member of each squad should be trained and equipped as a CLS. The squad leader is
          responsible for ensuring the casualty feeder card is filled out properly and provided to the platoon sergeant,
          as well as requesting evacuation for their personnel.

Combat Medics
307B




          1-74. EMT procedures performed by combat medics encompass critical interventions such as airway
          management, establishing intravenous or intraosseous access, hemorrhage control, shock prevention or
          treatment, splinting fractures, hypothermia management, and medication administration for pain or infection.
          1-75. Combat medics undergo training under the supervision of the battalion surgeon or physician assistant,
          focusing on medical tasks, while the medical platoon leader and platoon sergeant concentrate on tactical
          training. The platoon combat medic assumes responsibilities such as triaging injured personnel, conducting
          sick call screening, assisting in evacuations, training CLS, requisitioning medical supplies, recommending
          CCP locations, providing guidance on operational public health, and supporting CLS as needed.
          1-76. Combat medics are assigned to the battalion medical platoon and attached to the maneuver companies,
          typically with one combat medic per platoon and one senior combat medic per company, strategically located
          for rapid medical treatment of casualties.
          1-77. The company senior combat medic is positioned with the company trains, located 500 to 1000 meters.
          or one terrain feature to the rear of the company, ensuring immediate recovery and medical support, while
          remaining concealed from direct enemy fire. The company’s first sergeant or executive officer supervises
          evacuation activities and sustains operations within the platoon.
          1-78. During the planning phase, the senior combat medic or platoon combat medic provides
          recommendations and plans for medical support, Army Health System support, casualty response, and

text:
Chapter 1



            evacuation. They also coordinate CCP locations, medical task organization, evacuation plans, and conduct
            precombat inspections.
            1-79. During the execution phase, the senior combat medic or platoon combat medic implements triage,
            treatment, and monitoring, delegates treatment, requests assistance from other medical or unit assets, and
            offers guidance on casualty management and evacuation to support effective medical care in combat
            situations.

Combat Lifesavers
308B




            1-80. Immediate, far-forward medical care is critical on a widely dispersed and dynamic battlefield to prevent
            casualties from succumbing to wounds. Due to the unpredictable nature of combat, medical personnel may
            not always reach and treat wounded soldiers promptly. CLS play a crucial role in bridging this gap, as they
            can stabilize various types of casualties and mitigate the deterioration of a wounded soldier's condition until
            medical personnel arrive. Acting as CLS is a secondary mission conducted when the tactical situation allows,
            and they render enhanced first aid when a casualty occurs, either through self-aid, buddy aid, or CLS
            intervention.
            1-81. The CLS performs tier 2 TCCC skills, serving as a link between the tier 1 skills taught to all Soldiers
            and the advanced medical training, provided by combat medics or higher-level medical providers. This
            capability is organic and aims to fill the gap between basic life-saving skills and advanced medical care.
            Training CLS should be a priority for platoons to ensure that they can replicate essential medical techniques
            in the absence of a combat medic. Each squad or equivalent-sized unit should have at least one certified CLS,
            who must recertify annually according to AR 350-1.
            1-82. The primary role of a CLS is to address the most common causes of death on the battlefield, such as a
            massive hemorrhage, airway, and/or respiratory issues. They are trained to provide immediate care to save
            lives, including controlling bleeding and performing needle chest decompression for tension pneumothorax.
            The CLS may assist combat medics in patient care, evacuation preparation, or support medical personnel
            during prolonged care situations when not engaged in combat duties.
            1-83. A significant advantage of the CLS is their proximity to injured squad or crew members. During large
            scale combat operations, the battlefield is often spread out and fast-moving, making rapid casualty treatment
            challenging. CLS ensure that squad CLS bags and litters are properly maintained, identify medical supply
            shortages, participate in casualty treatment drills, use enhanced first aid skills in the field, and are familiar
            with CCP locations and tactical SOP for establishing them.
CONTAMINATED CASUALTY CARE
3B




            1-84. In a CBRN environment, Soldiers may need to employ self-aid, immediate lifesaving interventions,
            and decontamination measures. This includes administering correct antidotes for nerve agent exposure and
            assuming the appropriate Mission-Oriented Protective Posture level. Further guidance on contaminated
            casualty care can be found in Chapter 20 of this publication and refer to ATP 4-02.7/AFTTP 3-42.3.
            1-85. Buddy aid is crucial when individuals are unable to provide self-aid. In a CBRN environment, buddy
            aid actions involve:
                 • Treating immediate life-threatening injuries.
                 • Identifying the type of contamination (chemical, biological, or radiological).
                 • Administering appropriate medical CBRN defense material (prioritizing the casualty's own
                     supplies).
                 • Decontaminating exposed skin and contaminated gear using various methods such as Reactive Skin
                     Decontamination Lotion (RSDL) or the M291 Skin Decontamination Kit, which includes dry earth,
                     bleach and water for chemical contamination, soap and water for chemical, biological, and
                     radiological contamination, and brushing or vacuuming for radiological contamination.
                 • Assisting the casualty to do the remaining protective clothing, if required.
                 • Promptly moving the casualty to a decontamination point for further care.
            1-86. For comprehensive guidance on patient decontamination procedures, refer to ATP 4-02.7/AFTTP 3-
            42.3.

text:
Casualty Response



CASUALTY RESPONSE FOR UNITED STATES MARINE CORPS
19B




UNITS
          1-87. United States Marine Corps (USMC), Marine air-ground task forces require unit SOPs and operation
          orders address TCCC procedures, CASEVAC, and in-detail aid for chemical casualties with particular
          emphasis on lifesaving tasks. Wounded personnel should be treated at the appropriate role of care and
          returned to duty when possible. Hospital corpsmen evaluate sick and injured Marines, provide treatment, and
          arrange evacuation if necessary. CASEVAC and MEDEVAC are rehearsed like other critical parts of any
          operation. Casualty management begins at the POI or onset of illness throughout triage, treatment, and
          transport to the next role of medical care to include outside Service capabilities as necessary.
CASUALTY CARE
34B




          1-88. Health Service Support (HSS) is the employment of medical forces in support of the warfighter to
          deliver on-demand healthcare capabilities and ensure a healthy, fit, and medically ready force; counters the
          health threat to the deployed force; provide critical care for and management of combat casualties.
          1-89. The HSS directly supports the National Military Strategy of forward presence and power projection. It
          also strengthens the warfighting commander by providing essential care in theater and MEDEVAC of
          casualties across the continuum of care to MTFs in the continental United States for definitive care without
          sacrificing the quality of care.

Mission
309B




          1-90. The HSS mission is to minimize the effects that wounds, injuries, and diseases have on unit
          effectiveness, readiness, and morale. The mission is accomplished by an aggressive and proactive preventive
          medicine program that safeguards personnel against potential health risks and by establishing an HSS system
          that provides appropriate care from the POI or illness to the appropriate taxonomy of care.

Principles
310B




          1-91. The HSS principles are guides for planning, organizing, managing, and executing HSS. Seldom will
          all principles exert equal influence in each situation and the HSS is most effective when it can identify the
          priority principles and bring them to bear in support of the commander's mission. Refer to JP 4-02 for more
          information. The Marine Corps HSS system encompasses:
               • Conformity. The medical plan must integrate and comply with the commander's plan.
               • Proximity. The medical plan must provide HSS as close to combat operations as the tactical situation
                    permits.
               • Flexibility. The medical plan must shift HSS resources to meet changing requirements.
               • Mobility. The medical plan must anticipate requirements for rapid movements of HSS units to
                    support combat forces during operations.
               • Continuity. The medical plan must provide optimum, uninterrupted care and treatment to the
                    wounded, injured, and sick.
               • Coordination. The medical plan must ensure that HSS resources in short supply are efficiently
                    employed and used effectively to support the planned operations.

Casualty Care and Management
31B




          1-92. Marine Corps HSS deploys through task-organized units of employment to provide care throughout the
          continuum of healthcare. The taxonomy continuum of healthcare includes the following capabilities:
              • Policy and resource acquisition.
              • Prevention and protection.
              • First responder.
              • Damage Control Resuscitation.
              • Damage Control Surgery.
              • Theater hospitalization.
              • Definitive care.

Roles of Care for Marine Corps
312B




            1-93. Health Services Support within an area of operations is organized into roles of care that extend from
            forward to the rear of the area of responsibility. Each role of medical capability is designed to provide the
            mobility and capability that is required to meet basic health care needs of the supported operational units,

Point of Principal Treatment

Role 1 Care
314B




            1-96. Role 1 care is the first medical attention that military personnel receive and is also referred to as unit

            prevention and care, combat and operational stress preventive measures, and patient location and acquisition
