text:
Casualty Response



First Responder Self/Buddy Aid
41B




          1-97. The first responder provides unit level medical care. This is comprised of personnel from a unit and its
          organic BAS or squadron aid stations. In the case of organizations without organic medical elements, unit
          level care is provided by medical elements at the regimental, group, or support squadron level or other
          designated medical elements. TCCC has three phases and occurs during a combat mission and is the military
          counterpart to prehospital EMT.
          1-98. TCCC in the military is predominantly administered by enlisted personnel, encompassing a range of
          roles such as first responders, self-aid, buddy aid (first aid), CLS, unit corpsmen, independent duty corpsmen,
          and other medical personnel. TCCC emphasizes addressing the most probable threats, injuries, and conditions
          encountered in combat, focusing on a concise selection of interventions aimed at mitigating the most critical
          of these threats and conditions.

Combat Lifesaver for Marine Corps
415B




          1-99. The CLSs for the Marine Corps are nonmedical military personnel selected by their unit commander
          for additional training beyond basic first aid procedures. A minimum of two Marines should be trained per
          table of organization corpsmen. The primary duty of a CLS does not change. The additional duty as a CLS
          is to provide enhanced first aid for injuries, based on his training, before the corpsman arrives or to assist the
          corpsman. CLS training is normally provided by medical personnel organic to sustainment units. The senior
          medical person designated by the commander manages the CLS training program.

Unit Hospital Corpsman
416B




          1-100. The company or squadron corpsman represents the first point where a sick, injured, or wounded
          Marine receives care from trained medical personnel. If emergency or lifesaving measures are required before
          a Hospital Corpsman (HM) arrives, they must be performed by fellow Marines trained as a CLS, first
          responder self/buddy aid. Care from unit HM includes primary and secondary assessments, followed by
          emergency or lifesaving measures (such as establishing and maintaining an airway, control of bleeding,
          cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), treatment for shock, and fracture stabilization). The HMs duties
          include basic medical skills, use of medical equipment and supplies, and initiation of requests for assistance
          and evacuation.

The Aid Station
417B




          1-101. The aid station is the Role 1 for the Marine Corps. Treatment at the aid station is distinguished by the

AMPHIBIOUS OPERATIONS
35B

          constitutes the beach evacuation section(s) of the landing force support party. The primary role of a BAS is

          1-105. When evacuation stations attached to the landing force support party become operational ashore,
          established BASs are relieved to conduct their primary missions in supporting their parent battalions. The
          expansion of the HSS facilities follows the landing of supporting evacuation stations. The HSS assets are
          typically established at the beach service support area and follow-on combat service support areas, logistic
          support areas or forward arming and refueling points.

Assault Follow-on Echelon
316B




          1-106. While most logistic support capabilities during the assault follow-on echelon continue to be sea-based,
          projected HSS capabilities ashore expand along with the logistics combat element. Capabilities could be
          additional forward resuscitative surgery systems or shock trauma platoon with mobile combat logistics
          companies. When progress of assault units is such that the beachhead is relatively secure, HSS is enhanced
          from follow-on forces.

Follow-on Forces
317B




          1-107. The HSS shifts its posture to achieve shore-based health care consistent with the expected combat
          intensity and duration of sustained operations ashore, independent of sea-based facilities. This phasing is
          achieved by upgrading capabilities ashore by consolidating HSS capabilities once they come ashore. If a
          sustained land campaign is envisioned, additional HSS will normally be provided by theater hospitalization
          (expeditionary medical facilities, hospital ships, or other Service-equivalent facilities such as combat support
          hospitals and expeditionary medical support).

Casualty Evacuation
318B




          1-108. Timely movement of casualties from the operational environment is important for safety, care for the
          wounded, and troop morale. Unit leaders are responsible for coordination of CASEVAC from the POI to the
          appropriate role of care. The owning commands are responsible for CASEVAC from POI or illness to
          casualty treatment stations, and for casualty movement from the first responder capability to forward
          resuscitative care (also known as FRC) capabilities.
          1-109. CASEVAC can be accomplished through dedicated, designated, or opportune ground or air

text:
Chapter 2
                             Casualty Extraction and Movement

CASUALTY EXTRACTION
20B




         2-1. Transportation of casualties away from danger or to evacuation vehicles is a critical aspect of first aid,
         requiring careful attention to avoid exacerbating injuries. For comprehensive guidance on casualty transport
         and evacuation procedures, refer to Soldier Training Publication (STP) 8-68W13-SM-TG, ATP 4-02.13, and
         ATP 4-02.2. Risk assessment is essential during casualty movement, and for detailed information on this
         process, consult ATP 5-19.


                                                       WARNING
                       In cases where a casualty is involved in a vehicle crash, there is a
                       potential for spinal injury. Unless facing an immediate life-
                       threatening scenario (fire or explosion), they refrain from moving
                       a casualty suspected of a back or neck injury. Seek guidance
                       from medical personnel on appropriate transportation methods.


         2-2. Service members and CLS should adhere to the unit SOPs when extracting casualties from vehicles.
         Extraction methods will vary based on mission requirements and vehicle configurations in the operational
         area.
         2-3. Service members should familiarize themselves with safety principles, casualty assessment, and proper
         training procedures. For instance, if a casualty is on fire, extinguish the flames, address life-threatening
         bleeding with a tourniquet (TQ) if necessary, and promptly seek cover.
         2-4. To remove a casualty laterally from a vehicle—
              • With the assistance of another Service member, grip the casualty's arms and legs.
              • Stabilize the casualty's head and neck as much as possible.
              • Lift them clear of the vehicle and transfer to a safe area on the ground.

                 Note. If available, medical personnel may use a specialized board or splint to stabilize the
                 casualty's head, neck, and upper body.

         2-5. To remove a casualty upward from a vehicle—
              • Use a pistol belt or similar material to encircle the casualty's chest, aiding in their upward movement
                  from the vehicle.
              • With assistance from another Service member inside the vehicle, elevate the casualty using the pistol
                  belt or by grasping their arms.
              • While stabilizing the casualty's head and neck as much as possible, lift them free of the vehicle and
                  position them on the topmost side.

                 Note. If medical personnel are present, they may employ a specialized board or splint to stabilize
                 the casualty's head, neck, and upper body.

             •     Depending on the circumstances, relocate the casualty from the topmost side of the vehicle to a
                   secure area on the ground.

Chapter 2




                                                           WARNING
                         Avoid manual carries for casualties with suspected neck or spine
                         injuries, unless immediate life-threatening hazards are present.
                         Seek medical advice on appropriate movement and transportation
                         protocols.


CASUALTY MOVEMENT
201B




            2-6. Timely evacuation of casualties from the operational environment is crucial not only for their safety and
            care but also for maintaining troop morale. Squad leaders bear the responsibility for CASEVAC from the
            POI to the platoon CCP. At the CCP, the senior medic assists the platoon sergeant or first sergeant in
            coordinating MEDEVAC by ground or air ambulance, or by CASEVAC. It's imperative for leaders to
            minimize the number of Soldiers needed for CASEVAC.
CASUALTY MOVEMENT ROUTE
36B




            2-7. Casualties with minor wounds might still be able to walk or help carry more seriously injured comrades.
            In the field, Soldiers can create improvised litters by threading poles—such as tent poles or antenna poles—
            through the sleeves of zippered combat uniform blouses or ponchos. Another option is to use a travois or
            skid, which allows a wounded individual to be strapped on and pulled by one person. Casualties can be
            evacuated from the POI to the CCP or directly to the BAS by litter teams. Depending on the situation,
            casualties may stay with the unit until transportation is available, or they might be left at a designated location
            for later retrieval. For more information on making and using improvised litter, refer to ATP 4-02.13.
            2-8. From the platoon area, casualties are typically evacuated to the company CCP and then to the BAS. The
            company first sergeant, with support from the platoon sergeant, is usually tasked with moving casualties from
            the platoon CCP to the company CCP. Unit SOPs should cover this process, including casualty marking
            during limited visibility conditions. Small chemical lights can be effective for this purpose. Once casualties
            are gathered, assessed, and treated, they are transferred to the company CCP. Upon arrival, this process
            repeats until they are evacuated back to the BAS.
            2-9. In cases of wide dispersion within the company, casualties may be evacuated directly from the platoon
            CCP using ground or air platforms. Aeromedical evacuation could be limited due to weather, terrain, or
            enemy presence. Sometimes casualties must be moved to the company CCP or battalion combat trains before
            rotary-wing aircraft evacuation becomes feasible. If there aren't enough battalion ambulances, supply
            vehicles may transport casualties to the BAS after delivering supplies. Urgent casualties are prioritized for
            MEDEVAC, while less critical cases may be moved by other means. Occasionally, the platoon sergeant may
            direct aid and litter teams to carry casualties to the rear.
CASUALTY HANDLING
37B




            2-10. Casualties evacuated manually must be handled with care to avoid exacerbating their injuries. Rough
            handling could cause further harm, so movement efforts should be organized and methodical. Each
            movement should be deliberate and gentle, considering the casualties’ injuries and providing necessary first
            aid or TCCC as appropriate. Immediate movement may be necessary in certain safety-critical situations, such
            as a burning vehicle or enemy fire. However, manual carries should not be used for casualties with suspected
            neck or spine injuries unless there is an immediate life-threatening hazard, and medical advice should be
            sought.
            2-11. Various methods for carrying and dragging litters can be used, depending on the casualty's condition,
            the terrain, and the level of enemy threat. When planning how to move a casualty, factors to consider include
            cover and concealment, the weight of the casualty versus the size and strength of the rescuer, nature of the
            casualty's wounds, the distance to cover, the carrying technique, environmental hazards, and enemy activity.
            Rescuers must be prepared to adapt their plans quickly based on the changing dynamics of the situation to
            ensure the casualty is moved swiftly and safely. Special care is also necessary when moving casualties near

text:
Casualty Extraction and Movement



          different aircraft, vehicles, and ships, and responders should be knowledgeable about the specific hazards
          each platform presents.
          2-12. Once a casualty has been treated with a hasty TQ, if the tactical situation allows, priority shifts to
          getting them to cover and out of enemy fire. Carries and drags enable responders or the CLS to accomplish
          this swiftly without worsening the casualty's condition. When providing first aid and considering casualty
          transport, responders must carefully assess the situation, particularly in scenarios like motor vehicle accidents
          where spinal injuries are a concern. In such cases, moving the casualty may only be advisable if there's an
          immediate threat to their life, with trained medical personnel ultimately directing transportation decisions.

Manual Carries
319B




          2-13. Manual carries pose physical strain on the bearers and carries the risk of exacerbating the casualty's
          injuries. However, they can be crucial in saving a casualty's life when other means of transport are unavailable
          or impractical due to terrain or tactical considerations. Depending on factors such as the bearers' strength and
          endurance, the casualty's weight, nature of injuries, and obstacles encountered, the distance a casualty can be
          manually carried varies. Carries can be employed for both conscious and unconscious casualties by one or
          two bearers. When executed correctly, carries offer the casualty greater protection from additional harm
          compared to drags and can facilitate movement over longer distances, typically ranging from 50 to 300
          meters. For more information on manual carries refer to ATP 4-02.13.

Drags
320B




          2-14. Drags, on the other hand, are used when swift removal from dangerous or hostile environments is
          imperative. They allow the bearer and casualty to maintain a low profile, utilizing cover and concealment to
          evade hazards. Drags are generally employed for shorter distances, typically up to 50 meters. It's important
          to exercise caution during casualty handling to avoid causing further harm. For more information on drags
          refer to ATP 4-02.13.
LITTER EVACUATION
38B




          2-15. Whenever possible, transporting a casualty on a litter is preferred over manual carries. Litter transport
          offers greater comfort to the casualty and reduces the risk of worsening their injuries. It facilitates easier and
          faster evacuation and enables the casualty to be transported over longer distances compared to manual carries.
          Ideally, a standard litter should be used whenever available. In cases where standard litter is not accessible,
          an improvised litter can serve as a suitable alternative until the casualty can be transferred to a standard one.
          It's crucial to ensure that standard litter is always maintained in a serviceable condition. For further guidance
          on litter evacuation, refer to ATP 4-02.13.
EVACUATION PLATFORMS
39B




          2-16. In operational scenarios, ambulances may be insufficient in number to meet evacuation demands or
          may not be suitable for transporting patients over certain types of terrain. In such situations, many vehicles
          commonly used by units can be repurposed to transport casualties without significant modifications. Units
          should prioritize planning and training on how their existing vehicles can be used to transport casualties, both
          with and without litter. Leaders must assess not only their organic platforms but also explore the potential
          use of civilian, other Services, and coalition platforms. For detailed guidance on evacuation platforms and
          CASEVAC, refer to ATP 4-02.2, ATP 4-02.13, or STP 8-68W13-SM-TG.
          2-17. It's important to note that the current Standard Training Publication contains tasks and training guidance
          that are not aligned with the current standards for continuity training across the operational force. Once the
          revised STP 8-68W13-SG-TG is approved, it will be available for download on the Army Publishing
          Directorate and Central Army Register websites. In the meantime, for the most up-to-date Combat Medic
          Specialist tasks, refer to the Individual Critical Task Lists posted on the Central Army Register website. You
          can find these by searching for “68W ICTLs” in the search window. This ensures that you are using the most
          current and applicable training materials available.

PART TWO
                                                      290B




                    TACTICAL COMBAT CASUALTY CARE
                    293B




          TCCC is crucial for ensuring the safety and health of Service members in combat-
          related situations. Specifically designed for battlefield conditions, TCCC provides a
          comprehensive approach to casualty care, focusing on immediate treatment and
          management. In the fast-paced environment of warfare, adherence to TCCC principles
          can significantly improve survival outcomes. It equips military units and leaders with
          the necessary knowledge and skills to provide timely and effective care to injured
          personnel, thereby reducing fatalities and enhancing survival rates. This publication
          highlights the vital importance of TCCC in military operations, emphasizing its
          essential role in saving the lives of Service members and enhancing the overall
          effectiveness of units.

                                                             Chapter 3
               Fundamentals of Tactical Combat Casualty Care

TACTICAL COMBAT CASUALTY CARE OVERVIEW
20B




          3-1. In accordance with DODI 1322.24, medical readiness training (also known as MRT) encompasses all
          facets of medical support across the competition continuum and forms the cornerstone of effective force
          health protection. TCCC serves as the DOD standard of care for both nonmedical and medical first
          responders. The TCCC-All Service member course supersedes previous trauma skills taught in self-aid and
          buddy aid courses, mandating that all Service members receive role-based TCCC training and certification
          aligned with their assigned skill level as outlined by the JTS. DODI 6040.47 designates the JTS as the DOD’s
          Center of Excellence for trauma management.
          3-2. Service members performing self-aid, buddy aid, and CLS support prioritize their primary combat
          mission, rendering aid as a secondary mission when feasible. While these roles do not replace the specialized
          skills of combat medics, corpsmen, and healthcare technicians, they may assist in providing far-forward care
          and preparing casualties for evacuation if mission and time permit.
          3-3. Self-aid, buddy aid, and CLS support are integral components of a comprehensive plan aimed at caring
          for wounded Service members. A significant advantage of individual Service members providing such
          support is their proximity to injured squad or crew members. This proximity allows for more immediate care
          compared to waiting for a combat medic, especially in situations where the medic may be occupied with
          treating other seriously wounded personnel. First responders and CLS personnel are trained to administer
          critical immediate care, including addressing severe bleeding and performing needle chest decompression
          for tension pneumothorax, potentially saving lives in the crucial moments following injury.

SERVICE SPECIFIC SKILLS FOR TACTICAL COMBAT CASUALTY
203B




CARE
          3-4. Individual medical readiness training is built upon a foundation of knowledge, skills, and abilities
          tailored to operational medicine. Operational medical readiness training focuses on developing a core set of
          validated, operationally unique skills and abilities necessary to accomplish mission objectives. These core
          competencies are expanded as needed to address specific Service missions, informing unit readiness reporting
          as part of medical specialty team readiness. DODI 1322.24, published by the JTS, outlines basic TCCC skills

text:
Chapter 3



            for all Service members, allowing individual Services to augment these requirements based on their specific
            needs.
            3-5. TCCC skills are categorized into four tiers, spanning from all Service members to credentialed providers,
            with each tier building upon the knowledge and skills of the preceding tier. Each tier represents a progression
            in the complexity and scope of medical interventions, enabling Service members to provide increasingly
            advanced care to injured personnel. The tiered approach ensures that personnel are trained to the appropriate
            level based on their roles and responsibilities within their respective units or specialties.
            3-6. Tier 1, or All Service member skills, encompasses fundamental skills taught to all Service members,
            focusing on basic hemorrhage control and recognition of serious injuries. This tier aims to equip every
            Service member with essential lifesaving capabilities, enabling them to provide immediate care to injured
            comrades in the battlefield environment. Training in Tier 1 skills is critical for ensuring that all Service
            members are prepared to respond effectively to medical emergencies, regardless of their primary
            occupational specialties.
            3-7. Tier 2, or CLS skills, involves more advanced care aimed at addressing the most common causes of
            battlefield fatalities. This tier emphasizes recognizing, preventing, and communicating life-threatening
            complications to medical personnel. CLS training provides select Service members with enhanced
            capabilities to stabilize casualties and facilitate their evacuation to higher levels of care, thereby improving
            overall survival rates in combat environment.
            3-8. Tier 3 or Combat Medic and Corpsman skills contains the skills that are much more advanced and focus
            on invasive care. This tier of skills requires significantly more medical knowledge and skills than self-aid,
            buddy aid, or CLS.
            3-9. Tier 4 or Combat Paramedic and Provider skills are for combat paramedics and advanced providers. This
            tier provides the most sophisticated care to keep wounded Service members alive and get them to definitive
            care.
ADDITIONAL REQUIRED SKILLS FOR ARMY PERSONNEL
40B




            3-10. The U.S. Army has proactively expanded upon the foundational skills outlined in DODI 1322.24 by
            identifying additional Tier 1 and Tier 2 competencies critical for its personnel. This initiative highlights the
            Army's commitment to enhancing the skill sets of its members, ensuring they are well-prepared for the
            challenges they may face. The tracking and documentation of these competencies are meticulously managed
            through the Digital Training Management System. This system serves as the official record for all training
            activities within the Army, making it imperative that every course and task completion is recorded accurately
            in the Digital Training Management System. This process will continue until the Digital Training
            Management System is replaced by the forthcoming Army Training Information System, which promises to
            further streamline and optimize training management and record-keeping within the Army.

Tier 1 Skills for Army Personnel
321B




            3-11. The MEDCoE consistently evaluates and updates all relevant initial entry training and initial military
            training medical lesson plans to ensure compliance with TCCC-All Service member requirements. Soldiers
            who are not certified during initial training will receive certification upon arrival at their first assigned unit.
            This ensures that all personnel are adequately trained in TCCC before deployment.
            3-12. According to DODI 1322.31, the frequency of TCCC-All Service member training is determined by
            the Military Service, with the condition that all personnel receive training prior to deployment. Additionally,
            recertification and refresher training for Component 1 (Active Army) are required annually, while
            Component 2 (Reserve) and Component 3 (National Guard) require biannual recertification. Detailed task
            requirements and standards for the Army can be accessed through Central Army Registry website.
            3-13. In alignment with DODI 1322.24, the U.S. Army has integrated Warrior Tasks and Battle Drills for
            Perform Tactical Combat Casualty Care, into its training protocols. More information on Warrior Tasks and
            Battle Drills can be found in STP 21-1-SMCT and on the Central Army Registry website. This initiative
            ensures that Soldiers are proficient in providing critical medical care during combat situations, enhancing
            overall readiness and effectiveness in the field.

text:
Fundamentals of Tactical Combat Casualty Care



Tier 2 Skills for Army Personnel
32B




          3-14. Immediate and forward medical care is crucial in dynamic battlefield environments to prevent fatalities
          among wounded Soldiers. Given the challenges of reaching all casualties promptly, CLS plays a vital role in
          providing advanced lifesaving interventions. CLS training equips Soldiers with necessary skills and
          knowledge to stabilize various types of casualties and to mitigate the worsening of injuries until medical
          assistance arrives.
          3-15. It is essential to have at least one CLS per squad, crew, team, or similar-sized unit, ensuring readiness
          for medical emergencies. Recertification of CLS personnel every 12 months at the unit level is mandated by
          AR 350-1, ensuring proficiency and readiness. Additionally, comprehensive CLS and CASEVAC training
          for all Army personnel is imperative for small-unit operations with widely dispersed forces.

Combat Lifesaver Training
418B




          3-16. The U.S. Army MEDCoE developed the CLS course to ensure comprehensive medical support for
          Army personnel. This course is used by both active duty and reserve component Soldiers across all units
          throughout the force. Implementation of CLS training within corps, divisions, brigades, and battalions is
          overseen by designated credentialed providers, who supervise CLS programs and ensure adherence to
          established standards.
          3-17. Training support packages, containing student and instructor materials, facilitate CLS training at the
          unit and organizational levels. Training and testing are conducted based on the tasks, conditions, and
          standards set by the United States Army Training and Doctrine Command (also known as TRADOC). Proof
          of CLS course completion is documented IAW AR 600-8-104, with certificates issued to Soldiers who
          successfully complete the training, and records maintained in the Army Training Requirements and
          Resources System.
          3-18. Locations conducting CLS training are responsible for documenting completion through local systems
          or, if necessary, submitting records to the U.S. Army MEDCoE Instructional Technology Support Services
          Help Desk. The CLS course allows for retests following failed examinations, with a minimum of one retest
          opportunity provided. However, course managers may establish guidelines for retesting based on individual
          circumstances.
          3-19. Instructors responsible for CLS training must meet specific qualifications outlined in the individual
          critical task list Task: 081-68W-2003. Leaders are tasked with ensuring adequate training opportunities for
          nonmedical personnel within their units, coordinating with medical personnel for remedial training as needed.
          Enrollment procedures, facility requirements, course materials, and equipment procurement are essential
          considerations for successful CLS training implementation, ensuring Soldiers receive effective medical
          training and support.

Combat Lifesaver Recertification
419B




          3-20. CLS skills are perishable and must be recertified every 12 months to ensure proficiency in the
          performance-tested tasks. Unit instructors utilize the standards provided in the training support package for
          recertification purposes. Personnel staff, rather than medical platoon leaders, are responsible for updating
          personnel records after CLS training completion.
          3-21. Leaders should maintain records of CLS certification for all units under their supervision and notify
          unit commanders about upcoming certification expiration dates. Proper planning for recertification testing
          involves ensuring instructors have appropriate guides and tests, access to necessary facilities, personnel,
          equipment, and supplies. Personnel records must be updated following successful CLS training, a task
          entrusted to the personnel staff.
          3-22. To sustain skill proficiency, CLS training should be integrated into home station training activities,
          including field-training exercises, and deployment preparations. Additionally, CLS skills should be exercised
          during deployment for training, such as rotations through combat training centers. This ongoing training
          ensures that CLS personnel remain competent, and ready to provide lifesaving care in diverse operational
          environments.

title: U.S. Army: Casualty Response, Tactical Combat Casualty Care, and First Aid (ATP 4-02.11)
text:
Chapter 3



Combat Lifesaver Bag
420B




            3-23. Each certified CLS should ideally be equipped with a CLS aid bag, with its contents carefully regulated
            to prevent unauthorized alterations. While exceptions exist, for The United States Army Special Operations
            Command surgeons, modifications to aid bags must adhere to validated mission requirements and receive
            approval from The United States Army Special Operations Command Defense Collaboration Services,
            Surgeon. All necessary Class VIII supplies and materials for CLS operations are procured through standard
            supply channels, with detailed information available in Appendix A regarding CLS bag supplies.
            3-24. CLS aid bags are allocated to CLS personnel solely upon deployment, both for training exercises and
            actual missions. It remains the responsibility of each CLS to maintain their aid bag according to the prescribed
            packing list, ensuring all items are serviceable, and within their expiration dates. In combat scenarios, where
            medical supplies may be rapidly depleted, emergency resupply options include combat medics, ambulances,
            BAS, or nearby MTFs. However, it's important to exhaust supplies from the casualty's first aid kit before
            tapping into resources from the CLS bag.
ADDITIONAL REQUIRED SKILLS FOR MARINE CORPS PERSONNEL
41B




            3-25. The Marine Corps has expanded its training curriculum to include additional Tier 1 and Tier 2 skills,
            building on the foundation set by DODI 1322.31. This strategic enhancement ensures that Marines are
            equipped with a broader set of capabilities, tailored to meet the evolving demands of modern military
            engagements and operational responsibilities. The identification of these extra skills underlines the
            commitment of the Marine Corps to maintain superior readiness and effectiveness in all aspects of its mission.

Tier 1 Skills for Marine Corps Personnel
32B




            3-26. In accordance with TCCC-All Service Member Course curriculum developed by the JTS, the USMC
            will focus on the skills prescribed for All Service Members and the following additional skills described in
            subsequent chapters:
                 • Apply Rigid Eye Shield (paragraph 10-1).
                 • Perform Casualty Burn Care (paragraph 13-9).
                 • Record Treatment on a DD Form 1380 (paragraph 16-13).
            3-27. See Appendix A for details on the USMC first aid kit.

Tier 2 Skills for Marine Corps Personnel
324B




            3-28. In accordance with TCCC CLS course curriculum developed by the JTS, the USMC will focus only on
            the skills prescribed for CLS already described in this publication.
            3-29. A CLS kit is issued to CLS-trained Marines to assist the Navy Corpsman in multiple casualty situations
            or act as the primary first responder when HMs are not available, as in small unit operations.
            3-30. The CLS kit is a portable lightweight bag containing medical supplies that enables CLS-trained Marines
            to treat extremity hemorrhaging (treat one double limb and two single limb casualties), sucking chest wounds,
            and clear a wounded Marine’s airway.
            3-31. Using units are required to replenish the CLS Kit through standard supply (military standard
            requisitioning and issue procedures) requisitions; however, during combat, medical supplies can be quickly
            depleted. Additional supplies can be obtained from BASs or other nearby MTFs or in Line 4 of the 9-line
            MEDEVAC request.

                  Note. No Service manuals are required for the CLS Kit.

ADDITIONAL REQUIRED SKILLS FOR AIR FORCE PERSONNEL
42B




            3-32. The USAF assigns the same level of importance to TCCC training as its fellow Services, ensuring a
            standardized approach across the military. The USAF has not distinguished additional skills within the tier 1
            and tier 2 categories of TCCC competencies. For comprehensive TCCC information and specific training
            requirements, USAF personnel are advised to refer to DODI 1322.24, DODI 1322.31 and the Deployed

text:
Fundamentals of Tactical Combat Casualty Care



          Medicine website. It is also recommended that members familiarize themselves with any relevant Service-
          specific TCCC guidelines. The information provided in this publication is invaluable for general
          understanding and can be applied to the TCCC procedures, use of the expedient techniques detailed in each
          section, and for the administration of first aid for injuries not specifically covered under the TCCC protocols.

TACTICAL COMBAT CASUALTY CARE TRAINING
204B




          3-33. Continuous evolution characterizes TCCC, CLS, medical treatment, and interventions, aligning with
          shifts in medicine and operational contexts. To stay informed of the latest changes and updates, individuals
          should regularly consult the deployed medicine website and the United States Army Medical Material
          Agency website. Service members and Department of Defense-expeditionary civilian personnel, whether
          augmentees to operational units or individual augmentees, undergo comprehensive medical readiness training
          tailored to their deployment circumstances. This is done by encompassing triage, treatment, and management
          of various health hazards, including CBRN threats.
          3-34. A profound grasp of TCCC fundamentals can significantly impact outcomes by conserving fighting
          power, mass, and momentum to support the current fight and potentially saving lives, averting permanent
          disability, and minimizing hospitalization durations. Emphasizing what actions to take, what to avoid, and
          when to act. TCCC aims to treat casualties effectively, prevent further harm, and uphold mission completion.
          Central to TCCC's objectives is addressing and mitigating the causes of preventable death on the battlefield,
          with training targeting specific areas such as bleeding control, including junctional and noncompressible
          bleeding, as well as addressing tension pneumothorax and airway complications.
          3-35. Leveraging technology for enhanced accessibility and continuous learning, the deployed medicine
          website and mobile application by the Defense Health Agency offer invaluable resources. These platforms
          furnish on-demand multimedia content, facilitating lifelong learning and real-time updates in TCCC training
          and education. Among the resources provided are training and education materials, the TCCC-All Service
          member curriculum, updated videos, podcasts, and downloadable CPGs, empowering personnel with
          comprehensive support for optimal preparedness and skill development.

TACTICAL COMBAT CASUALTY CARE PHASES
205B




          3-36. The TCCC framework encompasses three critical phases of care tailored to the dynamic challenges of
          battlefield medicine. These phases, structured to address varying levels of urgency and complexity, are Care
          Under Fire (CUF), Tactical Field Care (TFC), and Tactical Evacuation Care (also known as TACEVAC).
          Mastery of these phases equips military units and leaders with the proficiency needed to deliver prompt and
          efficient medical assistance to injured Service members in combat scenarios. Such skills play a pivotal role
          in preserving life, mitigating the potential for long-term disability, and optimizing the prospects of full
          recovery for wounded personnel.
CARE UNDER FIRE
43B




          3-37. Care under fire is the first phase of care in tactical combat casualty care where very limited care
          is provided for the casualty while the enemy threat is still active. Also known as CUF or care under
          threat. During CUF, the primary focus is on providing immediate life-saving care while still under enemy
          fire. This phase involves skills such as returning fire, moving the casualty to a safer location, and controlling
          severe bleeding using techniques like TQs. The goal is to stabilize the casualty quickly to prevent further
          injury or death. In CUF, available medical equipment is limited to what is carried by individual responders
          or casualties, and the only medical priority is addressing massive extremity bleeding due to the ongoing threat
          in a potentially chaotic and dangerous situation.
          3-38. The order of actions during CUF is mission-variable dependent, with scene safety being paramount.
          For instance, if the threat is suppressed and the tactical situation allows massive life-threatening bleeding and
          extremity bleeding should be addressed prior to patient movement from the POI. However, each scenario is
          different, and the ordering of actions could vary accordingly. It's crucial to remember that in the combat
          environment, there is no "time-out" when casualties occur. Rapid medical and tactical decisions must be
          made simultaneously, as good medicine can sometimes be bad tactics. Potentially, endangering the lives of
          responders and jeopardizing the mission's success.

text:
Chapter 3



            3-39. The tactical situation dictates the initial actions during CUF, with little time available for casualty care
            while under effective enemy fire. Prioritizing suppressing hostile fire and gaining fire superiority is crucial
            to minimizing the risk of injury to personnel and preventing further harm to the casualty. Wounded Service
            members should be directed to continue returning fire, moving quickly to nearby cover, and performing self-
            aid if able. It's essential not to become a casualty oneself, assessing the situation, suppressing enemy fire, and
            developing a plan before moving to care for a casualty under fire.
            3-40. In CUF, early control of severe bleeding is the number one medical priority, as extremity hemorrhage
            is the most frequent cause of preventable battlefield deaths. Major vessel injuries can quickly lead to shock
            and death, making it crucial to identify and address life-threatening bleeding promptly. Only massive
            bleeding warrants intervention during CUF, with treatment of non-life-threatening bleeding deferred until
            the TFC phase. Despite the grave danger posed by enemy fire, applying a hasty TQ quickly and effectively
            remains essential in this phase (if this tactical situation allows) to save lives and prevent further casualties.

Scene Safety
325B




            3-41. CUF is defined as the aid rendered at the trauma scene while there is still an active threat. The scene in
            CUF is never safe, however, the active threat can be reduced. The responder can help others to reduce the
            threat (return gunfire, or firefighting) and to enable rescuers to reach the casualty and move the casualty to
            cover. The responder should not risk their personal safety or the safety of the casualty if the threat has not
            been reduced.

Control of Massive Bleeding
326B




            3-42. In the CUF phase, the primary focus is on controlling massive bleeding to prevent hypovolemic shock,
            a critical and potentially fatal condition. Effective management of severe bleeding is essential to stabilize the
            casualty and ensure survival until further medical treatment can be administered. For detailed strategies and
            techniques on controlling massive bleeding, see Chapter 4, which provides comprehensive guidance on the
            procedures and equipment necessary for this vital emergency intervention.

Casualty Movement
327B




            3-43. If a casualty is unresponsive or unable to move, a rescue plan should be devised and executed if
            tactically feasible. Do not put two people at risk if it can be avoided. If cover is not available or the wounded
            Service member cannot move to cover, they should lie flat and motionless. For more information on casualty
            movement techniques see chapter 2, paragraph 2-6 of this publication.

Proper Communication and Documentation
328B




            3-44. Communication is vital in providing effective care for casualties, involving interaction with the
            casualty, unit leaders, and on-scene medical personnel. Rescuers should communicate with the casualty as
            soon as they can safely reach them, by assessing their level of consciousness and orientation. It's crucial to
            reassure conscious casualties and request assistance from other responders or medics when available, as
            rescuers are rarely alone in such situations.
            3-45. Documentation of all care provided to casualties is essential, primarily utilizing DD Form 1380. This
            form should include details such as the casualty's name, sex, time of injury, the nature of the injury, along
            with findings from rapid casualty assessments and the medical aid provided. This information is critical for
            the continuity of care and should be securely attached to the casualty or recorded directly on them if the form
            is unavailable.
            3-46. Securing DD Form 1380 on the casualty, by attaching it to their belt loop or placing it in their pocket
            ensures it accompanies them to the next level of care. If the form is unavailable, pertinent information can be
            directly written on the casualty's body or on a strip of medical tape. This documentation is vital for ensuring
            comprehensive and effective care throughout the casualty's treatment process. (See figure 15-2 on page 154
            for an example of a completed DD Form 1380).

Fundamentals of Tactical Combat Casualty Care



Combat Lifesaver Role in Care Under Fire
329B




          3-47. In the context of CUF, the CLS assumes a role similar to individuals providing self-aid. Their primary
          objective is to suppress hostile fire to minimize the risk of injury to personnel and further harm to wounded
          Service members. The CLS utilizes available medical equipment, which is typically limited to what the
          individual responder, casualty's first aid kit, or CLS bag carries. It's emphasized that the first responder and
          CLS should prioritize the use of the casualty's first aid kit before resorting to other resources. See Appendix
          A, paragraph A-7 for further discussion on the CLS bag.
          3-48. Given the urgency of the situation, the sequence of actions in CUF is dictated by the tactical
          environment. With limited time available for casualty care amidst enemy fire, suppressing hostile fire and
          gaining fire superiority are prioritized to protect both personnel and casualties. This may involve personnel
          assisting in returning fire instead of immediately attending to casualties, especially if the casualty can still
          engage in combat. Wounded Service members exposed to enemy fire are directed to seek cover, perform
          self-aid if possible, and continue returning fire while moving to safety.
          3-49. In CUF, the primary focus is on recognizing and halting massive bleeding while seeking cover to shield
          oneself and the casualty from hostile fire. Signs of massive bleeding, such as pulsing or steady bleeding from
          wounds or traumatic amputations, must be promptly addressed. The immediate application of a hasty TQ is
          recommended if indicated, as injuries to major veins or arteries can lead to shock or death within minutes.
          Extremity hemorrhage, a common cause of preventable combat death, underscores the critical role of TQs in
          saving lives during CUF scenarios.
          3-50. Prompt application of TQs to halt life-threatening bleeding not only saves lives but also enables injured
          Service members to continue fighting while awaiting further medical care and evacuation. It's emphasized
          that all Service members with access to a first aid kit should be trained in TQ use, highlighting the importance
          of preparedness and training in combat lifesaving techniques.
TACTICAL FIELD CARE
4B




          3-51. Tactical field care is the second phase of care in tactical combat casualty care. Care provided once
          the threat has been neutralized, the scene is safe, or the casualty has moved or been moved out of the
          immediate threat situation. Also known as TFC. This phase permits more extensive medical interventions,
          including the assessment and management of airway, breathing, circulation, and other injuries. Essential
          skills such as wound dressing, pain management, blood or blood product resuscitation, and fluid resuscitation
          for burns are pivotal during this phase. TFC also encompasses scenarios in a combat or tactical environment
          not involving direct enemy fire, such as parachute injuries in a combat zone.
          3-52. Transitioning from CUF, TFC provides the opportunity for a more deliberate approach to casualty
          assessment and treatment, given the time and relative safety available. However, the tactical situation remains
          dynamic, and the potential for reverting to a CUF scenario always exists. In TFC, both the casualty and the
          first responder or CLS should maintain cover and concealment. The primary management plan involves
          maintaining tactical situational awareness, triaging casualties as needed, and conducting a thorough casualty
          assessment.
          3-53. Mission personnel are tasked with establishing a security perimeter according to unit tactical SOP or
          battle drills, maintaining security, and remaining vigilant for potential threats from hostile forces. Casualties
          in shock or under the influence of controlled substances pose risks to themselves and others. Hence, those
          with altered mental status should have their weapons cleared and secured, communications secured, and
          sensitive items redistributed.
          3-54. During the TFC phase, responders have more time and relatively greater safety to administer further
          medical care. They may need to continue treatment until medical personnel arrive, assisting them with
          continued treatment and preparation for evacuation. However, the anticipated time for evacuation to the next
          level of care may vary based on the operational situation, requiring CLS to remain prepared to reengage the
          enemy and resume the mission.
          3-55. While medical personnel prioritize casualty treatment, coordination between responders and unit
          leaders is crucial for requesting evacuation assets based on the operational situation. Despite the expanded
          scope of care in TFC, available medical equipment remains limited to what is carried into the field by the

           casualty's first aid kit, the CLS, and other responders' first aid kits or supplies in a medic's aid bag. It's
           emphasized that supplies within the casualty's first aid kit should be used first before resorting to other
           available supplies.
TACTICAL EVACUATION CARE
45B




           3-56. Tactical evacuation care is the third phase of care in tactical combat casualty care. Care provided
           during transportation from the battlefield to a medical treatment facility. Tactical evacuation care is the
           phase of TCCC focused on preparing the casualty for evacuation to a higher role of care, typically an MTF.
           This phase encompasses both preparing the casualty for evacuation and executing the evacuation process
           while ensuring continued monitoring and treatment of the casualty's condition. Skills required during tactical
           evacuation care include managing the casualty's airway and breathing, maintaining circulation, and providing
           ongoing medical interventions as necessary.
           3-57. The NATO term of tactical MEDEVAC refers to the intra-theater movement of patients between MTFs
           within the joint operational area. This process involves transferring patients from one MTF to another using
           ground, rotary, or fixed-wing assets, along the lines of communication within the joint operational area. In
           the U.S. Army, this includes MEDEVAC operations between different roles of care, from Role 1 through
           Role 3, supported by both ground and air ambulances. However, the term "TACEVAC" should not be used
           to describe the tactical evacuation care phase of TCCC and to prevent confusion between the evacuation
           process itself and a specific phase of TCCC.
           3-58. The primary principle in tactical evacuation care is to continue monitoring and providing appropriate
           assessment and treatment until the casualty is transferred to medical personnel or reaches a higher level of
           care. During this phase, first responders or CLSs conduct a deliberate assessment to identify and treat
           previously unrecognized life-threatening injuries. While similar to TFC in many aspects, the presence of
           additional medical personnel and equipment on the evacuation asset may enable the provision of more
           extensive care and casualty management.
           3-59. Non-medical first responders or CLSs are not expected to provide care during evacuation. However, if
           they do, the skills used in CUF and TFC still apply. Pre-evacuation procedures involve documenting all
           assessments and care provided during CUF and TFC on DD Form 1380. Additionally, an evacuation request
           using the 9-line format is initiated according to unit SOP to initiate MEDEVAC.
           3-60. During staging, each casualty is reassessed, and their medical condition is monitored to ensure they
           receive necessary care while waiting for evacuation. This step is vital for maintaining the stability of
           casualties and adjusting medical interventions as needed before they are transported to a higher level of
           medical care. Communication plays a key role during this phase, as it helps reduce the casualties' anxiety and
           provides them reassurance about the care, they are receiving While, keeping the casualty informed and as
           calm as possible under the circumstances.
           3-61. Overall, tactical evacuation care ensures that casualties receive continuous monitoring, assessment, and
           treatment during the evacuation process until they reach a higher level of care. It involves coordination
           between medical personnel, tactical leaders, and other responders to ensure a smooth and efficient evacuation
           process in challenging tactical environments.
           3-62. The proper procedure for performing a 9-line MEDEVAC request is critical in tactical environments
           to ensure timely evacuation support for casualties. Here's a detailed outline of the steps involved:
                • Collect Information: Gather all necessary information required for the MEDEVAC request,
                    including the casualty's condition, location, and other pertinent details, using authorized brevity
                    codes.
                • Initiate Contact: Clearly announce "I HAVE A MEDEVAC REQUEST" over the radio frequency
                    designated for communication with the unit controlling evacuation assets. Wait for one to three
                    seconds for a response. If there is no response, repeat the statement.
                • Transmit MEDEVAC Request: Contact the unit controlling evacuation assets using the proper call
                    sign and frequency assignment as specified in the signal operating instructions from an automated
                    net control device.
                • Sequence and Format: Transmit the MEDEVAC information in the proper sequence, stating all line
                    numbers clearly. Line numbers 1 through 5 must be transmitted within 25 seconds during the initial

TACTICAL COMBAT CASUALTY CARE DURING OPERATIONS
206B




          3-64. During operations, the battlefield is often widely dispersed and rapidly moving, posing challenges for
          the rapid acquisition of casualties and medical treatment. As a result, medical platoon personnel may face
          limitations in providing immediate, far-forward medical care. To address this, the plan is to integrate CLS
          into the system of providing care for wounded Service members. The three primary goals of TCCC are to
          treat casualties, prevent additional casualties, and complete the mission.
          3-65. When a nonmedical Service member encounters an unconscious or injured casualty, they must quickly
          assess the situation and casualty's condition to determine if it's safe and if immediate first aid measures are
          necessary to prevent further injury or death. They should ascertain if trained medical personnel are available
          or direct others at the scene to call for or locate trained medical personnel. Once first aid is initiated, efforts
          should continue without interruption until medical personnel take over. Service members may also need to
          rely on their own first aid skills for self-aid. The CLS serves as a link between the self-aid or buddy aid skills
          taught to all Service members and the medical training provided to medical personnel.
          3-66. Immediate medical care in far-forward positions is crucial in a dispersed and dynamic operational
          environment to prevent casualties from succumbing to wounds. In situations where medical personnel may
          not reach all wounded Service members promptly, the CLS plays a vital role in providing advanced lifesaving
          measures beyond basic self-aid or buddy aid. A well-trained CLS can stabilize various types of casualties
          and mitigate the deterioration of a wounded Service member's condition until medical personnel arrive.
          However, functioning as a CLS is a secondary mission undertaken when the tactical situation allows.
          3-67. One significant advantage of the CLS is their proximity to injured unit members. While medical
          personnel may take several minutes or longer to reach casualties, especially when attending to severely
          wounded individuals, the CLS can provide immediate lifesaving care, such as controlling severe bleeding
          and performing needle chest decompressions for tension pneumothorax.
          3-68. When not engaged in combat duties, CLS personnel may also assist medical personnel in providing
          care and preparing casualties for evacuation. The role and responsibilities of the CLS are delineated in
          different phases of care:
               • In CUF, the CLS responds by suppressing hostile fire to minimize the risk of injury to personnel
                    and prevent additional harm to previously injured Service members.
               • In TFC, the CLS maintains security and situational awareness while attending casualties and
                    preparing them for evacuation.
               • In Tactical Evacuation, support the Combat Medic or Corpsman, as directed.
          3-69. CLS personnel are specifically trained to tackle the primary causes of battlefield fatalities, which
          include massive hemorrhage and airway or respiratory issues. They possess the skills necessary to prevent
          complications and manage other injuries that, while not immediately life-threatening, could become serious

           combat situations, enhancing the survival chances of those injured in the field.
KEY FACTORS INFLUENCING TACTICAL COMBAT CASUALTY CARE
46B




           3-70. Prehospital care in the combat setting differs significantly from the civilian setting due to various
           factors that influence TCCC. These factors include:
                • Hostile Fire: Combat environments are characterized by the presence of hostile fire, posing an
                     immediate threat to both casualties and responders. This necessitates the integration of tactical
                     considerations into casualty care protocols.
                • Tactical Considerations: Tactical priorities and objectives often dictate the approach to casualty
                     care. The safety of personnel and the completion of the mission take precedence, influencing how
                     and when medical interventions are performed.
                • Environmental Considerations: Combat operations can occur in diverse environments, ranging from
                     urban areas to remote and hostile terrain. Responders must adapt their care techniques to address
                     environmental challenges such as extreme weather conditions, limited visibility, and difficult
                     terrain.
                • Wounding Patterns: In combat, injuries are often caused by explosive devices, firearms, and other
                     weapons unique to warfare. Understanding these specific wounding patterns is crucial for effective
                     casualty management and prioritization of care.
                • Equipment Constraints: Medical resources and equipment may be limited or unavailable in the
                     combat setting, requiring improvisation and prioritization of essential interventions. Responders
                     must work within the constraints of available resources to provide optimal care.
                • Delays Reaching Higher Roles of Care: Evacuation to higher levels of care may be delayed in
                     combat situations due to operational factors, such as ongoing enemy engagement or logistical
                     challenges. This necessitates prolonged on-site care and management of casualties by first
                     responders.
                • Level of First Responder Training and Experience: The training and experience level of first
                     responders, including CLS and medical personnel, significantly impacts the quality and
                     effectiveness of prehospital care in combat. Adequate training ensures responders are proficient in
                     TCCC principles and can adapt to dynamic battlefield conditions.
           3-71. Overall, these factors shape the unique challenges and considerations involved in providing prehospital
           care in the combat setting, highlighting the importance of specialized training and protocols like TCCC for
           managing battlefield casualties.
FIRE SUPERIORITY IN TACTICAL COMBAT CASUALTY CARE
47B




           3-72. Fire superiority is paramount on the battlefield, serving as the best medicine to mitigate threats and
           protect personnel. In the midst of combat, all individuals should prioritize returning fire and seeking cover.
           The sequence of initial actions must align with the tactical circumstances at hand. Given the limited time
           available amid effective enemy fire, providing casualty care becomes a secondary consideration.
           3-73. Suppression of hostile fire and establishment of fire superiority are critical objectives aimed at reducing
           the risk of harm to both personnel and casualties while accomplishing the mission. In certain situations,
           individuals may be required to engage in returning fire rather than immediately attending to casualties,
           including wounded personnel who retain combat capability. Those injured and exposed to enemy fire should
           be instructed to continue engaging the enemy, seek cover promptly, and administer self-aid measures if
           feasible. These actions are essential for maintaining operational effectiveness and safeguarding lives amidst
           combat conditions.
CASUALTY SELF-AID
48B




           3-74. The skills outlined in this publication equip Service members to administer initial medical care at the
           POI, sustaining casualties until further assistance arrives. Responsive casualties should be directed by the
           first responder or CLS to return fire, apply self-aid, re-engage, and seek cover if feasible.
           3-75. If cover is inaccessible or the wounded Service member cannot move to safety, they should lie flat and
           remain still. If self-aid is beyond the casualty's capability or cover is unattainable, implementing a rescue

          plan, if feasible, becomes imperative. A hasty TQ should be applied promptly and tightly to stop the bleeding
          (ideally within one minute), as the tactical situation dictates. The urgency of a TQ application is underscored
          by the potential for a casualty to succumb to exsanguination in as little as three minutes.
          3-76. Initial medical care within the military context is administered by Service members leveraging their
          trained basic skills, encompassing self-aid or buddy aid. These skills encompass immediate life-saving
          interventions, as well as treatment for non-combat related injuries or conditions affecting functional capacity.
          3-77. The CoTCCC has identified five critical life-saving skills, namely rapid casualty assessment, TQ
          application, wound packing with hemostatic dressing, application of pressure bandages, and basic airway
          maneuvers for airway management.
          3-78. Vital to sustaining life is maintaining an adequate blood volume to facilitate oxygen transport to tissues.
          Halting bleeding and ensuring open airways are pivotal first aid measures, as oxygen deprivation swiftly
          precipitates death.
          3-79. Shock denotes inadequate tissue and organ perfusion, which is left untreated, can culminate in fatality
          despite the non-lethal nature of the precipitating injury or condition. Preventing shock is a cornerstone of
          first aid, significantly enhancing casualty survival prospects.
          3-80. Effective wound management entails safeguarding injuries against infection, which can impede
          recovery and exacerbate morbidity. Understanding basic first aid principles include proficiency in wound
          dressing to avert infection and minimize contamination.
          3-81. TCCC serves as the benchmark in prehospital battlefield medicine. Rapid casualty assessment and
          application of life-saving skills are pivotal in preserving lives. During casualty response, Service members
          are urged to take decisive action, document provided medical aid for continuity of care and facilitate
          evacuation to expedite access to advanced medical treatment.
INITIAL ENCOUNTER
49B




          3-82. In many cases, the initial care a Service member receives is provided through self-aid, buddy aid, or by
          CLS. The effectiveness of the actions taken during the initial encounter with a casualty, along with proper
          movement and transportation, are crucial elements in the successful application of TCCC. Sound decision-
          making and proficient execution of TCCC tasks have a significant impact on the health outcomes of
          casualties.
          3-83. Upon first encountering a casualty, it is imperative for the responder to assess the situation, understand
          the nature and severity of the injuries, and determine the appropriate TCCC interventions required quickly
          and accurately. Accurate assessment is essential not only for the welfare of the casualty but also for the safety
          of the responder. For example, in the case of electrocution, the responder must avoid direct contact with the
          casualty to prevent becoming a casualty themselves. This initial assessment forms the foundation for all
          subsequent care and decisions in the management of battlefield casualties.

TACTICAL COMBAT CASUALTY CARE CLINICAL PRACTICE
207B




GUIDELINE
          3-84. The JTS is dedicated to establishing the standard of care for all aspects of battlefield medicine,
          including prehospital care. It operates as a Department of Defense Center of Excellence for Trauma and is
          responsible for providing the CPGs and performance improvement initiatives for all levels of military trauma
          care. Under JTS, the CoTCCC is tasked with developing the TCCC CPG.
          3-85. The TCCC CPG serves as the benchmark for contemporary battlefield medical care. While the
          guidelines serve as recommendations, they do not replace clinical judgment. Given that the guidelines
          undergo periodic review and updates, it is essential for healthcare providers to regularly review them and
          integrate any changes into their training. For more detailed information on the TCCC CPG, reference the
          deployed medicine website.

text:
Chapter 3



           authoritative resources for TCCC medical training. This application allows users to stay informed about the
           TCCC guidelines and updates.
TRIAGE OR SORTING OF CASUALTIES
50B




           3-87. Triage is the process of sorting casualties based on need for treatment, evacuation, and available
           resources (FM 4-02). It is performed in each role of medical care. Triage is the most effective means of
           establishing order and the best method for providing the greatest benefit to the greatest number of patients
           within the limitations of time, distance, and capability. Triage is a constant process as casualties move within
           and through the roles of medical care.
           3-88. During incidents that generate mass casualties, the need to withhold treatment from a severely injured
           casualty, in-order to redirect lifesaving resources to casualties whose wounds are more survivable, is a
           difficult decision to make. While such decisions have been infrequent in recent conflicts, they may become
           more common during large-scale combat operations or situations where evacuation is difficult. The
           overarching goal of triage is, aiming to provide the greatest good to the greatest number and should guide
           these difficult decisions. The mission, immediate tactical situation, followed by medical necessity should
           prioritize resource allocation and should not be influenced by a casualty’s nationality or combatant status.
           3-89. Triage, or sorting of casualties, is essential to maximize limited resources. It involves evaluating,
           categorizing, and prioritizing casualties for medical treatment and evacuation. Casualties are sorted into
           categories based on their treatment urgency: immediate, delayed, minimal, and expectant. The goal is to
           return the greatest number of Service members back to duty while preserving life, limb, and eyesight.

Immediate Category
30B




           3-90. Immediate injuries are those that require attention within minutes to two hours to prevent death or
           major disability. Examples include airway obstruction, tension pneumothorax, uncontrolled hemorrhage,
           torso, neck or pelvis injuries with shock, head injuries requiring emergent decompression, threatened limb
           loss, collection of blood behind the eye, and multiple extremity amputations.

Delayed
31B




           3-91. Delayed injuries are those requiring surgery but permitting delay without significant risk to life, limb,
           or eyesight. Examples include blunt or penetrating torso injuries without shock, fractures, soft tissue injuries,
           facial fractures without airway compromise, eye injuries, and survivable burns without immediate threat of
           life (airway, respiratory) or limb.

Minimal
32B




           3-92. Minimal injuries are those that can care for themselves or need minimal medical care. Examples include
           minor lacerations, abrasions, small bone fractures, and minor burns. These casualties may assist with the
           movement or care of more severely injured individuals.

Expectant
3B




           3-93. Expectant injuries are those casualties that have injuries that would overwhelm current medical
           resources, at the expense of treating salvageable patients. These casualties should receive comfort measures
           and intermittent reassessment. Examples include casualties without vital signs or signs of life, open pelvic
           injuries with controlled bleeding and shock, life-threatening burns, high cervical spinal cord injuries affecting
           respiration, and destructive cardiac injuries.
CASUALTY ASSESSMENT
51B




           3-94. When learning, training, or teaching emergency medical care for a medical condition the airway,
           breathing, and circulation is used to prioritize treatment and may still be applicable in some situations. Service
           members experiencing a trauma casualty often start with more problems than resources available. In these
           situations, casualty assessment and management in TCCC follows a deliberate framework to prioritize trauma
           care known as massive hemorrhaging, airway, respiration, circulation, and hypothermia (MARCH) - pain,
           wounds, antibiotics, and splinting (PAWS).

title: U.S. Army: Casualty Response, Tactical Combat Casualty Care, and First Aid (ATP 4-02.11)
text:
Fundamentals of Tactical Combat Casualty Care



         3-95. The implementation of TCCC in modern warfare reflects the military's commitment to enhancing the
         well-being and survival of personnel on the battlefield. TCCC provides a comprehensive approach to
         immediate medical intervention in combat environments, with a focus on the "MARCH" portion of the
         MARCH-PAWS treatment protocol. This protocol prioritizes the evaluation and control of:
             • Massive Bleeding or hemorrhaging (the top priority) (see Chapter 4).
             • Airway (see Chapter 5).
             • Respiration (breathing) (see Chapter 6).
             • Circulation (see Chapter 7).
             • Hypothermia and head injuries (see Chapter 8).
         3-96. The second portion of the MARCH-PAWS casualty assessment is PAWS, which is addressed after the
         MARCH portion. For instance, while treating a casualty, a first responder or CLS might identify a fractured
         arm during the circulation and second injury portion of the MARCH. However, splinting the fracture should
         occur during the PAWS portion of the assessment.
         3-97. The primary focus of the casualty assessment is to swiftly identify and address life-threatening injuries
         before treating secondary injuries. For example, if a first responder or CLS were to treat a simple wound or
         splint a fracture before completing the full MARCH assessment, they might overlook life-threatening
         bleeding to a lower extremity. Although the simple wound or fracture would be addressed, the casualty would
         still be at risk of death due to the untreated life-threatening bleed. After addressing life-threatening injuries,
         the PAWS portion of the framework should be completed.
         3-98. Following the MARCH-PAWS sequence guides Service members through the rapid casualty
         assessment and CLS through the trauma assessment. This involves either a rapid casualty assessment or a
         full tactical trauma assessment; both aimed at identifying and treating all life-threatening conditions and
         serious wounds. Rapid and accurate evaluation of casualties is crucial for providing effective first aid.

Rapid Casualty Assessment
34B




         3-99. When a casualty has transitioned from CUF into TFC, the Service member should treat all immediate
         and potential life threats discovered during the rapid casualty assessment. The rapid casualty assessment,
         performed by all Service members, is very similar to the tactical trauma assessment, which is performed by
         the CLS. Once the Service member has treated all immediate and potential life threats, the PAWS portion of
         the rapid casualty assessment should be performed, and all other injuries treated. These may include head
         injuries, eye trauma, fractures, and burns, among others.

Tactical Trauma Assessment
35B




         3-100. The CLS utilizes the tactical trauma assessment (a more in-depth assessment compared to the rapid
         casualty assessment) to reassess any hemorrhage control measures (hasty TQs) initiated in the CUF phase by
         first responders and identify any injuries that have not yet been treated. The tactical trauma assessment
         follows the MARCH-PAWS sequence, allowing the CLS to systematically evaluate and address any
         remaining life-threatening injuries and secondary injuries.
MEDICAL EQUIPMENT AND DOCUMENTATION FOR TACTICAL COMBAT CASUALTY CARE
52B




         3-101. Service members carry a large array of equipment, and survival on the battlefield depends heavily on
         the ability to properly use that equipment. One piece of equipment that is critically important is the joint first
         aid kit (JFAK), which is a standardized medical assembling.

               Note. The Army uses the individual first aid kit (IFAK) instead of the JFAK.


Medical Equipment
36B




         3-102. The JFAK contains both medical and documentation materials. Essential medical supplies for TCCC
         are typically found in the Service member's first aid kit or Service-specific first aid kit. It's vital for all Service
         members to be familiar with the contents and location of these kits, as well as any maintenance procedures
         for trauma supplies required by their unit. See Appendix A for further discussion on first aid kits.
