text:
Chapter 3



           3-103. CoTCCC-identified equipment required to treat injuries and conditions to execute specific aspects of
           the MARCH-PAWS sequence and can be found in the following chapters—
               • Chapter 4 Massive Bleeding.
               • Chapter 5 Airway Control.
               • Chapter 6 Respiration and Breathing control.
               • Chapter 7 Circulation Control.
               • Chapter 8 Hypothermia Prevention.
               • Chapter 9 Secondary Assessment.

Medical Documentation
37B




           3-104. The JFAK includes documentation material, primarily the DD Form 1380. This form is the standard
           for documenting all assessment and treatment provided to casualties before evacuation or handoff to medical
           personnel.
           3-105. Every piece of equipment in the JFAK is evidence-based, drawing from lessons learned in recent
           overseas contingency operations. The JFAK's contents support the provision of TCCC per current guidelines
           and enable first responders or CLS to address issues identified in various phases of casualty care. Each
           Service may have additional items in a Service-specific first aid kit. See Appendix A for Service-specific
           equipment.

Combat Lifesaver Aid Bag
38B




           3-106. The CLS carries a compact aid bag containing supplies for controlling bleeding, relieving tension
           pneumothorax, and performing other essential procedures. For a current list of supplies in the aid bag, refer
           to the medical materiel information portal website. CLS bags should be issued for training events and
           operational deployments.
           3-107. It's the responsibility of each CLS to:
               • Ensure their aid bag is stocked per the prescribed packing list.
               • Verifying all stocked items are serviceable and not expired.
               • Allocate aid bag supplies as needed.

                 Note. All supplies and materials required for CLS training should be obtained through normal
                 supply channels.

           3-108. The CLS should prioritize using the casualty’s first aid kit before using supplies from the CLS bag if
           the casualty's kit is depleted.
           3-109. Medical units should maintain stocks of medical materiel for resupplying CLS aid bags during
           operations. Resupply procedures during deployment mimic those during home station operations, involving
           bag inventories, supply requests, and emergency resupply from nearby medical units capable of helping.
MAINTENANCE AND RESUPPLY
53B




           3-110. Conducting precombat inspections or readiness checks is paramount for every piece of equipment
           carried or used by Service members. The readiness and serviceability of contents in first aid kits, CLS bags,
           or unit-specific kits can be a matter of life or death. Regular inspections before, during, and after training
           events and combat missions are crucial. Unit leaders should anticipate Class VIII resupply kits based on
           casualty estimates, and routine inventories must be conducted to ensure all required material is present.

Seals and wrappers
39B




           3-111. Replace items with broken or unsealed wrappers. If an item was vacuum sealed upon issuance but is
           no longer sealed during inspection, it should be replaced.

text:
Fundamentals of Tactical Combat Casualty Care



Check expiration dates
340B




          3-112. Medications and many medical-grade materials, such as hemostatic dressings, have expiration dates
          and lot numbers. Check all medications and medical-grade items for expiration dates and replace any expired
          items or those whose expiration dates do not extend beyond the expected deployment period. While items
          like TQs typically do not have expiration dates, ensure they are CoTCCC-approved, serviceable, reflect the
          current generation, and have not been replaced with newer models.

Unapproved or Fake Equipment
341B




          3-113. Only a few items in the first aid kit require specific recommendations from the CoTCCC. Ensure that
          kits are stocked only with CoTCCC-recommended or approved items and be wary of unapproved equipment.
          Beware of fraudulent manufacturers producing fake, misleading, or substandard medical equipment,
          especially TQs and hemostatic dressings.


                                                         CAUTION
                       Avoid deploying with equipment that is missing, expired, or previously
                       used in training.


Unit-Specific Evacuation Equipment
342B




          3-114. Unit-specific evacuation equipment may include ropes, harnesses, packing materials for mountain or
          extreme cold conditions, life jackets, or flotation devices. It's essential to incorporate precombat inspections
          of these unit-specific items into the unit's SOPs. After ensuring all specialized gear is accounted for, proceed
          to inspect litters for proper functioning and serviceability. Additionally, check the litter straps to ensure their
          locking functions and placements are correct. Inspect special evacuation equipment according to the
          manufacturers' instructions or unit guidelines and standards.

title: U.S. Army: Casualty Response, Tactical Combat Casualty Care, and First Aid (ATP 4-02.11)
text:
Chapter 4
                                      Massive Bleeding Control

OVERVIEW OF MASSIVE BLEEDING CONTROL
208B




          4-1. The number one medical priority in TCCC is early control of severe bleeding. Extremity hemorrhage is
          the most frequent cause of preventable battlefield deaths. Understanding the human body and how it works
          along with how casualties survive in combat results in efficient and proper TCCC skills application and an
          increased survivability of combat casualties.
          4-2. Injury to a major blood vessel can quickly lead to shock and death. Only life-threatening extremity
          bleeding warrants intervention during CUF (if the tactical situation allows). Casualties with injuries to large
          blood vessels in the extremities (such as the femoral artery in the thigh, or the brachial artery in the upper
          arm) can result in death in as little as three minutes if bleeding is allowed to continue. If life-threatening
          bleeding is encountered at the junctional areas (neck, axillary, or inguinal) treatment with a hemostatic
          dressing is not performed until the casualty transitions to TFC.
          4-3. Treatment priorities should follow MARCH-PAWS, with massive bleeding (M) always being the most
          important. The treatment priorities are not a linear process; if at any time massive bleeding is not controlled,
          go back to M.
          4-4. The initial casualty evaluation should be a rapid head-to-toe check for any unrecognized life-threatening
          bleeding (a blood sweep). This blood sweep is a systematic way to ensure rapid identification of any
          unrecognized life-threatening bleeding, and should include a visual and hands-on (palpation) inspection by
          checking the—
               • Neck.
               • Axillary (armpit).
               • Inguinal (groin).
               • Legs.
               • Arms.
               • Back.
          4-5. The priority in caring for a casualty, should be to identify and stop life-threatening bleeding and prevent
          them from bleeding to death. Bleeding is considered life-threatening when—
               • There is pulsing or steady bleeding from the wound.
               • The overlying clothes are soaked with blood.
               • Blood is pooling on the ground.
               • There is a traumatic amputation of an extremity.
               • Bandages or makeshift bandages used to cover the wound are ineffective and are steadily becoming
                   soaked with blood.
               • There was prior bleeding, and the patient is now in shock (unconscious, confused, and pale).
          4-6. A TQ is immediately needed when any of the above examples are present on an extremity. Injury to a
          major vein or artery can result in shock or death from blood loss in minutes. Extremity (arm or leg)
          hemorrhage is a leading cause of preventable combat death. Using TQ(s) to stop the bleeding is essential to
          the survival of casualties with these types of injuries.
          4-7. During CUF a TQ is the only medical intervention available to stop life-threatening bleeding from an
          extremity injury. Other wounds (such as neck, armpit, groin, or abdomen) are not treated during CUF. If the
          casualty is able, direct them to apply pressure to the wound as self-aid. Airway and other issues are not treated
          until the TFC phase.
          4-8. It may be difficult to determine whether hemorrhage is life-threatening until the TFC phase when the
          wound can be exposed and evaluated. A suspected life-threatening hemorrhage is immediately treated.
          4-9. During CUF, if a casualty shows to have massive bleeding, from an extremity, a hasty TQ is applied
          “high and tight” on the injured extremity and then cover should be acquired as quickly as possible. The

text:
Chapter 4



           equipment in the casualty’s first aid kit should be used and not that of the responder. Do not put a TQ directly
           over the knee or elbow, over a holster, or cargo pocket that contains bulky items.
           4-10. Direct pressure can and should be used as a temporary measure until a TQ or dressing is in place. It is
           difficult to use direct pressure alone to control significant bleeding or while moving the casualty. Direct
           pressure can be used if treatment no longer maintains control of the bleeding while a new treatment is started.
           4-11. In CUF, consider placing one or more hasty TQs in a “high and tight” manner to an arm or leg to control
           massive life-threatening bleeding. This should be accomplished in less than one minute. If the casualty is
           conscious, the responder should direct the casualty to render self-aid and apply a TQ to themselves, if they
           have one. A TQ applied in the CUF must be re-evaluated in TFC.
           4-12. To effectively perform first aid, Service members need a fundamental understanding of the key body
           systems, including their structures and functions. Knowledge of the respiratory, circulatory, and
           musculoskeletal systems is crucial as it helps in assessing injuries and providing the appropriate first aid
           without causing further harm to the casualty. Familiarity with these systems also aids in recognizing when
           they are damaged or not functioning properly. Injuries to or compromises of these vital systems can lead to
           severe, permanent injury or even death. Therefore, a solid grasp of these systems not only supports effective
           first aid intervention but also helps prevent intensifying the casualty's condition.
CIRCULATORY SYSTEM
54B




           4-13. The heart and the blood vessels (arteries, veins, and capillaries) circulate blood throughout the body.
           The heart is divided into two separate halves, each acting as a pump. The left side pumps oxygenated blood
           (bright red) through the arteries into the capillaries. Nutrients and oxygen pass from the blood through the
           walls of the capillaries and into the cells. At the same time, waste products and carbon dioxide leave the cells
           and enter the capillaries. From the capillaries, the blood is carried through the veins to the right side of the
           heart and then into the lungs where it expels the carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen. Blood in the veins is
           dark red because of its low oxygen content. Blood does not flow through the veins in spurts as it does through
           the arteries. The entire system of the heart, blood vessels, and lymphatics is called the circulatory system.
BLOOD VESSELS
5B




           4-14. The body has a complex network of blood vessels that are crucial for blood circulation. These vessels
           are three main types. First, arteries take oxygen-rich blood from the heart and branch into smaller arterioles,
           eventually leading to tiny capillaries. Next, capillaries play a key role in exchanging oxygen, nutrients, and
           wastes between blood and tissues. The blood, now lacking oxygen, moves into small veins called venules,
           which combine to form larger veins. Lastly, veins are responsible for carrying blood back to the heart,
           completing the circulation process.
           4-15. The blood vessels in the body are all connected and work together. They help deliver oxygen and
           nutrients to every part of the body and get rid of waste materials. This shows how each type of blood vessel
           depends on the others, highlighting their important roles in a Service member’s overall health.
BLOOD
56B




           4-16. Blood is a mixture of plasma (liquid component), white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. The
           body contains about 5 to 6 quarts (about 5 liters) of blood. Once blood is pumped out of the heart, it takes 20
           to 30 seconds to circulate through the body and return to the heart.
           4-17. Blood performs essential functions as it circulates through the body. It delivers oxygen and essential
           nutrients (such as fats, sugars, minerals, and vitamins) to the body's tissues. It carries carbon dioxide to the
           lungs and other waste products to the kidneys for elimination from the body. In addition, it carries
           components that fight infection and stop bleeding.

title: U.S. Army: Casualty Response, Tactical Combat Casualty Care, and First Aid (ATP 4-02.11)
text:
Massive Bleeding Control




                                                       WARNING
                      If bleeding is not stopped, excessive blood loss can quickly lead
                      to the death of the casualty. It is imperative that first aid providers
                      quickly determine if a casualty is losing blood. Many injuries can
                      result in blood vessels being torn which result in excessive blood
                      loss.


HEARTBEAT
57B




         4-18. The heart functions as a pump to circulate blood continuously through the blood vessels to all parts of
         the body. It contracts, forcing the blood from its chambers. The heart then relaxes, permitting its chambers
         to refill with blood.
         4-19. The rhythmical cycle of contraction and relaxation is called the heartbeat. The normal heart rate
         (heartbeats per minute) varies based on the age and physical condition of the individual at rest. For example—
             • Adults: 60 to 100 heartbeats per minute.
             • Children (1 to 6 years): 70 to 120 heartbeats per minute.
             • Infants (6 to 12 months): 80 to 140 heartbeats per minute.
             • Infants (0 to 5 months): 90 to 140 heartbeats per minute.

               Note. The typical pulse for Service members and athletes is 40 to 60 heart beats per minute and is
               lower than the average adult population due to physical conditioning.

         4-20. It is common for a Service member’s pulse to be elevated above the normal range during combat
         operations as this is both a stressful and high exertional state. Elevated pulse in combination with suspected
         injuries causing hemorrhage suggests developing shock.
PULSE
58B




         4-21. The heartbeat causes a rhythmical expansion and contraction of the arteries as it forces blood through
         them. This cycle of expansion and contraction can be felt (monitored) at various points in the body and is
         called the pulse. The common points for checking the pulse are at the—
              • Side of the neck (carotid).
              • Groin (femoral).
              • Wrist (radial).
              • Ankle (posterior tibial).

               Note. DO NOT use your thumb to check a casualty’s pulse because you may confuse the beat of
               your own pulse with that of the casualty.



                                                       WARNING
                      It is imperative that first aid providers quickly determine if the
                      casualty has a pulse (heartbeat). Absence of a pulse (heartbeat)
                      will lead to the death of the casualty if not quickly restored.


         4-22. The literature on combat casualty care raises questions about the reliability of traditional blood pressure
         measurements as indicators of specific pulse types. However, it underscores a crucial reality: as hemorrhage
         severity increases, more central pulses are likely to be lost, demanding prompt and decisive intervention.
         Identifying and responding to these central pulses swiftly is imperative in managing severe hemorrhage and
         ensuring the best possible outcomes for casualties.

Carotid Pulse
34B




            4-23. To ascertain the carotid pulse, locate the pulse on the casualty's neck nearest to you. Gently place the
            tips of your first two fingers alongside their thyroid cartilage, commonly referred to as the Adam's apple (see
            figure 4-1). This method allows for an effective assessment of the pulse, rhythm, and strength.

Femoral Pulse
34B




            4-24. To assess the femoral (groin) pulse, apply gentle pressure with the tips of your first two fingers to the
            center of the groin area (see figure 4-2). This method enables you to accurately detect the presence and
            strength of the femoral pulse.




                       Figure 4-1. Carotid pulse                              Figure 4-2. Femoral pulse


Radial Pulse
345B




            4-25. To ascertain the radial (wrist) pulse, position your first two fingers on the side of the casualty's wrist
            where the thumb is located (see figure 4-3 ). This technique allows for a precise assessment of the radial
            pulse's presence and strength.

Posterior Tibial Pulse
346B




            4-26. To assess the posterior tibial (ankle) pulse, position your first two fingers on the inner side of the
            casualty’s ankle (see figure 4-4). This method enables a reliable examination of the posterior tibial pulse’s
            rhythm and strength.

title: U.S. Army: Casualty Response, Tactical Combat Casualty Care, and First Aid (ATP 4-02.11)
text:
Massive Bleeding Control



EQUIPMENT USED FOR MASSIVE BLEEDING CONTROL
209B




          4-27. Specialized equipment plays a crucial role in effectively managing massive bleeding, offering
          immediate and life-saving interventions. TQs, junctional tourniquets, hemostatic agents, hemostatic gauze,
          and pressure dressings, are among the tools used for this purpose. These items form integral components of
          the TCCC approach to massive bleeding control, empowering military personnel to address severe
          hemorrhage swiftly and efficiently in the field and enhancing the likelihood of survival for wounded
          individuals.
TOURNIQUETS
59B




          4-28. TQs serve as critical devices for halting severe bleeding from extremities, such as arms or legs, by
          effectively restricting blood flow when applied higher to the injury site, thus preventing further blood loss.
          4-29. Considered the most vital lifesaving item in the first aid kit, TQs should be kept easily accessible and
          ready for use during combat missions. The "TQ, Nonpneumatic Combat Application One-Handed,"
          commonly known as the combat application TQ, is the most prevalent type in military inventory, featuring
          key components such as the windlass rod for twisting and tightening, a windlass clip to secure the rod, a
          windlass safety strap for added security, and a routing buckle for TQ band management after looping it
          around an arm or leg.
          4-30. It's imperative that all personnel deployed on combat missions have a CoTCCC recommended TQ
          readily available in a standard location on their battle gear and are trained in its proper usage. Additionally,
          casualties should be capable of easily and swiftly accessing and applying their own TQs, emphasizing the
          importance of not storing TQs at the bottom of the pack, and prioritizing the use of the casualty’s first aid kit
          TQ first.
HEMOSTATIC DRESSING AND WOUND PACKING
60B




          4-31. Hemostatic dressings, engineered with clotting agents like kaolin or chitosan, are purpose-built to
          staunch bleeding efficiently. These dressings are either packed directly into deep or narrow wounds or applied
          directly onto a bleeding wound, accelerating blood clotting far more effectively than traditional dressings.
          4-32. When severe bleeding is noted from a junctional area, such as the neck, axillary or inguinal locations
          of the body (areas were TQs cannot be applied) hemostatic dressings should be used for massive bleeding
          control. It's essential to note that they should not be used inside the abdomen or chest, where emergency
          bandages or other trauma dressings are more appropriate.
          4-33. Each first aid kit is typically equipped with one hemostatic dressing and one dry sterile gauze. The
          hemostatic dressings recommended by the CoTCCC are known to be safe and include active ingredients that
          help blood to clot at the wound site. Hemostatic dressings are available in various types, one type of
          hemostatic dressing is impregnated with kaolin, another type contains celox granules, or the third type
          contains chitosan. Chitosan works by binding red blood cells and platelets to the surface of the dressing,
          enhancing clot formation. Importantly, despite being derived from shellfish, chitosan does not trigger allergic
          reactions in individuals with shellfish allergies.
PRESSURE DRESSINGS
61B




          4-34. Pressure dressings play a crucial role in stemming bleeding by applying direct pressure on wounds.
          Typically comprised of an elastic bandage and a sterile pad, they are placed over the wound and securely
          fastened to maintain pressure on the injured area. These dressings not only aid in blood clotting but also
          compress the open blood vessel, assisting in controlling bleeding effectively. After bleeding has been
          stemmed with a hemostatic dressing or packing material, it's imperative to maintain pressure on the wound.
          This is achieved by applying a pressure dressing directly on top of the hemostatic dressing or packing material
          and wrapping it around the limb, ensuring comprehensive coverage of the wound and gauze applied
          previously.
          4-35. The CoTCCC-recommended emergency bandage or trauma dressing serves as a versatile solution for
          most wounds, particularly those not severe enough to require a TQ. These dressings can be used alone or in
          conjunction with other hemorrhage control methods, such as hemostatic gauze and normal gauze, to bolster
          their effectiveness in controlling bleeding by providing consistent pressure to the wound.

title: U.S. Army: Casualty Response, Tactical Combat Casualty Care, and First Aid (ATP 4-02.11)
text:
Chapter 4



TIER 1 SKILLS FOR MASSIVE BLEEDING CONTROL
210B




            4-36. The urgency of promptly stopping massive external bleeding cannot be overstated, as the longer a
            Service member bleeds from a major wound, the lower their chances of survival become. Severe injuries
            have the potential to cause death in as little as three minutes due to blood loss. During TFC, when evaluating
            the casualty for the location, type, and size of the wound or injury, it is essential to cut or tear their clothing
            and carefully expose the entire area of the wound. This procedure ensures proper visualization of the injury
            while minimizing the risk of further contamination. It's crucial not to touch the wound directly and to keep it
            as clean as possible to prevent complications. It's important to note that in a chemical environment, protective
            clothing should not be removed, and dressings should be applied over the protective clothing. The skills used
            by all Service members to control massive bleeding include the application of TQs, hemostatic dressings,
            and pressure bandages.
APPLICATION OF TOURNIQUETS
62B




            4-37. In combat scenarios, especially while under enemy fire, a TQ stands as the primary means to control
            massive extremity bleeding, enabling individuals, battle buddies, or combat medics to swiftly manage life-
            threatening hemorrhages until the casualty can be moved away from the firefight. Always prioritize treating
            life-threatening hemorrhage while seeking cover. The application of a TQ to a massive bleed is time-
            sensitive, with the TQ aiming to halt bleeding within one minute and be fully secured within three minutes,
            casualties with uncontrolled massive bleeding can succumb within these initial minutes. Expecting pain
            during application is crucial as it signifies proper TQ application.
            4-38. The casualty may need to apply a one-handed TQ (see figure 4-5) to an upper extremity when applying
            self-aid. One-handed TQs are used to apply self-aid for bleeding from an injury to the upper arm or forearm.
            (One-handed windlass and one-handed ratchet TQs are the TQs of choice; they are effective and can be
            applied quickly).




                                      Figure 4-5. Windlass and Ratchet Tourniquets
            4-39. A hasty TQ is implemented as "high and tight" on the wounded extremity or when the bleeding source
            is ambiguous during the CUF phase. However, during TFC, all TQs should be deliberate, placed two to three
            inches above the wound directly on the skin, not over clothing. Once the casualty is in a safer position, the
            bleeding source should be reassessed, and the effectiveness of the TQs verified. If bleeding remains
            uncontrolled, a second TQ may be necessary, particularly for severe bleeding wounds of the thigh.
            4-40. It is crucial to recognize that TQs should be used cautiously, with the optimal safe duration being less
            than two hours. Beyond this timeframe, tissues may start to die, potentially leading to limb loss after six
            hours. Regular reassessment of TQ effectiveness is necessary, including checking for stopped bleeding,
            absent distal pulse, and ensuring no pulse below the TQ on the limb. Common errors when applying TQs
            include not using one, when necessary, not tightening it adequately, and using it for minimal bleeding.
            Additionally, TQs should never be removed except by medical personnel at a higher role of care. If the source
            of massive bleeding is evident, such as from an amputation or major wound, immediate bleeding control
            measures like applying a TQ or wound packing should be initiated, especially in areas where a TQ cannot be

   Service Members, CLS, and medical personnel.
   4-41. One-Handed (Windlass) TQ Application CUF:
       • Remove TQ from JFAK and/or carrying pouch.
       • Insert the wounded extremity through the loop of the self-adhering band.
       • Position the TQ above the bleeding site, high on the extremity over the clothing/uniform.
       • Ensure that all the slack in the self-adhering band is pulled through the routing buckle before the
           band is fastened back on itself and the windlass is twisted.
       • Twist the rod until bleeding has stopped (complete steps 1-5 in under 1 min).
       • Lock the windlass rod in place with the windlass clip.
       • Route the self-adhering band around the rod and between the clips.
       • Secure the windlass safety strap.
       • If no other major bleeding is present, move to cover.

         Note. Do not document the TQ application time until the TFC phase.

   4-42. One-Handed (Ratchet) TQ Application CUF:
       • Remove TQ from the JFAK and/or carrying pouch.
       • Insert the wounded extremity through the loop of the TQ band.
       • Position the TQ above the bleeding site, high on the extremity over the clothing/uniform.
       • Grasp the TQ loop with your teeth (or if able lean against a hard surface) to prevent slipping when
           tightening.
       • Tighten the TQ strap as much as possible.
       • Lift the lever arm of the ratcheting buckle and tighten by ratcheting the TQ until bleeding has
           stopped (complete steps 1-5 in under 1 min).
       • Lock the ratchet on itself (it will click into place).
       • If no other major bleeding is present, move to cover.

         Note. If bleeding is not controlled, continue to ratchet the maneuver device until bleeding has
         stopped. Do not document TQ application time until the TFC phase.

   4-43. Two-Handed (Windlass) TQ Application CUF:
       • Remove TQ from JFAK and/or carrying pouch.
       • Insert the wounded extremity through the loop of the self-adhering band or route the band around
           the limb, passing the tip through the slit of the routing buckle.
       • Position the TQ above the bleeding site, high on the extremity over the clothing/uniform.
       • Ensure that all the slack in the self-adhering band is pulled through the routing buckle before the
           band is fastened back on itself and the windlass is twisted.
       • Twist the rod until bleeding has stopped (complete steps 1-5 in under 1 min).
       • Lock the windlass rod in place with the windlass clip.
       • Route the self-adhering band around the rod and between the clips.
       • Secure the windlass safety strap.
       • If no other major bleeding is present, move to cover.

         Note. Do not document TQ application time until the TFC phase.

   4-44. Two-Handed (Ratchet) TQ Application CUF:
       • Remove the TQ from the casualty’s JFAK and/or carrying pouch.
       • Insert the wounded limb through the TQ strap loop or route the strap around the limb; pass the tip
           through the buckle.
       • Position the TQ above the bleeding site, high on the extremity over the clothing/uniform.
       • Pull the strap as tightly as possible, removing all excess slack.

           armpit, and groin, use a CoTCCC-recommended hemostatic dressing.

         4-51. Depending on the nature of the injuries, the first responder may need to pack wounds and apply a
         pressure bandage. Hemostatic dressings, containing special clotting agents, are ideal for wound packing to
         promote blood clotting. If hemostatic dressings are unavailable, gauze bandage can be used to pack wounds.

                                 Avoid packing wounds in the chest or abdomen.


         4-52. Pressure dressings are crucial for maintaining the effectiveness of hemostatic dressings, ensuring
         sustained pressure on the bleeding sources. In situations where pressure dressings are not available,
         maintaining firm, direct pressure is essential until medical assistance arrives.
         4-53. When applying a pressure bandage over a packed wound, use short tugs while wrapping and continue
         with tension. Care should be taken to avoid wrapping the bandage too tightly, ensuring the skin below remains
         pink and warm, with a present pulse.

                 Note. Service members assess tightness based on skin coolness and paleness rather than “capillary
                 refill.”

         4-54. Hemostatic dressings are only applied during the TFC phase. The steps for wound packing and pressure
         bandage are as follows:
             • Expose the wound, if not previously exposed.
             • Remove clothing and equipment as required.
             • Locate the source of the most active bleeding and apply direct pressure.
             • Remove the hemostatic dressing from its sterile package.
             • If a hemostatic dressing is not available, use gauze or clean, dry cloth material.
             • Pack the hemostatic dressing tightly into the wound directly over the site that has the most active
                 bleeding.

                 Note. Fill and pack the whole wound cavity tightly while keeping firm pressure on the wound.
                 More than one hemostatic dressing or gauze may be required to stop the blood flow.

                       place. Do not remove the object.

APPLICATION OF TOURNIQUETS
65B




         4-59. The CLS must possess proficiency in executing all Tier 1 massive bleeding control skills and be capable
         of directing or assisting Service members in their application. Emphasizing TQs as the primary method for
         bleeding control during CUF.
         4-60. During TFC, where time allows for thorough assessment, exposing the wound becomes feasible, aiding
         in and pinpointing the precise site of bleeding. Deliberate TQs applied in this phase, positioned two to three
         inches above the wound directly on the skin, optimize effectiveness while minimizing unnecessary impact
         on healthy tissue.
         4-61. The CLS conducts reassessment of TQs applied during CUF to ensure their efficacy. TQs hastily
         applied "high and tight" may need adjustment as medical personnel intervene, addressing the placement for
         optimal effectiveness.
         4-62. If bleeding persists despite a previously applied TQ, the CLS should promptly apply a second deliberate
         TQ adjacent to the original, positioned higher on the limb. Bleeding cessation is expected within one minute,
         with full TQ securing achieved within three minutes. Any life-threatening bleeding not identified during CUF
         warrants immediate intervention with a TQ, hemostatic, or pressure dressing.
         4-63. Documenting the time of TQ placement on both the TQ itself and the DD Form 1380 during TFC,
         rather than CUF, is crucial for subsequent medical personnel. Care should be taken to avoid placing TQs
         over joints or pockets containing bulky items, ensuring the TQs effectiveness.
APPLICATION OF HEMOSTATIC DRESSING
6B




         4-64. While hemostatic dressings should be packed into wounds of the limbs, when the source of bleeding is
         too high on the limb for TQ application (such as the neck, armpit, and groin) they should NOT be packed
         into the abdomen or chest. For compressible (external) hemorrhage, places where a TQ cannot be effectively
         applied, use a CoTCCC-recommended hemostatic dressing.
         4-65. Although the hemostatic dressing contains the active hemostatic agents, direct pressure must be applied
         for at least three minutes. Non-CoTCCC-recommended supplies may be available; however, they have not
         been shown to be effective in controlling massive hemorrhaging.
APPLICATION OF DIRECT PRESSURE
67B




         4-66. After packing the wound with a hemostatic dressing or gauze, hold direct pressure for three minutes.
         Direct pressure can and should be used as a temporary measure until a TQ or dressing is in place. It is difficult
         to use direct pressure alone to control significant bleeding, or while moving the casualty. While packing a
         wound, maintain constant, direct pressure, at the source of the bleeding to be effective.
APPLICATION OF WOUND PACKING
68B




         4-67. Wounds should not be blindly packed. Effort must be taken to locate the source of bleeding and apply
         direct pressure immediately while preparing the gauze.
         4-68. Wound packing:
             • Identify and expose the wound.
             • Locate the source of the most active bleeding and apply direct pressure, while preparing the
                 hemostatic dressing.
             • Remove the hemostatic dressing from its sterile package and pack it into the wound tightly, directly
                 over the site of the most active bleeding.
             • Fill and pack the whole wound cavity tightly while keeping firm pressure on the wound.
             • Ensure the hemostatic dressing extends one to two inches above the skin.
             • Hold continuous direct pressure for a minimum of three minutes.
             • Reassess the wound to ensure that the bleeding has stopped.
             • Apply a pressure bandage over the hemostatic dressing to secure it in place.
             • Reassess the wound to ensure that the bleeding has stopped. If blood is seeping through or around
                 the hemostatic dressing, the bleeding is not controlled, and the following steps should be applied:

           skin is cool. If circulation is blocked or stopped, loosen, and re-tie the bandage. Dressings and bandages

APPLICATION OF JUNCTIONAL PRESSURE
70B




           4-73. Junctional pressure is an alternative method to control bleeding. This method uses pressure to press at
           the site or point where a main artery supplying the wounded area lies near the skin surface or over bone (see
           figure 4-6 on page 55). These areas are known as junctional areas and are difficult to stop the bleeding even
           though the vessels are larger than in the extremities. Junctional areas are located at the junction of the
           extremities and neck with the torso.

text:
Massive Bleeding Control



EXPEDIENT TECHNIQUES FOR HEMORRHAGE CONTROL
21B




         4-78. Expedient techniques for hemorrhage control are of paramount importance in TCCC due to their ability
         to rapidly address life-threatening bleeding in high-stress and time-critical combat situations. Expedient
         techniques enable military personnel to intervene quickly and effectively control hemorrhage and prevent
         further blood loss. These techniques, such as the use of TQs, pressure dressings, and hemostatic agents, are
         specifically designed to be simple, easily applied, and accessible to all Service members, regardless of
         medical training. By swiftly initiating hemorrhage control, expedient techniques significantly increase the
         chances of survival, allowing injured individuals to receive timely care, and ultimately improving their
         overall mission success, and preserving the fighting strength of the military forces.
IMPROVISED TOURNIQUET
71B




         4-79. Using one of the CoTCCC-recommended TQs is the safe and preferred procedure for hemorrhage
         control. Improvised TQs are much less effective than commercially available TQs discussed in paragraph
         4-37 on page 48. Improvised TQs are difficult to make and apply without extensive practice, however they
         may be needed in situations where commercially produced TQs are unavailable, or supplies have been
         exhausted.


                                                      CAUTION
                      The risks associated with using improvised TQs include:
                      • Damage may occur to the skin if the band is too narrow.
                      • Bleeding may worsen.
                      • Bleeding may not be completely controlled.
                      • Likely to loosen overtime from not being properly secured.


         4-80. If a TQ is not available, pack the wound and hold direct pressure over the source of the heaviest bleed,
         FIRST. If this fails to control the bleeding in an arm or leg, only then consider an alternate improvised TQ.
         4-81. An alternate improvised TQ uses other materials on hand. In constructing one, it is recommended that
         you fold a cravat (or other pliable material) to a width of approximately 1 ½ to 2 inches and tighten it with
         some sort of windlass rod (a straight rod that can be used to twist the material tighter). Then secure the rod
         to ensure it does not loosen.

               Note. The cravat is included in the JFAK, however it is not part of the Army IFAK Generation 1
               or 2. To resource the cravat for the Army IFAK, the nomenclature is: Sterile Burn Dressing Cravat,
               NSN: 6510-01-587-6579; Muslin Compressed Bandage NSN: 6510-00-201-1755.

         4-82. An improvised TQ should not be used except as an absolute last resort when there is no other option to
         control life-threatening bleeding. If no TQ is available, pack the wound and hold direct pressure over the
         main source of bleeding.
         4-83. Continue to check the TQ, as improvised TQs are prone to loosening due to (but not limited to) casualty
         movement, shifting fluid, and quality of improvised material.
INGUINAL HEMORRHAGE CONTROL WITH AN IMPROVISED PRESSURE DELIVERY DEVICE
72B




         4-84. A pressure delivery device (PDD) is made using improvised materials, such as a shoe or boot, full water

     4-87. Inguinal (Groin) Hemorrhage Control with Improvised Junctional Pressure Device:
         • Consider body substance isolation.
         • Expose the injury and assess the bleeding source.
         • Apply direct pressure to the wound using a hand, fist, or elbow and open the hemostatic gauze
              package.
         • Tightly pack the wound with hemostatic gauze until the wound cavity is filled (finishing the packing
              within 90 seconds).
         • Hold pressure for a minimum of 3 minutes.
         • Reassess to ensure that the bleeding has been controlled while maintaining pressure.
         • If packed with hemostatic dressing, and extra hemostatic dressings are available, remove and repack.
         • If packed with gauze or initially packed with hemostatic dressing and no more hemostatic dressing
              is available, apply additional gauze and pressure (for three minutes) until bleeding stops.
         • Select and position a pressure delivery device, such as a canteen, into the inguinal gutter while
              maintaining pressure.
         • Select a TQ that can wrap around the casualty’s waist/hip area or connect the two tourniquets
              together.
         • Place the windlass or ratchet TQ directly over the middle of the pressure delivery device; ensure
              that the routing buckle is located towards the middle of the body.
         • Remove all slack from the band or strap using a pushing motion across the casualty’s body before
              tightening the TQ.
         • Tighten the TQ and ensure that the bleeding is still controlled, and the distal pulse is absent.


             Note. If the bleeding is not controlled and the distal pulse (a pulse located below the TQ) is present,
             remove any remaining slack in the strapping (if possible) and twist or ratchet the TQ device until
             bleeding is controlled and/or a distal pulse is absent.

               place and the windlass or ratchet is properly positioned over the device.

Chapter 5
                                                Airway Control

OVERVIEW OF AIRWAY CONTROL
213B




          5-1. After massive bleeding is controlled, the responder can move on to airway control, the first “A” in the
          MARCH-PAWS sequence. The casualty must have an open (unobstructed) airway. If the casualty is awake
          and talking, you can assume the casualty’s airway is open. However, the casualty may still have difficulty
          breathing. If the casualty is unconscious, their airway must be inspected for any obvious blockages.
          5-2. Humans must have oxygen to live. Through the breathing process, the lungs draw oxygen from the air
          and put it into the blood. The heart pumps the blood through the body to be used by the cells that require a
          constant supply of oxygen. Some cells are more dependent on a constant supply of oxygen than others. For
          example, cells of the brain may die within five minutes without oxygen. The brain, heart and lungs are very
          intolerant to lack of oxygen. The brain is considered one of the organs that is least tolerant to oxygen
          deprivation. Once these cells die, they are lost forever and do not regenerate. This could result in permanent
          brain damage, paralysis, or death.
          5-3. Airway obstruction on the battlefield is often due to facial trauma. If the casualty is breathing on their
          own but unconscious or semi-conscious, and there is no airway obstruction, further airway management is
          achieved through a nasopharyngeal airway (NPA). First responders must assess casualties with facial trauma
          when contraindications exist to NPA use (such as basilar skull fractures, disruption of the midface,
          nasopharynx, or roof of the mouth).
          5-4. Unconscious casualties can also lose their airway as the muscles of their tongue may have relaxed. This
          causes the tongue to block the airway by sliding to the back of the mouth and covering the opening to the
          windpipe. The signs and symptoms of airway obstruction include:
               • Casualty is in distress and indicating that they cannot breathe properly.
               • Casualty making snoring or gurgling sounds.
               • Visible blood or foreign objects are present in the airway.
               • Severe trauma to the face is observed.
RESPIRATION
73B




          5-5. Respiration is the process where we breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide. The efficiency
          of this process can vary depending on someone's age and physical health. Generally, adults breathe 12 to 20
          times a minute. But children and infants have different rates. For instance, children aged one to 10 years take
          15 to 30 breaths per minute. Infants who are six to 12 months old breath faster, at a rate of 25 to 50 times per
          minute. Meanwhile, the youngest infants, those aged zero to five months, have a rate of 25 to 40 breaths per
          minute.
ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY OF THE RESPIRATORY SYSTEM
74B




          5-6. The respiratory system consists of the airway, lungs, and rib cage. The airway consists of the nose,
          mouth, throat, voice box, and windpipe. Air passes to and from the lungs through the canal. The lungs are
          two elastic organs made up of thousands of tiny air spaces or sacs and covered by an airtight membrane. The
          bronchial tree is a part of the lungs. The rib cage is the structure that joins the spine in the back and the
          breastbone in front, which protects the heart and lungs. The top part of the rib cage is closed by the structure
          of the neck, and the bottom part is separated from the abdominal cavity by a large dome-shaped muscle called
          the diaphragm (figure 5-1 on page 60).

            5-7. The diaphragm and rib muscles, which are under the control of the respiratory center in the brain,
            automatically contract and relax. Inspiration increases and expiration decreases the size of the rib cage. When
            the rib cage increases and then decreases, the air pressure in the lungs is first less and then more than the
            atmospheric pressure, thus causing the air to rush into and out of the lungs to equalize the pressure.

EQUIPMENT USED FOR AIRWAY CONTROL
214B




            5-8. The CoTCCC-recommended NPA with lubricant is a nonsterile, rubber tube-shaped device that is
            inserted into the nostril of a casualty. It acts as a wedge to keep the airway open by keeping the tongue from
            falling back into the space behind the mouth leading to the windpipe. Only an NPA, size 32 French, is found
            within the standard issued JFAKs. Sizing the NPA before insertion is not necessary but is important to
            minimize nasopharyngeal trauma or elicit the casualty’s gag reflex. The lubricant is a water-based substance
            that assists in inserting the device into the nose. Use of an NPA is a Tier 2 skill.


                                                          CAUTION
                               Do NOT use blood or other body fluids to lubricate the NPA.


TIER 1 SKILLS FOR AIRWAY CONTROL
215B




            5-9. Tier 1 TCCC skills for airway control encompass techniques and procedures designed to address various
            challenges, including airway obstructions and respiratory distress. Proficiency in these skills is imperative
            for Service members operating in high-stakes, dynamic situations, and where swift and precise intervention
            can mean the difference between life, and death on the battlefield.
SAFELY POSITION THE CASUALTY TO OPEN THE AIRWAY
75B




            5-10. Check for responsiveness (figure 5-2 step A on page 61) and establish whether the casualty is conscious
            by gently shaking them and asking, “Are you OK?” Call for help (figure 5-2 step B on page 61) and then
            position the unconscious casualty so that they are lying in the recovery position, head tilted back; chin away
            from chest (figure 5-2 step C on page 61) by —
                • Straightening the casualty’s legs.
                • Moving the casualty’s arm that is nearest to you. Move it so that it is straight and above their head.
                     Repeat the procedure for the other arm placing it by their side.
                • Kneeling beside the casualty with your knees near their shoulders (leave space to roll their body).
                • Placing one hand behind their head and neck for support. On your other hand, grasp the casualty
                     under their arm (figure 5-2 step C on page 61).
                • Rolling the casualty towards you using a steady, even pull. The casualty’s head and neck should
                     stay in line with their back.

         5-12. Oxygen flows to and from the lungs requires an unobstructed airway, yet obstructions can arise due to
         various factors:

                •    Unconsciousness may lead to the tongue falling back into the throat, obstructing the airway if not
                     properly managed.
                •    Foreign objects, particularly food, may become lodged in the throat during eating, especially when
                     large pieces are swallowed without proper chewing, exacerbated by factors like alcohol

            5-13. Upper airway obstruction, a potentially life-threatening emergency, can occur as either a partial or
            complete blockage. The severity and nature of the obstruction underscore the importance of rapid recognition
            and immediate intervention to prevent respiratory compromise. Identifying the signs early and responding
            effectively are crucial in maintaining the airway and supporting breathing, which are vital for the casualty's
            survival. This situation demands prompt and decisive action to alleviate the obstruction and ensure an open
            airway.

Partial Airway Obstruction
349B




            5-14. The casualty may still have an air exchange. A good air exchange means that the casualty can cough
            forcefully, though they may be wheezing between coughs. The rescuer should not interfere and should
            encourage the casualty to cough up the object obstructing their airway on their own. Weak coughing with a
            high-pitched noise between coughs may indicate a poor air exchange. You should assist the casualty and treat
            them as though they had a complete obstruction.

Complete Airway Obstruction
350B




            5-15. A complete obstruction (no air exchange) is indicated if the casualty cannot speak, breathe, or cough
            at all. They may be clutching their neck and moving erratically. In an unconscious casualty, a complete
            obstruction is also indicated if after opening their airway you cannot ventilate them. A casualty, experiencing
            a partial foreign body airway obstruction, with poor air exchange, or a complete airway obstruction will not
            survive without medical intervention. Both conditions are treated the same.
OPENING THE AIRWAY OF AN UNCONSCIOUS OR NOT BREATHING CASUALTY
7B




            5-16. The tongue is the single most common cause of an airway obstruction (see figure 5-3). In most cases,
            simply using the head-tilt/chin-lift or jaw thrust technique can open the airway. This action pulls the tongue
            away from the air passage in the throat (see figure 5-4).




                    Figure 5-3. Airway, blocked                              Figure 5-4. Airway, opened

            5-17. Call for help and then position the casualty. Move (roll) the casualty onto their back as described in
            paragraph 5-10 on page 60.

Jaw-Thrust Method
352B




            5-20. The jaw-thrust method may be accomplished by the rescuer grasping the angles of the casualty’s lower
            jaw and lifting with both hands, one on each side, displacing the jaw forward and up (see figure 5-6). The
            rescuer’s elbows should rest on the surface on which the casualty is lying. If the lips close, the lower lip can
            be retracted with the thumb. If mouth-to-mouth breathing is necessary, close the nostrils by placing your
            cheek tightly against them. The head should be carefully supported without tilting it backwards or turning it
            from side-to-side. If this is unsuccessful, the head should be tilted back slightly. The jaw-thrust is the safest
            first approach to opening the airway of a casualty who has a suspected neck injury because in most cases it
            can be accomplished without extending the neck.




                                Figure 5-6. Jaw-thrust technique of opening the airway

                  Note. If the casualty’s lips are still closed after the jaw has been moved forward, use your thumbs
                  to retract the lower lip, and allow air to enter the casualty’s mouth.

            5-21. The jaw-thrust method, commonly emphasized in training, can sometimes serve as a distraction in the
            field. Neck injuries in trauma cases are typically associated with dramatic incidents such as falls and motor
            vehicle accidents. Most neck injuries occur upon impact, and the extent of injury is usually immediate and
            unchangeable at the scene. If neck trauma is present, it is often necessary to perform a jaw-thrust maneuver
            to secure an airway and maintain that position until additional personnel arrive. This intervention allows the
            responder to proceed with the MARCH sequence.
MANAGING THE AIRWAY
78B




            5-22. If the casualty is breathing independently yet is unconscious or semiconscious, and there is no airway
            obstruction, managing the airway is best accomplished using an NPA. An NPA is suitable for both conscious
            and unconscious individuals and is effective in helping to open or maintain an open airway. This method
            ensures that the airway remains clear, facilitating easier breathing and potentially preventing further
            complications.
            5-23. Casualties with severe facial trauma can often protect their own airways by sitting up and leaning
            forward. Assisting a conscious casualty by helping them assume any comfortable sitting-up position that
            allows them to breathe easily. If the casualty is unconscious but breathing, the casualty should be placed in
            the recovery position (figure 5-7 on page 65).

          the addition of Tier 2 insertion of a nasopharyngeal airway and monitor the casualty for any signs of airway
          compromise, as outlined in paragraph 5-3. If the casualty shows signs of not breathing spontaneously, it's

          CLS in administering breathing assistance using a bag valve mask (BVM) device, as depicted in figure 5-8.

          administered a sedating pain medication, might indicate an injury or condition warranting earlier or
          immediate evacuation (such as severe traumatic brain injury or TBI). If definitive treatment or evacuation is
          not available, consider triaging the casualty to expectant if resources are limited or better applied to more
          likely survivable casualties.

          “E-C” holding technique (figure 5-9 on page 66). The mask is sealed over the casualty’s mouth so that air
          does not escape (figure 5-10 on page 66). The mask is then squeezed firmly for one to two seconds and five

EXPEDIENT TECHNIQUES FOR AIRWAY CONTROL
217B




            5-28. Expedient techniques for airway control are critically important in TCCC due to the immediate threat
            posed by compromised airways in combat situations. Injured Service members may experience airway
            obstructions, respiratory distress, or loss of consciousness, which can rapidly progress to life-threatening
            situations. Expedient airway control techniques, such as the head tilt/chin lift, jaw thrust maneuver and use
            of NPAs may enable prompt restoration of adequate breathing and oxygenation. These techniques can be
            quickly implemented by trained personnel, ensuring timely intervention even in chaotic and high-stress
            environments. By swiftly addressing airway compromises, through the use of expedient techniques in TCCC
            play a vital role in preserving life, preventing further complications, and maximizing the chances of survival
            for injured military personnel on the battlefield.
OPENING THE OBSTRUCTED AIRWAY – CONSCIOUS CASUALTY
79B




            5-29. Clearing an airway obstruction in a conscious casualty can be managed while they are either standing
            or sitting. However, it's critical to recognize that an obstructed airway can lead to oxygen deficiency in the
            brain, resulting in respiratory arrest, unconsciousness and, if not promptly corrected, death.
            5-30. To assess and manage airway obstruction, start by asking the casualty if they can speak or if they are
            choking. Additionally, check for the universal choking sign (see figure 5-11 on page 67). If the casualty can
            speak or cough effectively, encourage them to continue coughing. This indicates that they still have good air
            exchange, and you should not interfere with their efforts to expel the obstruction.

80B




         5-35. When an individual who is choking becomes unresponsive while lying down, or if an unconscious
         person is discovered and the cause of their condition is unknown, specific emergency protocols must be
         followed to address potential airway obstruction.
         5-36. If a conscious individual begins choking and subsequently loses consciousness, immediate action is
         required:
             • Summon help right away to ensure assistance is on the way.
             • Open the casualty's airway to assess and manage the obstruction.
             • Perform a finger sweep only if there is visible obstruction in the mouth to avoid pushing the
                   obstruction deeper.
             • Attempt to rescue breathing, which involves assessing whether the air can flow into the lungs. Refer
                   to detailed instructions on mouth-to-mouth resuscitation provided in paragraph 6-49 on page 81. If
                   breathing efforts fail due to a blockage, swiftly move to clear the airway using procedures outlined
                   in paragraph 5-39.
         5-37. In scenarios where a casualty is found already unresponsive, the procedure slightly differs:
             • Quickly assess the situation to understand the context and severity.
             • Call for immediate assistance.
             • Position the casualty on their back to manage and secure the airway effectively.
             • Check for a pulse to determine the urgency of cardiovascular support.
             • Open the airway using recommended techniques.
             • Confirm if the casualty is not breathing and, if so, proceed to attempt rescue breathing as per the
                  guidelines detailed in paragraph 6-49 on page 81.
         5-38. These critical steps are designed to maximize the chances of recovery by ensuring that the airway is
         cleared, and that breathing is restored at the earliest possible opportunity. Quick and effective intervention is
         crucial in such emergencies, underscoring the importance of thorough training and readiness.

             finger on the lower edge of the casualty’s breastbone.
         • Place the heel of the other hand on the lower half of the breastbone next to the two fingers
             (figure 5-16 step B on page 71).

             breastbone, extending or interlocking the fingers (figure 5-16 step C on page 71).

Chapter 6
                              Respiration and Breathing Control

OVERVIEW OF RESPIRATION AND BREATHING
218B




          6-1. After establishing an open airway, it is important to evaluate the casualty's respirations and maintain that
          airway in an open position. This is the “R” of MARCH-PAWS. Respiratory distress means difficulty
          breathing (rapid or abnormally slow breathing), in other words, it is difficult for the casualty to get air in or
          out. Airway and respiration are not addressed in CUF; however, they must be addressed in TFC.
          6-2. The pleural space between the lungs and chest wall naturally has negative pressure, which helps the
          lungs to collapse (exhale) and expand (inhale). With either a blunt or penetrating injury to the chest wall or
          lungs, air may counteract the lung’s natural tendency to expand and collapse. This is due to positive pressure
          replacing negative pressure. It results in air being trapped in the pleural space, putting pressure on the affected
          lung. This forces the lungs to collapse and reduces the ability to get oxygen to the body.
          6-3. While it may be easy to see a gunshot wound or shrapnel wound to the chest, it is important to evaluate
          casualties for additional injuries from blunt force trauma which may have been caused from an explosive
          device or from the chest hitting the steering wheel during a high-impact vehicle accident.
          6-4. Signs of future life-threatening respiration issues include bruising, contusions (swelling around the chest,
          back, or rib cage), crepitus (crackling, popping, grating) that are felt or heard, or other deformities of the
          chest not normally seen without removing the clothing. Signs of respiratory distress include:
               • Difficulty in breathing.
               • Struggling to get air in and out.
               • Breathing is too weak to be effective (less than six times per minute).
               • Rapid breathing (greater than 20 times per minute).

                Note. The above signs may also indicate a penetrating chest wound injury. Report findings of
                respiratory distress to medical personnel.


EQUIPMENT USED FOR RESPIRATION AND BREATHING
219B




CONTROL
          6-5. In TCCC, various specialized equipment is used to address respiration and breathing control in combat
          situations. These tools are designed to promptly manage compromised airways and provide respiratory
          support. The primary equipment used includes:
               • NPA.
               • BVM.
               • Chest Seal.
               • 10–14-gauge catheter over needle device.
          6-6. An NPA is a flexible tube inserted through the nose into the oropharynx to maintain an open airway and
          facilitate adequate breathing. It is particularly useful when there is a risk of tongue obstruction or in cases
          where the patient is conscious and able to maintain their own airway.
          6-7. A BVM device consists of a self-inflating bag and a mask that is manually squeezed to deliver positive
          pressure ventilation. It is used when there is a need for artificial respiration to support or control the patient's
          breathing.
          6-8. A chest seal is an airtight dressing that is applied over a penetrating chest wound to prevent the entry of
          air into the pleural cavity, reducing the risk of a tension pneumothorax. It allows for the restoration of normal
          respiratory function by maintaining appropriate chest pressure. The CoTCCC-recommended chest seal is a
          vented (preferred) self-adhering chest seal (see figure 6-1 on page 74) is used for treating and sucking chest
          wounds or open pneumothorax.

           6-17. At this point in the MARCH-PAWS protocol, the responder's role is to carefully roll the casualty to
           examine both the front and back of the torso for any signs of chest trauma. It is crucial for the responder to
           identify and acknowledge if the casualty has a potentially life-threatening chest injury that is causing
           respiratory distress. The responder must then effectively communicate these findings to the medical
           personnel arriving on the scene, ensuring that the casualty receives the appropriate medical attention
           promptly.

TIER 2 SKILLS FOR RESPIRATION AND BREATHING CONTROL
21B




           6-18. The Tier 2 skills do not replace all Service member skills for respiration and breathing control. The
           CLS must reassess respiration and breathing control in TFC and start more advanced respiration and
           breathing control interventions. The CLS must be ready to treat an open pneumothorax, a tension
           pneumothorax, and identify if the treatment for those injuries was successful.
OPEN PNEUMOTHORAX
81B




           6-19. An open pneumothorax is also known as a sucking chest wound. An open pneumothorax occurs when
           air enters the pleural space. The pleural space is the thin area between the lungs and chest wall.
           6-20. When a casualty experiences penetrating torso trauma the elastic lung deflates and pulls away from the
           chest wall. If the hole, through the chest wall, is at least the size of a nickel or 2/3 the diameter of the trachea,
           on inspiration, the air now enters the chest through the hole instead of into the lungs through the normal
           airways of the mouth and nose. As a result, the affected lung cannot be fully re-inflated by inhalation.
           6-21. An open pneumothorax usually occurs with a hole in the chest the size of a nickel or bigger. Not all
           chest wounds are sucking chest wounds; some do not penetrate as deeply as the lung cavity.
           6-22. The first responders check the casualty's respiration and ability to breathe. All open or sucking chest
           wounds are treated by immediately applying a vented chest seal to cover the defect. If a determination cannot
           be made if the wound has penetrated the chest wall completely, treat the wound as though it were an open
           chest wound. A casualty with an open chest wound will exhibit one or more of the following signs and
           symptoms:
               • A “sucking” or “hissing” sound when the casualty inhales.
               • Difficulty breathing.
               • A puncture wound of the chest.
               • Froth or bubbles around the injury.
               • Coughing up blood.
               • Blood-tinged sputum (spit).
           6-23. For respiratory distress not resolved by a chest seal or in a casualty with known or suspected chest or
           back trauma without an open sucking chest wound, consider a tension pneumothorax, and perform a needle
           decompression of the chest (NDC). Injuries to the chest are very serious and can be life-threatening. The
           casualty's condition can change quickly with a chest injury.
           6-24. An open chest wound should be treated with a CoTCCC- recommended commercial chest seal found
           within the first aid kit, which maybe vented or non-vented. Vented chest seals are for treating penetrating
           wounds to the chest. The vented chest seals allow air to escape out of the chest while non-vented chest seals
           do not. The injured lung will remain partially collapsed, but the mechanics of respiration will be better.
           6-25. Recommended treatment for open or sucking chest wounds is prompt application of a vented chest seal.
           If a vented chest seal is NOT available, a non-vented chest seal should be used. When the casualty inhales,

TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX
82B




         6-29. Tension pneumothorax is caused by significant torso (chest) trauma, or a blast injury resulting in severe
         and progressive respiratory distress. Progressive difficulty breathing is labored, and rapid breathing worsens
         overtime.
         6-30. A tension pneumothorax is the second-leading cause of preventable deaths on the battlefield. As a
         tension pneumothorax develops, air enters the chest cavity through the wound with every inspiration but does
         not leave with expiration and is trapped. Every breath adds more air to the air space inside the rib cage and
         outside the lung, and the pressure inside the chest builds up (figure 6-4).

                                            Figure 6-4. Tension Pneumothorax
           6-31. When a lung is injured, it can act like a one-way valve, trapping air between the lung and chest wall.
           This trapped air builds pressure, potentially compressing both lungs and the heart, impairing their function
           and leading to respiratory distress and shock. In tension pneumothorax, this elevated pressure stops the lungs
           and heart from expanding normally, which can be fatal. Signs of tension pneumothorax vary from early to
           late stages:
                • Early signs include:
                     ▪ Increasing difficulty breathing over time.
                     ▪ Shortness of breath.
                     ▪ Confusion, lightheadedness, or agitation from low oxygen.
                     ▪ Bluish discoloration around the mouth and lips.
                     ▪ Rapid pulse.
                • Late signs, which may appear as the condition worsens, include:
                     ▪ Swollen neck veins.
                     ▪ Tracheal deviation (the windpipe shifting to one side).
                     ▪ Severe difficulty breathing, often with chest pain or anxiety.
           6-32. These signs might be hard to detect in a combat situation. Responders must be vigilant for tension
           pneumothorax if there is any chest wound accompanied by increasing breathing difficulties.
           6-33. It's crucial to monitor these signs during TFC. Like controlling bleeding, treating a tension
           pneumothorax is crucial; if left untreated, it can lead to severe respiratory issues, shock, and death. The initial
           treatment for a suspected tension pneumothorax is NDC. After this, any chest injury, whether an open
           pneumothorax or tension pneumothorax, needs further evaluation by medical personnel and likely evacuation
UNSUCCESSFUL TREATMENT OR RECURRENCE OF TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX
83B




           6-34. Casualties with a tension pneumothorax must be continuously monitored for reoccurring symptoms.
           The condition may initially be treated unsuccessfully and then spontaneously recur. The immediate remedy
           for the unsuccessful treatment or recurrence of a tension pneumothorax is to burp the chest seal, if one is in
           place.
           6-35. If initial treatment of tension pneumothorax with NDC does not result in improvement, a second NDC
           should be attempted at the alternate recommended site. If tension pneumothorax initially responds to NDC,
           but symptoms later recur, then repeat NDC at the same site right beside the original NDC. If no improvement
           is noted after the second NDC, proceed with circulation assessment and treatment following the MARCH-
           PAWS protocol.

        6-39. Expedient techniques for respiration and breathing control in TCCC are crucial for immediate and

PENETRATING CHEST INJURIES
84B




           6-40. Penetrating chest injuries involve the intrusion of foreign objects such as bullets, knives, or projectiles
           through the chest wall, penetrating into the thoracic cavity. This breach can lead to severe damage to vital
           structures including the lungs, heart, major blood vessels, or other organs within the thoracic cavity.
           6-41. Penetrating chest injuries can result in significant internal bleeding, pneumothorax (collapsed lung),
           hemothorax (accumulation of blood in the chest cavity), tension pneumothorax (air buildup under pressure
           in the chest), or cardiac tamponade (compression of the heart due to blood accumulation). They are
           considered severe and life-threatening, requiring immediate intervention to stabilize the casualty and prevent
           further complications. Penetrating chest injuries can also be referred to as an open chest wound.
           6-42. A CoTCCC vented commercial chest seal is the preferred type of chest seal. However, if one is
           unavailable, a non-vented commercial chest seal may be applied in the same manner as a vented commercial
           chest seal. If there is not a commercial chest seal available, the following examples can be used as occlusive
           (airtight) materials:
                • Plastics such as the outer wrapper of the emergency dressing from the first aid kit.
                • The combat ration packing.
                • Cellophane.
           6-43. An improvised chest seal may be used to treat an open chest wound by—
               • Wiping any dirt, blood, or sweat from the skin with gauze or any available clothing.
               • Instructing the casualty to fully exhale and then place the inner surface of the outer wrapper or other
                   occlusive material directly over the wound.

                   Note. Do not touch the inner surface of the occlusive material. Ensure that the edges of the
                   occlusive material extend two inches beyond the wound.

               •     Applying two-inch tape from the casualty’s first aid kit to three sides of the occlusive material and
                     secure it firmly to the casualty’s chest. Leave the side nearest to the ground un-taped.
               •     Rolling the casualty on their side or have the conscious casualty sit up and examine the back for any
                     wounds.
               •     Checking the casualty for any wounds on the back and treating it as a chest injury with a large
                     improvised occlusive chest seal (such as the plastic wrapper from the emergency dressing in the first
                     aid kit).
               •     Placing the casualty in a position of comfort (usually sitting) if conscious, or in the recovery position
                     (on the casualty’s side) with the injured side down if unconscious.
               •     Continuing to monitor the casualty for signs of respiratory distress (increased difficulty breathing).

                   Note. If the casualty has increased difficulty breathing, lift the chest seal, release any trapped air
                   by wiping blood or debris from the wound, and reseal or replace the chest seal upon exhalation.

EXTERNAL CHEST COMPRESSIONS
85B




           6-44. External chest compressions, also known as Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR), in combat
           casualties is nearly always the result of hemorrhagic or obstructive shock, neither of which will respond to
           standard CPR. Conducting CPR may delay definitive treatment in nearly all cases. The CoTCCC guidelines
           recommend performing bilateral needle decompression and expedite blood product administration. Mission
           variables or the credentialed provider may guide exceptions to this rule in support of CPR on combat
           casualties. The administration of CPR on a combat casualty should be a rare circumstance and not the
           standard of care in this trauma population.
           6-45. CPR is conducted using a specific technique to provide manual circulation support during cardiac arrest
           or when the heart has stopped beating effectively. A general outline of the steps involved in conducting
           external chest compressions is:
               • Position: Ensure the person is lying on a firm, flat surface, such as the ground or a CPR board. Kneel
                    beside the person's chest.
