             •    Hand Placement: Place the heel of one hand on the center of the person's chest, between the nipples.
                  For infants or children, use two or three fingers instead of the entire hand.
             •    Compression Depth: Press down firmly and smoothly. For adults, compress the chest at least two
                  inches (five centimeters) deep. For infants or children, compress the chest about one-third to one-
                  half of its depth.
             •    Compression Rate: Perform compressions at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute. This
                  equates to about two compressions per second.
             •    Complete Chest Recoil: Allow the chest to fully recoil between each compression, without lifting
                  your hands off the chest. This allows the heart to refill with blood.
             •    Compression to Ventilation Ratio: If you are performing CPR alone, do cycles of 30 chest
                  compressions to two rescue breaths (mouth-to-mouth or mouth-to-mask). If there are two rescuers,
                  the ratio can be 30:2 or continuous chest compressions with ventilation being delivered by the other
                  rescuer.
             •    Continue until Help Arrives: Keep performing chest compressions until professional medical help
                  arrives, or until the person shows signs of movement or starts breathing.
         6-46. It is important to note that these steps provide a general overview of external chest compressions.
         Proper CPR training and certification are needed to gain a thorough understanding of the technique and to
         ensure accurate and effective application during emergency situations.
         6-47. The duration of CPR can vary depending on the circumstances and response of the individual being
         treated. In general, CPR should be continued until one of the following conditions is met:
              • Signs of Life: If the person shows obvious signs of life, such as breathing normally, coughing, or
                   moving, CPR can be stopped.
              • Professional Medical Help Arrives: CPR should be continued until professional medical personnel
                   take over the resuscitation efforts.
              • Provider Fatigue: If the person performing CPR becomes too exhausted to continue effectively, they
                   can switch with another trained individual to maintain the quality of compression.
         6-48. In many cases, CPR is performed continuously without interruptions until one of the above conditions
         is met. However, it is important to note that high-quality chest compressions are crucial for improving the
         chances of survival. Therefore, proper training in CPR techniques and regular updates on the latest guidelines
         are recommended to ensure effective and efficient resuscitation efforts.
RESCUE BREATHING
86B




         6-49. Rescue breathing, also known as artificial ventilation, is a technique used in CPR to provide oxygen to
         a person who is not breathing or has inadequate breathing. It involves delivering breaths into the person's
         lungs to support their respiratory function. Rescue breathing is conducted executing the following:
             • Position: Ensure the casualty is lying on a flat surface, preferably with their head tilted back slightly
                  to open the airway.
             • Clear the Airway: Check for any visible obstructions in the person's mouth or throat, and if present,
                  gently remove them if possible.
             • Seal the Mouth: If the casualty's mouth is open, use your hand to gently lift the chin upward to
                  maintain an open airway. With your other hand, pinch the person's nose closed to prevent air from
                  escaping.
             • Breathing Technique: Place your mouth over the casualty's mouth, forming a seal, and blow into
                  their mouth while watching for the chest to rise. Deliver the breath over one second and make sure
                  it is sufficient to visibly inflate the chest.
             • Breathing Rate: Provide rescue breaths at a rate of about one breath every five to six seconds
                  (10 to 12 breaths per minute).
             • Chest Recoil: Allow the chest to fully recoil between breaths. This enables the chest to return to its
                  resting position, which helps in the exchange of gases during respiration.
             • Continue Until Help Arrives: Perform rescue breathing until professional medical help arrives or
                  until the person starts breathing on their own.
         6-50. There are several methods for rescue breathing, each suitable for different situations and age groups.
         The main methods include:

              mouth with their own and delivering breaths into their lungs.
         •    Mouth-to-Nose: Used when the casualty's mouth is injured, obstructed, or inaccessible, the rescuer
              closes the casualty's mouth and breathes into their nose to create a seal.
         •    Mouth-to-Mask: In situations like professional CPR or with specialized equipment, a pocket mask
              or BVM device is used. The mask covers the casualty's mouth and nose, and the rescuer delivers
              breaths by squeezing the bag or using the valve.
         •    Mouth-to-Stoma: For individuals with a tracheostomy or a surgical stoma in the neck for breathing,
              rescue breaths can be delivered directly into the stoma using the rescuer's mouth or a specialized
              device.
     6-51. It is important to note that the technique and ratio of rescue breaths may vary depending on the age of
     the person receiving CPR (such as an adult, child, or infant) and the specific guidelines in the area or
     operation. Proper training in CPR techniques, including rescue breathing, is crucial to ensure accurate and
     effective administration of artificial ventilation during emergency situations.
     6-52. It is important to follow the specific guidelines and protocols for rescue breathing based on the person's
     age, condition, and the resources available. Proper training and certification in CPR techniques are essential
     to gain proficiency in rescue breathing and to ensure the best possible outcomes during resuscitation efforts.

Chapter 7
                                            Circulation Control

OVERVIEW OF CIRCULATION CONTROL
23B




         7-1. Hemorrhage control assessment and management in TFC falls under the “C,” for Circulation, in the
         MARCH-PAWS sequence. The body requires good blood flow throughout, and a lack of good blood flow
         may cause the casualty to go into hypovolemic shock.
         7-2. Hemorrhage control in the TFC phase takes place after massive bleeding control that occurs in the CUF
         phase. It is possible that it did not occur, and this may be the first opportunity to address massive bleeding as
         well, so there is significant urgency. The first step is to reassess all prior hemorrhage control interventions
         for effectiveness.
         7-3. The casualty’s hemorrhage control interventions must be frequently reassessed to ensure continued
         hemorrhage control. This includes reassessments at frequent time intervals and any time the casualty is
         moved or the casualty’s status changes. The casualty must be continually watched for signs of shock.
         7-4. Controlling shock is the primary method of circulation control. Shock is the inadequate blood flow to
         body tissues. Inadequate blood volume inside the circulatory system results in inadequate oxygen delivery to
         the body’s cells. As cells, tissues, and organs cease to function, eventually the whole body will fail, and death
         follows.

               Note. Hypovolemic shock can also result from blood loss due to internal bleeding into the
               abdominal or chest cavity. The first responder or CLS will not be able to control internal bleeding.
               This condition requires rapid evacuation of the casualty.

         7-5. Shock is caused by a decrease in the amount of blood volume circulating in the casualty's blood
         circulatory system. Shocks can have many causes such as:
              • Low blood volume or hypovolemia (such as dehydration or blood loss).
              • Low blood pressure.
              • Heart failure (pump failure).
              • Neurologic damage (infection, allergic reaction).
              • Obstructive causes (such as tension pneumothorax or pericardial tamponade causes obstruction of
                  the heart).
INDICATORS OF SHOCK
87B




         7-6. Shock is usually caused by severe bleeding, but it can also be caused by severe burns classified as partial
         thickness burns (2nd degree) or full thickness burns (3rd degree) on 20 percent or more of the body surface.
         On the battlefield, assume shock is from severe blood loss (also called hemorrhagic shock). The signs and
         symptoms of shock include:
              • Mental confusion.
              • Weak or absent radial pulse.
              • Rapid breathing.
              • Nausea.
              • Sweaty, cool, or clammy skin.
              • Excessive thirst.
              • Pale or gray skin.
              • Previous severe bleeding

PREVENTION OF SHOCK
8B




           7-8. It is more effective to prevent shock through hemorrhage control than to treat it once it has developed.
           Even in cases where shock is already present, the most critical first action is to control any bleeding.
           Continuously reassess all bleeding control measures, such as tourniquets and pressure dressings, to ensure
           they remain effective and are adjusted tightly as soon as possible. This is a crucial step in treating shock.
           7-9. Internal bleeding caused by blunt or penetrating trauma to the chest or abdomen may not be immediately
           controlled and can lead to shock later on. Continuous assessment of the casualty is essential. Even if a casualty
           is not currently in shock but has sustained serious injuries, they should be carefully monitored for signs of
           developing shock. It's important not to wait until signs and symptoms of shock appear. While medical
           personnel will provide comprehensive treatments, controlling any external bleeding early can save valuable
           time.

EQUIPMENT USED FOR CIRCULATION CONTROL
24B




           7-10. At present, no specialized equipment has been designated exclusively for managing circulation control.
           The equipment mentioned in the earlier section of this publication serves to support and enhance circulation
           control measures.

TIER 1 SKILLS FOR CIRCULATION CONTROL
25B




         7-11. The best way to prevent shock is to control bleeding. Responders should continuously monitor and
         reassess the effectiveness of bleeding control measures to ensure they are working, TQ application, wound
         packing with hemostatic dressing, a pressure dressing, or a combination of these.
         7-12. After reassessing TQs and hemostatic dressings, the TCCC guideline on shock states: “Assess for
         hemorrhagic shock” (altered mental status in the absence of brain injury or weak and absent radial pulse).
         Reassess all bleeding control measures are still effective and TQs remain tight.
BASIC MEASURES TO CONTROL CIRCULATION
89B




         7-13. Control bleeding and then take steps to prevent shock by elevating the casualty’s legs higher than the
         casualty's heart if their airway tolerates lying flat on their back.
         7-14. Conduct a bleeding re-check by:
             • Reassess every TQ and dressing that may have been applied earlier.
             • Expose the area and determine if bleeding is controlled.
             • Expose and clearly mark all TQ sites with the time of TQ application if not previously done.
             • When time and the tactical situation permit, check for further bleeding, and for pulses further out
                 on the limb than the TQ.
POSITION THE CASUALTY FOR SHOCK
90B




         7-15. Move the casualty under a permanent or improvised shelter to shade them from direct sunlight. If the
         casualty is conscious, place the casualty in the shock recovery position (see figure 7-1), which is on their
         back with their feet elevated slightly above the level of their heart. This will help their blood circulation. A
         log, field pack, box, rolled field jacket, or other stable objects can be used to elevate their feet. If a sitting
         position makes it easier for the casualty to breathe, that is fine.




                                         Figure 7-1. Shock recovery position
         7-16. The following steps will also significantly help in the prevention of shock:
             • Loosen clothing at the neck, waist, or anywhere is binding.


                                                        WARNING
                       Do not loosen clothing if in a chemically contaminated area.


             •     Prevent the casualty from getting chilled or overheated. Using a blanket or clothing, cover the
                   casualty to avoid loss of body heat by wrapping the blanket completely around the casualty.

                 Note. Ensure no part of the casualty is touching the ground, as this increases loss of body heat.

PRESSURE BANDAGE REASSESSMENT
93B




         7-21. The regular reassessment of pressure bandages is crucial in managing wounds effectively. The CLS are
         tasked with ensuring that there is no ongoing bleeding from the wound site. Additionally, it's important to
         check for circulation below the pressure bandage by feeling for a distal pulse—that is, a pulse found below
         the level of the bandage.
         7-22. If the skin below the bandage is cool, bluish, numb, or if the distal pulse is absent, these may be signs
         that the bandage is applied too tightly, potentially hindering blood flow. In such cases, the bandage should
         be loosened and then securely retied to ensure proper circulation is restored.
         7-23. All dressings and bandages must be checked routinely, especially every time a casualty is moved. This
         practice helps to monitor the effectiveness of the initial treatment and to make timely adjustments as needed.
         7-24. In situations where a pressure bandage or hemostatic dressing fails to control bleeding, a TQ should be
         applied approximately two to three inches above the site of bleeding, if feasible. If placing a TQ is not
         possible and the existing bandage is either ineffective or saturated with blood, replace it with a fresh
         hemostatic dressing. Ensure to pack the wound thoroughly with the hemostatic material, applying constant,
         direct pressure at the bleeding source for optimal effectiveness.

EXPEDIENT TECHNIQUES FOR CIRCULATION CONTROL
27B




         7-25. Medical personnel may not always be readily available. Nonmedical personnel must rely on
         themselves, other Service members’ knowledge, fundamentals of first aid for circulation control, until
         medical assistance arrives. This section will provide additional first aid, non-TCCC, procedures that
         nonmedical personnel can use for circulation control.
TECHNIQUES FOR NON-MEDICAL PERSONNEL
94B




         7-26. When medical personnel are not immediately available, non-medical personnel must depend on
         themselves and the knowledge of other Service members. The fundamentals of first aid for controlling
         circulation are crucial until professional medical help arrives. This section aims to provide essential, non-
         TCCC first aid procedures that non-medical personnel can use effectively to maintain circulation control.
         7-27. Non-medical personnel are often the first responders in critical situations, making it essential for them
         to be familiar with basic first aid techniques. Understanding and applying these methods can be lifesaving
         when delays in professional medical treatment occur. Training in these expedient techniques empowers
         individuals to act confidently and efficiently, providing critical care in emergencies.
         7-28. The guidance provided here includes several key first aid actions that non-medical personnel can take
         to manage circulation issues effectively. These include methods to minimize bleeding, stabilize the affected
         individual, and prepare for the arrival of medical professionals. Each technique has been chosen for its
         simplicity and effectiveness, ensuring that those with minimal medical training can apply them under
         pressure.
         7-29. It is vital for all personnel, especially those in high-risk environments, to be trained in these techniques.
         Such training ensures that every member of a team can provide essential care in emergencies, enhancing
         overall safety and increasing the likelihood of positive outcomes in critical situations.
TREATMENT FOR ANAPHYLACTIC SHOCK
95B




         7-30. Anaphylactic shock is a severe and life-threatening allergic reaction that significantly impacts the
         circulatory system. This medical emergency is marked by a swift release of histamines and other chemicals
         into the body, leading to vasodilation and increased permeability in blood vessels. Such changes can disrupt
         the adequate perfusion of vital organs and tissues, putting the casualty's life at great risk.
         7-31. Vasodilation, a key feature of anaphylactic shock, involves the relaxation of smooth muscle cells within
         blood vessel walls, causing these vessels to widen and blood pressure to drop significantly. This physiological
         process can rapidly deteriorate the casualty’s condition.
         7-32. The treatment of anaphylactic shock is urgent and time sensitive. Immediate actions include calling for
         medical help and, if available, using the casualty’s epinephrine auto-injector. Anaphylactic reactions can

     manifest within seconds or minutes after exposure to an allergen, affecting the skin, respiratory, and
     circulatory systems.
     7-33. Prompt recognition and response to anaphylactic shock are critical. Assessing both the signs and
     symptoms early on is essential for effective intervention. Quick and accurate identification of the condition
     allows for the necessary steps to be taken to mitigate its life-threatening effects.
     7-34. To effectively check for anaphylactic shock, Service members should follow a systematic approach:
         • Assess Symptoms:
              ▪ Observe for sudden and severe symptoms like difficulty breathing, wheezing, or shortness of
                  breath.
              ▪ Check for a rapid or weak pulse.
              ▪ Look for swelling of the face, lips, or tongue.
              ▪ Note any hives or widespread skin redness.
              ▪ Be alert to signs of confusion, dizziness, or loss of consciousness.
         • Ask Questions:
              ▪ Inquire about any known allergies or recent exposures to potential allergens.
              ▪ Ask if they have ingested or come into contact with a known allergen recently.
         • Observe Breathing:
              ▪ Check for signs of respiratory distress, such as rapid or labored breathing.
              ▪ Listen for wheezing or other abnormal breathing sounds.
         • Check Circulation:
              ▪ Assess the pulse to determine its rate and strength.
              ▪ Look for signs of poor circulation, such as pale or bluish skin.
         • Look for Other Symptoms:
              ▪ Be aware of nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, or a feeling of impending doom.
     7-35. If anaphylactic shock is suspected, immediate medical assistance is crucial. The primary treatment
     involves administering epinephrine (adrenaline). If an epinephrine auto-injector is available, assist the
     affected individual in using it, or administer it yourself if you are allowed and trained. Dosage guidelines are
     typically provided with the injector—0.15 milligrams (mg) for children and 0.3 mg for adults weighing more
     than 66 pounds.
     7-36. Further doses of epinephrine may be necessary, administered every 5 to 10 minutes if prescribed and
     symptoms persist. Additionally, provide supportive measures for treating shock, respiratory failure,
     circulatory collapse, or cardiac arrest:
          • Position the casualty supine with legs elevated if injuries permit.
          • Perform rescue breathing and external chest compressions if required.
          • Monitor vital signs every three to five minutes until the casualty is stable.
     7-37. Record all first aid actions on DD Form 1380 and request MEDEVAC immediately. Use CASEVAC
     only if MEDEVAC is unavailable and transport the casualty to the nearest MTF as soon as possible.
     Anaphylaxis is life-threatening, and immediate action is crucial. Seek professional medical help promptly
     and provide supportive care while awaiting arrival of medical personnel.

text:
Chapter 8
                                         Hypothermia Control

OVERVIEW OF HYPOTHERMIA CONTROL
28B




         8-1. The “H” in MARCH-PAWS stands for hypothermia prevention. Hypothermia begins when the body’s
         core temperature drops below 97° Fahrenheit (F). It can be mild (93-96°F), moderate (89-93°F), or severe
         (less than 89°F), depending on the temperature. To accurately diagnose hypothermia, the core temperature
         must be measured rectally with a special low-range thermometer, as mouth and ear measurements won't work
         well in cold environments.
         8-2. Hypothermia can be caused by being in a cold environment or by losing a lot of blood, a condition
         known as hypovolemia. This is when there’s a significant drop in the volume of blood circulating in the body.
         Both environmental exposure and loss of blood can lead to dangerously low body temperatures, which can
         be life-threatening if not treated.
         8-3. Environmental hypothermia happens when the body loses heat faster than it can produce it, often from
         being in cold weather for too long. Hypothermia from hypovolemic shock happens due to a large loss of
         blood or fluids, making it hard for the body to keep warm. Both causes can lead to serious health issues,
         including death, if not managed quickly.
         8-4. Hypothermia can happen suddenly, like from falling into cold water, or slowly, if someone is exposed
         to cold conditions for a long time. It can even happen in mild temperatures if a person is wet, which makes
         it easier to lose body heat. Factors like wet clothing, not enough food, exhaustion, and drinking alcohol or
         using drugs can make hypothermia worse.
         8-5. Massive bleeding can cause hypothermia, which in turn can cause more bleeding because cold
         temperatures can prevent blood from clotting properly. This is a problem even in warm weather, and
         especially for people in shock who can’t generate enough body heat. It’s crucial to stop this cycle to save the
         person’s life.
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS OF HYPOTHERMIA
96B




         8-6. In the TFC phase of care, the focus has shifted from immediate life-threatening hemorrhage control
         during CUF phase, to the reassessment of all previous interventions. This is followed by the prevention and
         treatment of other injuries and complications such as hypothermia. It is important to identify the signs of
         hypothermia. Some easily recognizable signs of hypothermia are:
              • Vigorous shivering is typically present.
              • Shivering may decrease or cease as the core temperature continues to fall.
              • Conscious, but usually apathetic or lethargic.
              • Confusion.
              • Sleepiness.
              • Slurred speech or mumbling.
              • Slow breathing and drowsiness.
              • Weak pulse.
              • Low or unattainable blood pressure.
              • Change in behavior with or without poor control over body movements, and with or without slow
                   reactions.
         8-7. The signs and symptoms of hypothermia may vary depending on the severity and can be categorized
         into mild, moderate, and severe stages:
              • Mild Hypothermia:
                  ▪ Shivering.
                  ▪ Cold and pale skin.
                  ▪ Numbness or tingling in extremities.
                  ▪ Fatigue and drowsiness.

FIRST AID FOR HYPOTHERMIA
97B




           8-8. The goals for first aid for hypothermia are to rescue, examine, insulate, and rapidly transport. If
           untreated, hypothermia is a true medical emergency and requires evacuation. Evacuate as soon as possible
           with the casualty lying down.


                                                         CAUTION
                            Do not allow the casualty to use tobacco, consume alcohol, or
                                                 caffeinated drinks.


           8-9. Re-warming techniques include—
                • Remove the casualty from the cold environment.
                • Replace wet clothing with dry clothing.
                • Cover the casualty with insulating material or blanket.
                • Wrap the casualty from head to toe.
                • Avoid unnecessary movement from the casualty.
                • If the casualty is conscious, slowly give high caloric sweet warm fluids.
                • Seek medical aid.
           8-10. Hypothermia is a serious condition that requires professional evaluation and treatment. Attempting to
           rewarm a severely hypothermic person should be done by medical professionals using appropriate
           techniques. While waiting for help to arrive, focus on preventing further heat loss and providing support to
           the person.
PREVENTION OF HYPOTHERMIA
98B




           8-11. Preventing hypothermia is critical in reducing the effects of heat loss and preventing deaths from
           uncontrolled bleeding. Immediate action to prevent hypothermia should commence right after an injury
           occurs. Without preventative measures, there is a real risk that a casualty may succumb to hemorrhage from
           a wound that could otherwise be survivable. As blood loss itself can lead to hypothermia, it is vital for first
           responders and CLS to control bleeding and actively engage in both passive and active measures to prevent
           the casualty’s body temperature from dropping.
           8-12. The quicker hypothermia prevention begins, the less severe its impact will be on the casualty’s bleeding
           and potential shock. Minimizing exposure to the elements is essential. Actions such as replacing wet clothing
           with dry ones and placing the casualty on an insulated surface should be prioritized. Environmental factors
           such as daily temperature fluctuations, nightfall, changes in altitude, and wind exposure must also be
           considered as they can significantly affect body heat retention.

title: U.S. Army: Casualty Response, Tactical Combat Casualty Care, and First Aid (ATP 4-02.11)
text:
Hypothermia Control



         8-13. Prevention of hypothermia is far more manageable than treating it once it has set in. Starting
         hypothermia prevention measures early is crucial because a decreased body temperature can adversely affect
         blood clotting processes, heightening the risk of continued bleeding—even in warm conditions.
         8-14. CLS personnel must be proactive in assuming that every casualty is at risk of developing hypothermia,
         utilizing all known prevention techniques. If a casualty is already hypothermic, the response should be even
         more aggressive, treating the condition as a direct threat to the casualty’s life.
MANAGEMENT OF HYPOTHERMIA
9B




         8-15. To prevent hypothermia, it is essential to keep the casualty warm, even in very hot environments. This
         is particularly crucial when a casualty is suffering from hemorrhagic shock due to blood loss, as they are at
         an extreme risk for developing hypothermia. Both active and passive methods should be employed to ensure
         the casualty's body temperature is maintained. This involves proactive measures such as providing thermal
         blankets, using heat packs, and minimizing exposure to cold or windy conditions. Maintaining warmth not
         only aids in preventing hypothermia but also helps stabilize the casualty’s overall condition.

EQUIPMENT USED FOR HYPOTHERMIA CONTROL
29B




         8-16. The hypothermia control equipment falls into either active warming (external source of heat) or passive
         warming blankets, or a poncho liner to treat or prevent hypothermia. The most common equipment seen is
         the hypothermia prevention and management kit, blankets, or ponchos.
ACTIVE HYPOTHERMIA MANAGEMENT AND MATERIAL
10B




         8-17. Medical personnel will distribute active hypothermia blankets based on the unit mission and load.
         Active hypothermia blankets are activated when their heating elements are exposed to air and can produce
         temperatures reaching 104° F for up to eight hours. Active hypothermia blankets are applied to a casualty
         who cannot generate their own heat, but not directly on their skin, because the activated blankets can cause
         burns.
         8-18. Apply the active warming blanket from the active hypothermia materials to the casualty’s torso, not
         directly on the skin, and cover the casualty with the passive hypothermia shell. Continue to reassess the
         casualty to determine if additional methods are needed to prevent or treat hypothermia. The heat reflective
         shell will help to retain the heat produced by the ready-heat blanket. It has an incorporated hood and Velcro
         closures down each side to allow exposure of an arm or a leg. Such exposure allows the medic to attend to
         IVs and TQs.
         8-19. If an active hypothermia device is not available, a combination of the passive warming blanket and
         active warming blanket may be used. Active hypothermia treatment uses heating sources such as the ready-
         heat blanket to warm the casualty. This requires a chemical reaction with oxygen, so at higher altitudes there
         may not be enough oxygen to sustain the chemical reaction required to generate heat.
         8-20. You must determine based on the environmental conditions whether the casualty needs both the outer
         shell and the heating blanket. It is sufficient to just keep them covered with the shell, because it is already
         hot outside.
         8-21. If no active rewarming equipment is available, then use passive warming devices that will retain heat
         and keep the casualty dry. The casualty should be assessed for hemorrhagic shock and ensure bleeding is
         controlled.


                                                      WARNING:
                      Active warming is contraindicated in a casualty who is showing
                      signs and symptoms of hyperthermia from heat related illness.

title: U.S. Army: Casualty Response, Tactical Combat Casualty Care, and First Aid (ATP 4-02.11)
text:
Chapter 8



PASSIVE HYPOTHERMIA MANAGEMENT AND MATERIAL
10B




            8-22. Passive hypothermia blankets are designed to retain the casualty’s body heat by enclosing them within
            a thermal barrier, keeping them off the cold ground. While passive strategies prevent further cooling, they do
            not actively warm the casualty. Therefore, it's critical to avoid placing the casualty directly onto cold, wet,
            or damp surfaces; instead, a blanket or poncho should be positioned underneath them to provide insulation.
            In the absence of specialized re-warming equipment, dry blankets, poncho liners, sleeping bags, or similar
            items should be used to retain heat and keep the casualty dry and elevated from the ground.
            8-23. Key considerations include recognizing that blood loss can significantly reduce body temperature, even
            in warmer climates. When using a blanket or any passive heating material, it is crucial to wrap the casualty
            completely, including their head, but ensure the face remains uncovered to prevent breathing obstructions.
            Leaving any part of the body exposed can result in heat loss and worsen hypothermia. These measures are
            vital in managing a hypothermic casualty, especially in the absence of active warming tools.

TIER 1 SKILLS USED FOR HYPOTHERMIA CONTROL
230B




            8-24. The first responder must prevent, and address hypothermia compounded by massive blood loss. This
            is not hypothermia due to cold weather, but can be prevented by—
                 • Keeping clothing or uniform on the casualty.
                 • Replacing extremely wet clothing if possible and keeping the casualty dry.
                 • Keeping the casualty off the ground, by placing a barrier between the casualty and the ground or
                     lifting them off the ground, if possible.

                    Note. Contact with the ground increases loss of body heat.

                •     Using dry blankets, poncho liners, sleeping bags, or anything that will retain heat.
                •     Minimizing the casualty’s exposure to the environment.

TIER 2 SKILLS USED FOR HYPOTHERMIA CONTROL
231B




            8-25. The Tier 2 TCCC skills emphasize advanced yet practical approaches to managing battlefield casualties
            under hypothermic conditions. Personnel trained in Tier 2 TCCC are equipped with the knowledge and skills
            to effectively use available medical equipment to prevent and treat hypothermia. This includes the application
            of specialized gear such as hypothermia prevention and management kits, which are designed to maintain
            body temperature and prevent further heat loss in injured soldiers. In addition, Tier 2 personnel are trained
            to monitor vital signs closely, ensuring that the core body temperature is maintained within a safe range,
            thereby reducing the risk of hypothermia-related complications.

EXPEDIENT SKILLS USED FOR HYPOTHERMIA CONTROL
23B




            8-26. In situations where standard medical supplies are not available, field expedient techniques for
            hypothermia control become crucial. Soldiers are taught to use their environment and available resources to
            prevent and manage hypothermia. For instance, using space blankets or even regular blankets to wrap the
            victim can significantly reduce heat loss. If these are not available, utilizing materials such as leaves, grass,
            or even newspapers as insulation can be a life-saving improvisation. Creating a barrier between the victim
            and the cold ground, such as with a sleeping pad, backpack, or any available material, can also prevent further
            body heat loss. These improvised methods are essential skills in TCCC, enabling soldiers to provide effective
            hypothermia care even in resource-limited settings.

23B

SYMPTOMS, AND TREATMENTS
          9-1. As discussed in paragraph 3-96 on page 39, PAWS is the second part of the MARCH-PAWS casualty
          assessment and is conducted after the MARCH portion. The MIST reporting was introduced as a standard
          component of the MEDEVAC request during Operation Enduring Freedom in Afghanistan.
          9-2. While not officially part of the NATO and U.S. standard MEDEVAC request, MIST reporting has
          become customary in some operations. Often referred to as the 10th line in the 9-line MEDEVAC request,
          the completed DD Form 1380 serves as the MIST report. However, the high volume of casualties expected
          during large scale combat operations may make it challenging to complete MIST reporting for each casualty.
          9-3. The MIST report facilitates the transfer of medical information to the receiving health care provider by
          providing a structured approach to the casualty handoff. A MIST report delivers additional evacuation
          information that might be required by theater commanders and assists the receiving MTF in preparing for
          specific inbound casualties. However, transmitting a MIST report for each casualty during operations and
          mass casualty incidents may not always be timely or feasible.
MANAGEMENT OF PAIN AND ANTIBIOTICS
102B




          9-4. The combat wound medication pack (CWMP) is both the “P” (pain) and the “A” (antibiotics) in the
          MARCH-PAWS sequence. Pain is common with battlefield injuries. Some injuries and levels of pain can be
          treated safely by using pain medications (also known as analgesics) in the CWMP. These include fractures,
          burns, and eye injuries.
          9-5. The CWMP is a prepackaged medication packet with drugs and dosages specifically chosen for use in
          combat casualty care. The CWMP contains drugs for mild to moderate pain (Meloxicam and Acetaminophen)
          and an antibiotic specific for penetrating wounds (Moxifloxacin). The CWMP should be used only for combat
          related injuries and is not for routine use. It may be procured through medical logistics systems as a pre-
          packaged blister pack or, may be locally packaged by medical personnel.
          9-6. For pain relief on the battlefield of mild to moderate pain that will not keep the casualty out of the fight,
          ensure they take their CWMP. The casualty should take all three medications in the CWMP. This can give
          significant pain relief and will not alter the casualty’s mental status. This is a good option when the casualty’s
          pain and wounds are not severe enough to keep them out of the fight.

                Note. If the casualty has wounds or pain severe enough to render them unable to fight, then medical
                personnel have other options for more effective pain relief. The medications given by medical
                personnel will generally require that the casualty be disarmed because the medications can alter
                the casualty’s mental status.

          9-7. CWMP is a prepackaged pill pack containing CoTCCC-recommended medications for use in combat
          casualty care. The CWMP is found in the casualty’s first aid kit. It contains medications for pain and
          antibiotics that can be taken by mouth.
          9-8. The medication in the CWMP should be taken as soon as possible after life-threatening conditions have
          been addressed. All medications administered should be documented along with the time given on the DD
          Form 1380.

            9-9. The CWMP contains the following components:
                 • Two 500mg caplets of acetaminophen (total 1,000mg) in extended-release form.
                 • One 400mg tablet of moxifloxacin.
                 • One 15mg tablet of meloxicam.
            9-10. Each of the three medications in these dosages is contained in a blister pack.

                  Note. The popular nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin
                  interfere with platelet function and blood clotting and can significantly increase the risk of
                  bleeding in combat casualties.

            9-11. Acetaminophen and meloxicam do not alter platelet function and are safe and effective for use in
            combat casualties. Meloxicam does not alter platelet function and is the preferred Non-Steroidal Anti-
            Inflammatory Drug for personnel who may see combat in the next 7-10 days.
            9-12. The CWMP should be given when the casualty:
                • Is conscious and able to swallow.
                • It has mild to moderate pain.
                • Is still able to fight if needed.
                • Has any penetrating wounds or break of the skin.
            9-13. The CWMP should NOT be given if the casualty:
                • Is unable to swallow or take oral meds, such as when the casualty is unconscious, or has severe
                    facial trauma, or burns.
                • Has known allergies to the CWMP medications.
                • If the casualty is unconscious, refer them to medical personnel as soon as possible.

                  Note. If the casualty has a break in the skin in a traumatic injury, they should take the CWMP.
                  Otherwise, consult with medical personnel before giving it.

            9-14. Battlefield wounds are often dirty and susceptible to infection. Early administration of antibiotics from
            the CWMP may reduce the chance of later infections. Wound infections can kill the casualty or delay their
            recovery. The CWMP should be given as soon as possible for wounds after life-threatening issues have been
            addressed.
MANAGEMENT OF WOUNDS
103B




            9-15. Beyond MARCH, there are additional or secondary injuries that should be identified and may need
            treatment. The secondary injuries identified in TCCC are organized by eye trauma, head injury, burns, and
            fractures. These secondary injuries are treated in TFC.
            9-16. Wound management is the “W” in the MARCH-PAWS sequence. Once the casualty's hemorrhage has
            been controlled, earlier control interventions are completed, and wound management must be rechecked. All
            wounds must be frequently reassessed to ensure continued hemorrhage control.
            9-17. The first responder or CLS should confirm all wounds have been addressed and reassess for re-bleeding
            under gauze or bandages to ensure bleeding has been controlled. The first responder or CLS must look for
            blood flowing around or under TQs, bandages, and dressings. If the bleeding has not been controlled, tighten
            the TQ or pressure bandage for that wound if possible, and redress any wounds as necessary. Also, check
            other wounds to make sure that:
                • Eye injuries are shielded.
                • Open chest wounds are accounted for.
                • All wounds are wrapped.
                • Fractures are splinted.
            9-18. Wounds should always be monitored and frequently reassessed to ensure hemorrhage has been
            controlled. Any wounds that continue to bleed must be packed with new hemostatic dressing. Once the
            dressing has been applied with pressure for three minutes, carefully observe for blood continuing to flow

Chapter 10
                                                    Eye Trauma

OVERVIEW OF EYE TRAUMA
234B




          10-1. The eye is a vital sensory organ, and blindness is a severe physical handicap. Timely first aid for eye
          injuries may relieve pain and may help prevent shock, permanent eye injury, and possible loss of vision. The
          eye is very sensitive: any injury can be easily aggravated if it is improperly handled. Injuries in the eye may
          be quite severe. Cuts of the eyelids can appear to be very serious, but if the eyeball is not involved, a person's
          vision usually will not be damaged. However, lacerations (cuts) of the eyeball can cause permanent damage
          or loss of sight.
          10-2. Exposure to intense light can burn an individual. Infrared rays, eclipse light (if the casualty has looked
          directly at the sun), or laser burns cause injuries of the exposed eyeball. Ultraviolet (UV) rays from arc
          welding can cause a superficial burn to the surface of the eye. These injuries are generally not painful but
          may cause permanent damage to the eyes. Immediate first aid is usually not required. Loosely bandaging the
          eyes may make the casualty more comfortable and protect their eyes from further injury caused by exposure
          to other bright lights or sunlight. Eyesight is one of our most important senses. Damage to an eye can be
          irreversible if not treated correctly and as early as possible. The following signs should make you suspect a
          penetrating eye injury:
               • Bleeding surrounding the eye, inside the eyeball, or coming from the eyeball.
               • Obvious penetration of shrapnel or debris into the eyeball or eye socket.
               • Protruding objects from the globe of the eyeball.
               • Swelling or lacerations of the globe of the eyeball.
               • Protrusion of the globe of the eyeball from the eye socket.
               • Reduced vision and swelling of the eye area.
               • Misshapen or distorted parts of the eye from normal.

EQUIPMENT USED FOR THE TREATMENT OF EYE TRAUMA
235B




          10-3. The rigid eye shield is a barrier to environmental hazards and to protect the eye by providing a safe
          enclosure, until additional medical attention is available. The rigid eye shield is normally plastic or metallic,
          with a domed shape to enhance the protection of eye injuries, without applying pressure. It may be self-
          adhering or require tape. If a rigid eye shield is not available, or already used, the following may be used as
          an improvised or expedient rigid eye shield:
              • Protective glasses.
              • Clean cup.
              • Dip can.
          10-4. The Military Acute Concussion Evaluation 2 Card is an acute assessment tool for all medically trained
          personnel who treat Service members involved in a potentially concussive event. The Military Acute
          Concussion Evaluation 2 incorporates current state-of-the-science traumatic brain injury information, which
          looks at the systems in charge of integrating balance, vision, and movement.

TIER 1 SKILLS USED TO TREAT EYE TRAUMA
236B




          10-5. If a penetrating eye injury is seen or suspected, the first responder must shield the injured eye. The
          casualties injured eye must be covered with a rigid eye shield, not a pressure patch. In typical situations, a
          concave shield is placed over the injured eye, (not both eyes), and taped in place. If there is a protruding
          object in the eye, bandage in place — do not remove the object. Do not waste critical time by conducting
          further treatment. The casualty should be evacuated as soon as possible.

            10-6. The rigid eye shield is secured over the injured eye with tape at a 45-degree angle across the forehead
            and cheek. Rigid eye shields should be placed over both eyes only when you are sure and at least suspect that
            both eyes have been injured. If a rigid eye shield is not available, tactical eyewear may be used to protect the
            eyes from further trauma.

            movement. Movement has not been shown to worsen the outcome for the injured eye. Blindness, resulting
            from placing eye shields over both eyes unnecessarily, makes an otherwise ambulatory casualty a litter
            casualty, and is psychologically stressful. The first responder should be prepared to render first aid for
            lacerations of the eyelid, foreign bodies in the eye, extrusions of the eye, and chemical burns of the eye.
INITIATE FIRST AID FOR LACERATIONS OF THE EYELID OR EYEBALL WITH EYE-SHIELD
104B




            10-8. Lacerated or torn eyelids may bleed heavily, but bleeding usually stops quickly. Cover the injured eye
            with a sterile dressing. DO NOT put pressure on the wound because you may injure the eyeball. Handle torn
            eyelids very carefully to prevent further injury. Place any detached pieces of the eyelid on a clean bandage
            or dressing and immediately send them with the casualty to the medical facility.
            10-9. Lacerations or cuts to the eyeball may cause serious and permanent eye damage. Cover the injury with
            a loose sterile dressing. DO NOT put pressure on the eyeball because additional damage may occur.


                                                          CAUTION
                        DO NOT apply pressure when there is a possible laceration of the
                        eyeball. The eyeball contains fluid. Pressure applied over the eye will
                        force the fluid out, resulting in permanent injury. APPLY A
                        PROTECTIVE DRESSING WITHOUT ADDED PRESSURE.


            10-10. Survey the situation; if the injury is from chemical exposure, immediately wash the eye. Otherwise,
            DO NOT put anything on the eye ITSELF, especially if you think the eye is cut.
            10-11. If necessary, remove the casualty’s headgear. Position and treat the casualty as follows:
                • The conscious casualty will be placed in a seated position.
                • The unconscious casualty will be placed in a supine position with their head slightly elevated.
                • Gently clean any dirt or blood from the affected area around the eye.


                                                          WARNING
                        DO NOT put pressure on the eye or remove anything from the eye
                        surface. This could cause additional harm, such as loss of
                        eyesight or loss of the eye.


            10-12. Examine the eyes for the following:
                • Objects protruding from the eyes.
                • Look for foreign objects in or on the eyes and damage to the eyes.
                • Swelling or lacerations of the eyes.
                • Bloodshot appearance of the white of the eyes.
                • Bleeding—
                    ▪ Surrounding the eye.

          10-41. Injuries from chemical burns require immediate first aid. Mainly acids or alkalis cause chemical burns.
          The first aid measures consist of flushing the eyes immediately with large amounts of water for at least 5 to
          20 minutes, or as long as necessary to flush out the chemical and, once flushed, bandaging the eyes. If the
          burn is an acid burn, you should flush the eye for at least 5 to 10 minutes. If the burn is an alkali burn, you
          should flush the eye for at least 20 minutes. After the eye has been flushed, evacuate the casualty immediately.
          10-42. When an individual suffers burns of the face from a fire, the eyes will close quickly due to extreme
          heat. This reaction is a natural reflex to protect the eyeballs; however, the eyelids remain exposed to possibly
          being burned. If a casualty receives burns of the eyelids or face—
               • DO NOT apply dressing.
               • DO NOT touch.
               • SEEK medical assistance immediately.


                                                         WARNING
                        DO NOT attempt to force open the eyes with thermal burns.


          10-43. Reassure the casualty and quickly survey the situation.
          10-44. Quickly identify the substance that the casualty was exposed to such as—

                  Note. Do not delay first aid to perform this step. Time is critical and the eyes must be irrigated as

text:
Chapter 11
                                                     Head Injury

OVERVIEW OF HEAD INJURIES
239B




          11-1. Head injuries are a common concern that can occur due to accidents, falls, or sports-related incidents.
          When the head experiences a forceful impact, it can result in different types of injuries. Understanding head
          injuries can help Service members take the necessary precautions to protect themselves or others from
          potential harm. It is critically important to report findings of a head injury to medical personnel at the scene
          since a lack of rapid, and appropriate medical care can worsen the head injury, and the eventual outcome.
          Head trauma can be either blunt or penetrating. Head injuries can be broadly classified as open or closed
          head injuries.
OPEN HEAD INJURY
108B




          11-2. An open head injury, also known as an open skull injury, is a type of injury that occurs when there is a
          break or penetration of the skull, exposing the brain to the external environment. It typically involves visible
          damage to the scalp, skull, or meninges (protective coverings of the brain). The signs and symptoms of an
          open head injury can vary depending on the severity and specific location of the injury. Open head injuries
          are considered medical emergencies. If an open head injury is suspected, it is crucial to seek immediate
          medical attention for evaluation, diagnosis, and appropriate treatment.
          11-3. The common signs and symptoms associated with an open head injury are:
              • Visible head wound. An open head injury often involves a visible wound or laceration on the scalp
                  or skull. There may be bleeding, or an open fracture where the bone is exposed.
              • Profuse bleeding. Open head injuries can cause significant bleeding due to damage to blood vessels.
                  Blood may be visible on the scalp, face, or in severe cases, there may be profuse bleeding from the
                  head wound.
              • Skull deformity. In some cases, an open head injury may cause a visible deformity or depression in
                  the skull, indicating a skull fracture or bone displacement.
              • Loss of consciousness. Depending on the severity of the injury, loss of consciousness can occur,
                  ranging from a brief period to an extended duration.
              • Clear fluid or blood drainage. Leakage of clear fluid (cerebrospinal fluid) or blood from the nose,
                  ears, or wound can indicate a more severe injury and should be treated as an emergency.
              • Severe headache. An intense and persistent headache is common following an open head injury.
              • Nausea and vomiting. Feelings of nausea and vomiting may be present after an open head injury.
              • Confusion and disorientation. The Service member may exhibit confusion, memory loss, difficulty
                  concentrating, or may appear disoriented.
              • Seizures. Seizures can occur after an open head injury, especially if the brain is directly affected.
              • Changes in speech or vision. The person may have difficulties with speech, vision problems, double
                  vision, or other sensory disturbances.
              • Weaknesses or numbness. Weakness or numbness in certain body parts can be a sign of nerve
                  damage resulting from the head injury.
CLOSED HEAD INJURY
109B




          11-4. A closed head injury refers to trauma to the head that does not involve an open wound or penetration
          of the skull. Instead, the injury occurs internally, within the skull. Closed head injuries are often the result of
          blunt force impacts, falls, or accidents, where the brain is subjected to sudden acceleration, deceleration, or
          rotational forces. Concussions are the most common type of a closed head injury. Closed head injuries may
          not be obvious or detectable.
          11-5. Closed head injuries can range in severity from mild concussions to more severe forms, such as
          contusions, diffuse axonal injuries, or intracranial hemorrhages. It is essential to seek medical attention if a

text:
Chapter 11



            closed head injury is suspected, as the impact on the brain can have serious consequences and requires
            appropriate evaluation and management.
            11-6. The signs and symptoms of a closed head injury can vary depending on the severity of the injury. Mild
            cases may be present with subtle symptoms, while more severe injuries can have immediate and pronounced
            effects. The common signs and symptoms associated with a closed head injury are:
                 • Headache or pressure in the head.
                 • Nausea and vomiting.
                 • Dizziness and balance problems.
                 • Confusion and disorientation.
                 • Memory loss or difficulty concentrating.
                 • Mood and behavior changes.
                 • Sensory changes, such as blurred vision, or ringing in the ears.
                 • Sensitivity to light and sound.
                 • Loss of consciousness (in severe cases).
            11-7. It is important to seek medical attention if any of these signs are present after a head injury, as they can
            indicate a range of severity from a mild concussion to more serious brain trauma. The above symptoms can
            occur immediately after the injury or may develop gradually over time. Symptoms may vary from person to
            person.
CONCUSSIONS
10B




            11-8. A concussion is a type of traumatic brain injury that occurs when the brain experiences a sudden and
            forceful movement within the skull. It is typically caused by a blow, jolt, or bump to the head or body, which
            can disrupt the normal functioning of the brain.
            11-9. Concussions can occur in various situations, such as sports-related injuries, falls, motor vehicle
            accidents, or any other incident involving a significant impact to the head. Concussions can happen even
            without a direct impact to the head. The forceful movement or shaking of the body can still cause the brain
            to move inside the skull, leading to a concussion.
            11-10. The primary characteristic of a concussion is a temporary disruption of brain function. Concussions
            may not always involve a loss of consciousness. In fact, most concussions occur without a person losing
            consciousness. Common symptoms of a concussion can include:
                • Headache or pressure in the head.
                • Dizziness or feeling lightheaded.
                • Confusion or feeling mentally foggy.
                • Memory problems or difficulty concentrating.
                • Fatigue or feeling tired.
                • Nausea or vomiting.
                • Sensitivity to light or noise.
                • Changes in sleep patterns.
                • Irritability or changes in mood.
                • Blurred vision or difficulty with balance.
            11-11. It’s important to seek medical attention if a concussion is suspected, as health care professionals can
            evaluate the severity of the injury and provide appropriate guidance for recovery. The initial management of
            a concussion involves rest and avoiding activities that could further injure the brain. Physical and cognitive
            rest are recommended to allow the brain to heal properly. In some cases, individuals may need to temporarily
            limit activities like school or work to promote recovery. A gradual return to normal activities is typically
            recommended under the guidance of a health care professional.
            11-12. Every concussion is unique, and the symptoms and recovery time can vary from person to person.
            With proper rest, most individuals recover fully from a concussion. However, in some cases, symptoms may
            persist or worsen, and a condition known as post-concussion syndrome may develop.

text:
Head Injury



CONTUSIONS RELATED TO HEAD INJURIES
1B




          11-13. A contusion refers to a type of injury characterized by damage to the tissue or blood vessels beneath
          the skin, usually resulting from a blunt force impact. It is commonly known as a bruise. When a contusion
          occurs, blood vessels are damaged, leading to bleeding and the subsequent discoloration of the skin.
          11-14. In relation to head injuries, contusions can occur because of a direct blow or trauma to the head. When
          the head experiences a significant impact, the brain can collide with the inner surface of the skull, leading to
          contusions. These types of injuries are known as cerebral contusions.
          11-15. Cerebral contusions can be classified as coup-contrecoup injuries, which means that contusions can
          occur both at the site of impact (coup) and on the opposite side of the brain due to the brain rebounding and
          hitting the skull (contrecoup). These injuries are concerning because they involve damage to the brain tissue
          itself.
          11-16. The severity of a cerebral contusion can vary, ranging from mild to severe. In more severe cases,
          contusions can lead to increased pressure within the skull, swelling of the brain, and potentially life-
          threatening complications.
          11-17. It is crucial to seek immediate medical attention if a head injury is suspected, as prompt evaluation
          and treatment are essential to prevent further complications. Symptoms of a cerebral contusion may include:
              • Changes in vision.
              • Confusion.
              • Difficulty speaking.
              • Dizziness.
              • Headache.
              • Loss of consciousness.
              • Nausea.
              • Seizures.
              • Vomiting.
              • Weaknesses.
          11-18. Treatment for cerebral contusions focuses on managing the underlying injury and preventing further
          damage. It may involve measures such as rest, pain management, observation, close monitoring of
          neurological status, and, in more severe cases, surgical intervention to relieve pressure and remove any blood
          clots or damaged tissue.

EQUIPMENT USED FOR THE TREATMENT OF A HEAD INJURY
240B




          11-19. Treating a head wound requires few essential pieces of equipment. Service members will need
          disposable gloves to protect themselves and the injured person from any potential infection. Sterile gauze
          pads or clean clothes are vital for covering and applying pressure to the wound to stop the bleeding. Adhesive
          bandages or medical tape are used to secure the gauze in place. Additionally, a mild antiseptic solution or
          wipes are important for cleaning the wound to prevent infection. Lastly, a cravat or gauze bandage can be
          used to create a makeshift dressing or sling to support the head if there is a suspected skull or neck injury.

TIER 1 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF A HEAD INJURY
241B




          11-20. Service members may not have the time or expertise to conduct extensive treatment for a head injury.
          Service members experiencing any of the symptoms explained in paragraph 11-17 should be evacuated as
          soon as tactically feasible.

TIER 2 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF A HEAD INJURY
24B




          11-21. Service members experiencing any of the symptoms explained in paragraph 11-17 should be
          evacuated as soon as tactically feasible. However, the CLS should complete the injury/evaluation/distance
          (commonly known as I.E.D.) checklist that is outlined in DODI 6490.11. This checklist is used to gather
          information, and to identify the signs and symptoms of a head injury.

NECK, AND FACIAL INJURIES

         11-28. Prompt first aid measures should be initiated for casualties with suspected head and neck injuries. The
         conscious casualty may be able to provide information on the extent of their injuries. However, because of
         the head injury, they may be confused and unable to provide accurate information. The signs and symptoms
         that a first aid provider might observe are:
              • Nausea and vomiting.
              • Convulsions or twitches.
              • Slurred speech.
              • Confusion and loss of memory. (Do they know who they are? Do they know where they are?
                    Do they know what day it is?).
              • Recent unconsciousness.
              • Dizziness.
              • Drowsiness.
              • Blurred vision, unequal pupils, or bruising (black eyes).
              • Paralysis (partial or full).
              • Complaint of headache.
              • Bleeding or other fluid discharge from the scalp, nose, or ears.
              • Deformity of the head (depression or swelling).
              • Staggering while walking.
UNCONSCIOUS CASUALTY
12B




         11-29. When encountering an unconscious casualty, it is essential to act swiftly and methodically, as their
         condition may be critical. Unconsciousness can result from various causes, such as trauma, medical
         emergencies, or underlying health conditions. The primary objective of first aid for an unconscious patient is
         to ensure their immediate safety, preserve their airway, and seek professional medical help. By following
         specific guidelines and employing basic life support techniques, first responders can play a vital role in
         providing initial assistance until medical professionals arrive. An unconscious casualty does not have control
         of all their functions and may choke on their tongue, blood, vomitus, or other substances resulting in:
              • Loss of Breathing. The brain requires a constant supply of oxygen. A bluish (or an individual with
                   dark skin-grayish) color of skin around the lips and nail beds indicates that the casualty is not
                   receiving enough oxygen. Immediate action must be taken to clear the airway, to position the
                   casualty on their side, or to initiate rescue breathing.
              • Bleeding. Bleeding from a head injury usually comes from blood vessels within the scalp. Bleeding
                   can also develop inside the skull or within the brain. In most instances visible bleeding from the
                   head can be controlled by application of the field first aid dressing.


                                                       CAUTION
                       DO NOT attempt to put unnecessary pressure on the wound or attempt
                       to push any brain matter back into the head (skull). DO NOT apply
                       pressure dressing.

             •     Convulsions. Convulsions (seizures or involuntary jerking) may occur even after a mild head injury.
                   When a casualty is convulsing, protect them from hurting themselves. Take the following measures:
                   ▪ Ease them to the ground if they are standing or sitting.
                   ▪ Support their head and neck.
                   ▪ Maintain their airway.
                   ▪ Protect them from further injury (such as hitting close-by objects).

                 Note. DO NOT forcefully hold their arms and legs if they are jerking because this can lead to
                 broken bones. DO NOT force anything between the casualties’ teeth-especially if they are tightly
                 clenched because this may obstruct the casualty’s airway. Maintain the casualty’s airway if
                 necessary.

NECK INJURIES
14B




          11-35. Neck injuries may result in heavy bleeding. Apply pressure above and below the injury. Do not
          interfere with the breathing process and attempt to control the bleeding. Apply a dressing. When blunt trauma
          occurs, always evaluate the casualty for a possible neck fracture or spinal cord injury; if suspected, seek
          medical treatment immediately.

                  Note. Establish and maintain the airway in cases of facial or neck injuries. If a neck fracture or
                  spinal cord injury is suspected, immobilize the injury and, if necessary, perform basic life support
                  measures.

FACIAL INJURIES
15B




          11-36. Soft tissue injuries of the face and scalp are common. Abrasions (scrapes) of the skin do not cause
          serious problems. Contusions (injury without a break in the skin) usually cause swelling. A contusion of the
          scalp looks and feels like a lump. Laceration (cut) and avulsion (torn away tissue) injuries are common.
          Avulsions are frequently caused when a sharp blow separates the scalp from the skull beneath it. The face
          and scalp are richly supplied with blood vessels (arteries and veins) and the wounds of these areas usually
          bleed heavily.

Ear Injuries
357B




          11-37. Lacerated (cut) or avulsed (torn) ear tissue may not be a serious injury. Bleeding, or the drainage of
          fluids from the ear canal, however, may be a sign of a head injury, such as a skull fracture. DO NOT attempt
          to stop the flow from the inner ear canal or put anything into the ear canal to block it. Instead, you should
          cover the ear lightly with a dressing. For minor cuts or wounds to the external ear, apply a cravat or gauze
          bandage as follows:
               • Place the middle of the bandage over the ear (figure 11-2 step A).
               • Cross the ends, wrap them in opposite directions around the head, and tie them (figure 11-2 step B
                    and figure 11-2 step C).




                                      Figure 11-2. Applying a bandage to the ear
              •     If possible, place some dressing material between the back of the ear and the side of the head to
                    avoid crushing the ear against the head with the bandage.

Nose Injuries
358B




          11-38. Nose injuries generally produce bleeding. The bleeding may be controlled by placing an ice pack (if
          available) over the nose or pinching the nostrils together. The bleeding may also be controlled by placing
          torn gauze (rolled) between the upper teeth and the lip.

                         DO NOT attempt to remove objects inhaled into the nose. An untrained

             11-39. Before applying a bandage to a casualty's jaw, remove all loose or free-floating foreign material from

text:
Chapter 12
                                                       Burns

OVERVIEW OF BURNS
24B




         12-1. A burned trauma casualty should be treated for all other life-threatening injuries first, following the
         MARCH-PAWS sequence, before addressing burns. Even if the skin is burned, trauma treatments can still
         be performed on or through it.
         12-2. Burns can result from various causes:
             • Friction Burns. These are common in situations where skin is rubbed off against a hard surface,
                 often seen in road accidents where motorcycle riders, cyclists, or skateboarders slide across
                 pavement, getting what's known as "road rash." Carpet burns occur from skin scraping against
                 carpet, often during indoor sports or play. Rope burns are common during activities like climbing
                 or tug-of-war, and sliding burns frequently happen in sports like baseball when sliding into bases.
             • Cold Burns. Also known as frostbite, these burns damage the skin by freezing it. Frostbite can occur
                 from prolonged exposure to freezing temperatures or direct contact with extremely cold objects.
             • Thermal Burns. These occur when the skin touches something very hot, like hot metals, scalding
                 liquids, flames, or steam, raising the skin temperature high enough to kill skin cells.
             • Radiation Burns. Sunburn is a typical example. Other sources include X-rays or radiation therapy
                 for cancer.
             • Chemical Burns. These happen when strong acids, solvents, or detergents come into contact with
                 the skin.
             • Electrical Burns. These burns are the result of contact with electrical currents.
         12-3. Burns are classified based on how deeply they damage the skin:
             • Superficial or First Degree Burns (figure 12-1 on page 116): Superficial burns affect only the outer
                 layer of the skin, causing redness, pain, and mild swelling. They are like mild sunburn and usually
                 heal within a few days without leaving scars.
             • Partial thickness or Second Degree Burns (figure 12-2 on page 116): Partial thickness burns reach
                 the second layer of the skin and can cause blisters, severe pain, redness, and swelling. Healing times
                 vary, and these burns may leave scars.
             • Full thickness or Third Degree Burns (figure 12-3 on page 116): Full thickness burns are the most
                 severe, these burns go through the entire thickness of the skin and can damage muscles or bones
                 underneath. The skin may look white, blackened, or charred, and there might be no feeling in the
                 area because of nerve damage. These burns require immediate medical attention and often need skin
                 grafts to heal.

      12-4. The size of or percentage of the burn area will be documented on DD Form 1380. The “Rule of Nines”

           • Arms – 9 percent each.
           • Legs – 18 percent each.
           • Pubic area – 1 percent.

            Note. First degree or superficial burns are not part of the burn percentage calculation and are rarely
            of medical significance.

text:
Burns



          12-5. General guidelines are that the size of the casualty’s palm of the hand represents approximately 1
          percent of the burned area. When estimating, it is easiest to round up to the nearest 10 percent. If half of the
          front or rear area is burned, the area would be half of the area value. For example, if half of the front upper
          leg or front lower leg were burned, it would be half of 9 percent, or 4.5 percent. If half of the front torso were
          burned, say either the upper or the lower part of the front torso, then it would be half of 18 percent or 9
          percent. Remember, the higher the percentage burned, the higher the chance is for hypothermia.

EQUIPMENT USED FOR THE TREATMENT OF BURNS
245B




          12-6. The CoTCCC-recommended compressed gauze and or gauze rolls are 6-ply sterile cotton that has been
          compressed. They are used to stop minor bleeding, cover wounds or burns, pack wounds, act as bulky
          material for pressure dressings, or pad pressure points in splinting.
          12-7. The CoTCCC-recommended elastic bandage is a stretchable bandage. They are used to hold dressings
          or splints in place or can be applied more tightly to apply localized pressure on a wound. Elastic or restrictive
          bandages are normally not applied to a burn casualty. The application of these types of bandages are very
          painful and swelling secondary to the injury may restrict circulation.
          12-8. The cravat is a sterile triangular shaped bandage. It can be used as both a bandage and a sling. It is
          commonly used to secure a splint, create a sling, or swath for an injured limb.

TIER 1 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF BURNS
246B




          12-9. Burn care in TCCC is very basic. Eliminating the source of the burn should be the initial priority.
          Providing any treatment prior to removing the casualty from the source of the burn or extinguishing the cause
          of the burn will be ineffective and harmful to the casualty and casualty response personnel.
          12-10. Electrical burn care consists of—
              • Eliminating the source of electrical burns.
              • Turning off any sources of electricity that have been exposed to the casualty (if applicable).
              • Using nonconductive material to drag the casualty away from the electrical source
                  (if it cannot be turned off).

                  Note. Types of nonconductive material include rope, clothing, and dry wood.

              •     Moving the casualty to a safe place.


                                                        WARNING
                       Do not touch the casualty or the electrical source with your bare
                       hands. You will be injured too! High voltage electrical burns from
                       an electrical source or lightning may cause temporary
                       unconsciousness, difficulties in breathing, or difficulties with the
                       heart (irregular heartbeat).


          12-11. Thermal burn care consists of—
              • Stopping the source of the thermal burn and remove the casualty from the source of the burn.
              • Extinguishing any flames on the casualty, cut the clothing around the burned area, and gently lift
                  away.


                                                           CAUTION
                       If clothing is stuck to the burn, ensure you cut around the clothing and
                       leave the stuck clothing in place.
