text:
Chapter 12



                 •    Avoid grabbing the burned area while moving or picking up the casualty.
             12-12. Chemical burn care consists of—
                 • Eliminating the source of chemical burns.
                 • Brushing off dry chemicals (carefully) with a clean, dry cloth.
                 • Flush the burned area with copious amounts of flowing water to remove any liquid chemicals.
                 • Applying a wet barrier (water-soaked gauze, clothing, or mud) with an occlusive dressing.
                 • Advising medical personnel immediately.


                                                          WARNING
                         Do not submerge a chemical burn casualty in water. This will
                         greatly contribute to hypothermia and spread the irritation.


             12-13. All burn care consists of—
                 • Monitoring the casualty for life-threatening conditions.
                 • Checking for additional injuries.
                 • Treating for shock (if applicable).
                 • Seeking medical aid.
                 • Annotating all treatment and care on DD Form 1380.
             12-14. Close attention to the casualty’s airway, breathing is required and always assess for secondary injuries
             and shock.

TIER 2 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF BURNS
247B




             12-15. Along with the treatment measures outlined in paragraph 13-9 through 13-14 extra emphasis should
             be placed on heat loss prevention methods. Burn patients are particularly susceptible to hypothermia.
             Casualties should be kept off the ground and placed onto an insulated surface as soon as possible.
             12-16. For extensive burns, those with greater than 20 percent of the area burned place the casualty in the
             Heat Reflective Shield to cover the burned areas and prevent hypothermia. Preventing and managing
             hypothermia for burn patients is important and occurs regardless of the ambient temperature in the
             environment.
             12-17. Facial burns, especially those that occur in closed spaces, may be associated with an inhalation injury.
             These casualties should be monitored closely for potential airway issues. Do not place an NPA in a casualty
             with signs of inhalation burns. Notify medical personnel as soon as possible if an inhalation injury is
             suspected.
             12-18. Analgesia may be administered to treat burn pain. Antibiotic therapy is not solely indicated for burns;
             it should also be given to prevent infection in penetrating wounds. Consider giving the entire combat pill
             pack if medical treatment takes more than three hours from the time of injury, and if giving the medication
             to the casualty does not cause nausea.
             12-19. Interventions for warm and cool weather should be considered. The addition of blood loss can cause
             the body’s temperature to drop even when it is hot outside. The TQs should not be covered; keep them visible
             so medical personnel can easily see it.

EXPEDIENT SKILLS USED FOR THE TREATMENT OF BURNS
248B




             12-20. In emergency scenarios, especially in remote or combat zones, effectively managing burn injuries
             with limited resources is essential. Basic materials such as gauze bandage, clean clothing, and cravats can be
             used to cover burns and control bleeding. Cooling and cleaning burns should be done with available clean
             water, avoiding ice to prevent further skin damage. For thermal burns, it's crucial to remove the casualty from
             the heat source and cut away clothing gently around the burn area. In cases of electrical burns, disconnecting
             the power and using non-conductive materials to move the casualty is vital, while chemical burns require
             immediate decontamination by brushing off dry chemicals and flushing the area thoroughly with water.

   12-21. Preventing hypothermia is critical in burn care due to the high risk posed by skin damage. Using
   emergency blankets, reflective heat shields, or makeshift insulation from natural materials can help maintain
   body temperature. Pain management, when possible, should include safe administration of over-the-counter
   pain relievers, and continuous monitoring for shock is essential. These field expedient techniques are pivotal
   in stabilizing burn victims and preventing further injury until more advanced medical help can be accessed,
   underscoring the importance of training and preparedness in these emergency interventions.

text:
Chapter 13
                                         Fractures and Splinting

OVERVIEW OF FRACTURES
249B




          13-1. Prompt and appropriate management of fractures, or breaks in bones, is essential to minimize further
          harm and optimize the chances of survival for injured individuals. TCCC emphasizes a systematic approach
          to fracture care, incorporating principles such as rapid assessment, stabilization, and pain management. The
          goal is to provide efficient and effective treatment, considering the challenges of the tactical environment
          where resources may be limited, and evacuation to definitive care may be delayed. Mastery of fracture
          management in TCCC equips military personnel and first responders with the skills necessary to stabilize
          fractures, prevent complications, and facilitate the evacuation process, ultimately improving the overall
          outcomes for casualties in the field.
MUSCULOSKELETAL SYSTEM
16B




          13-2. The musculoskeletal system provides a structural framework for the body and, because bones are rigid,
          provides support and protection for vital organs and softer tissues. Skeletal muscles and bones work together
          to make body movement possible.
          13-3. The musculoskeletal system is composed of—
              • Bones.
              • Joints.
              • Muscles.
              • Cartilage.
              • Ligaments.
              • Tendons.

Bones
360B




          13-4. Bones are the substance that forms the skeleton of the body. It is composed chiefly of calcium
          phosphate and calcium carbonate. The human body has 206 bones. There are 80 axial (head and trunk) bones
          and 126 appendicular (upper and lower extremity) bones. Bones provide structural support for the body.
          Individual and groups of bones provide structure for the attachment of soft tissues and protect organs.

Joints
361B




          13-5. The human body's mobility hinges on its joints, where bones connect and facilitate movement. These
          pivotal junctures come in various forms, each serving distinct functions in enabling motion.

Muscles
362B




          13-6. The body's muscles serve as its powerhouse, providing the force needed for movement and various
          physiological functions. Within the body, there exist three main types of muscles, each with its unique roles
          and characteristics. These include skeletal muscles, which control movement in the extremities and outer
          body areas, cardiac muscles, found exclusively in the heart, and smooth muscles, lining the walls of arteries
          and the gastrointestinal tract.

Cartilage
36B




          13-7. Cartilage serves as a resilient and pliable tissue that provides cushioning and support between bones
          at the joints, facilitating smooth movement. In addition to its role in joint function, cartilage also forms
          essential structures elsewhere in the body, such as the larynx and the external portions of the ears, contributing
          to their flexibility and shape.

title: U.S. Army: Casualty Response, Tactical Combat Casualty Care, and First Aid (ATP 4-02.11)
text:
Chapter 13



Ligaments
364B




             13-8. Ligaments play a crucial role in the body's structural integrity, serving as sturdy bands of connective
             tissue that link bones together at joints. They provide stability and support, helping to prevent excessive
             movement and potential joint injuries.

Tendons
365B




             13-9. Tendons serve as soft tissue connectors that attach muscles to bones, enabling movement and
             transmitting the force generated by muscles to the bones they are connected to. Despite their flexibility,
             tendons possess considerable toughness, providing durability to withstand the stresses of movement and
             physical activity.
TYPES OF FRACTURES
17B




             13-10. A fracture can be a closed or open fracture. A closed fracture (see figure 13-1) means that there is no
             external wound associated with the fracture. An open fracture (see figure 13-2) means that there is a break in
             the skin in conjunction with the fracture, often with protruding bone. The warning signs that an arm or leg
             might be fractured include:
                  • Significant pain along with marked swelling.
                  • An audible or perceived “snap.”
                  • Different length or shape of limb.
                  • Loss of pulse or sensation in the injured arm or leg.
                  • Crepitus (a crackling or popping sound under the skin).




                     Figure 13-1. Closed Fracture                            Figure 13-2. Open Fracture

EQUIPMENT USED FOR THE TREATMENT OF FRACTURES
250B




             13-11. The CoTCCC endorses the use of the semi-rigid splint, a 36-inch-long malleable device comprised of
             moldable aluminum, encased in foam padding. This type of splint is designed for versatility in the field and
             is most commonly employed for stabilizing fractures. Its flexible yet sturdy structure allows it to be shaped
             according to the specific contours of the injury site, providing effective support and immobilization needed
             to prevent further injury during transport or until more definitive care can be administered.

title: U.S. Army: Casualty Response, Tactical Combat Casualty Care, and First Aid (ATP 4-02.11)
text:
Fractures and Splinting



TIER 1 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF FRACTURES
251B




          13-12. During the TFC phase, it is highly advisable to splint all fractures if circumstances permit. Splinting
          is crucial to immobilize the affected area, preventing further damage, and minimizing pain for the casualty.
          Proper splinting techniques ensure that fractures are adequately supported until the injured individual
          receives comprehensive medical treatment. For detailed guidance on how to correctly apply splints, refer to
          paragraph 14-13, which provides specific instructions and considerations for effective splintering in a tactical
          environment.

TIER 2 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF FRACTURES
25B




          13-13. The "S" in MARCH-PAWS protocol denotes splinting, a crucial step in managing both open and
          closed fractures. For more information on fractures see paragraph 14-10 on page 122. Splinting involves
          immobilizing the injured limb to prevent further movement, typically using semi-rigid splints or improvised
          materials like boards or tree limbs. It's essential to incorporate the joints above and below the fracture site
          for stability and secure the splint firmly with wraps, belts, or tape. Additionally, securing arm fractures to the
          shirt using the sleeve as a sling can provide added support. However, caution must be exercised to avoid
          excessive tightness, which can compromise circulation to the fingers or toes.
          13-14. Caution must be taken when splinting to ensure that it is not wrapped too tightly. If wrapped too
          tightly, the splint may cut off circulation below the splint. If there is numbness, tingling or increased pain, or
          if the fingers or toes turn pale or bluish, loosen the bandage. Increased swelling may occur; continued
          monitoring of the splintered fracture is required.
          13-15. When splinting, first responders or CLS should avoid—
              • Manipulating the fracture site too much, resulting in pain, additional damage to blood vessels, and
                  nerves.
              • Securing too tightly and cutting off blood flow.
              • Failing to immobilize the joint above and below the fracture when possible.
              • Causing further injury.
              • Making the casualty uncomfortable during transport or evacuation.
              • Splinting near or over a wound that has not been properly treated.
SPLINTING LEG FRACTURES
18B




          13-16. Care should be taken on cravat placement. First responders or CLS should not apply a cravat on the
          fracture site, as the pressure from the cravat could cause additional injury to the fracture site.
          13-17. The ends of the splint should not be placed against the groin, as this could interfere with blood
          circulation. Extra padding is used for joints or sensitive areas, such as the groin.
          13-18. Before splinting a suspected fracture, the first responder or CLS should—
              • Identify the location of the fracture.
              • Check the pulse below the fracture.
              • Watch for signs of poor circulation, including coolness, numbness, or lack of a pulse.
              • Ensure the ends of the rigid objects are not interfering with blood circulation.
              • If there are any signs of poor circulation, loosen the splint, reposition, and reapply.
          13-19. The first responder or CLS should follow the below when applying a leg splint:
              • Apply the splint to the injured extremity with the limb in the position of function or a normal resting
                  position if possible.
              • Secure the splint in place with appropriate materials.
              • Ensure the joints above and below the fracture are immobilized in the splint whenever possible.
              • Recheck the pulse after applying the splint.
              • Watch for signs of poor circulation, including coolness, numbness, or lack of a pulse. Ensure the
                  ends of the rigid objects are not interfering with blood circulation. If there are any signs of poor
                  circulation, loosen the splint, reposition, and reapply.
              • Administering the CWMP as needed.
              • Document all treatment on a DD Form 1380 and attach it to the casualty.

title: U.S. Army: Casualty Response, Tactical Combat Casualty Care, and First Aid (ATP 4-02.11)
text:
Chapter 13



SPLINTING ARM FRACTURES
19B




             13-20. Movement or manipulation of a fractured extremity may result in increased pain. The following will
             help to reduce the casualty’s pain:
                 • If possible, have the casualty support their injured arm while preparing the equipment.
                 • Mold the padded splint using the casualty's unaffected limb to avoid unnecessary manipulation.
                 • Use cravats or gauze bandages to immobilize the fracture and secure the limb to the body to
                       minimize unnecessary movement during transport.
             13-21. The first responder or CLS should follow the following when applying an arm splint:
                 • Place rigid objects so that one is on each side of the injured arm or forearm.
                 • Positioning the rigid objects so that the joint above the fracture and the joint below the fracture will
                     be immobilized.
                 • Apply padding between the arm and the splint.
                 • Secure the splint with cravats, gauze bandages, strips of cloth, or other securing materials.
                 • If possible, place two cravats above and two below the fracture site.
                 • Use square knots to secure bandages tied away from the body on the splint.
                 • Check pulses lower to the affected extremity before and after the application of the splint.
                 • Administering the CWMP as needed.
                 • Document all treatment on a DD Form 1380 and attach it to the casualty.

EXPEDIENT TECHNIQUES FOR SPLINTS, PADDING, BANDAGES,
253B




SLINGS, AND SWATHES
             13-22. Splints may be improvised from such items such as boards, poles, sticks, tree limbs, or cardboard. If
             nothing is available for a splint, the chest wall can be used to immobilize a fractured arm, and the uninjured
             leg can be used to immobilize (to some extent) the fractured leg.
             13-23. Padding may be improvised from such items as a jacket, blanket, poncho, shelter half, or leafy
             vegetation. Padding when splinting a fracture is essential for the well-being of the casualty. It promotes
             comfort, even pressure distribution, stability, protection against skin issues, and helps manage swelling, all
             of which contributes to an effective and safer management of fractures, especially in situations where
             immediate medical care may not be readily available.
             13-24. Bandages may be improvised from belts, rifle slings, handkerchiefs, or strips torn from clothing, or
             blankets. Narrow materials such as wire, or cord should not be used to secure a splint in place. The application
             of wire or narrow material to an extremity could cause tissue damage and a TQ effect.
             13-25. A sling is a bandage suspended from the neck to support an upper extremity. If a bandage is not
             available, a sling can be improvised by using the tail of a coat, shirt, or pieces of cloth torn from such items
             as clothing and blankets. The cravat is ideal for this purpose. Remember that the casualty’s hand should be
             higher than their elbow, and their fingers should be always showing. The sling should be applied so that the
             supporting pressure is on the uninjured side.
             13-26. Swathes are any bands (pieces of cloth or straps) that are used to further immobilize a splinted fracture.
             Cravats are often used and are called swathe bandages. The purpose of the swathe is to immobilize; therefore,
             the swathe bandage is placed above or below the fracture, not on top of the fracture.
PROCEDURES FOR SPLINTING SUSPECTED FRACTURE
120B




             13-27. Before beginning first aid procedures for a fracture, gather whatever splinting materials are available.
             Ensure that splints are long enough to immobilize the joint above and below the suspected fracture. If
             possible, use at least four ties (two above and two below the fracture) to secure the splints. The ties should
             be square knots and should be tied away from the body on the splint. Distal pulses of the affected extremity
             should be checked before and after the application of the splint.
             13-28. Evaluate the casualty and be prepared to perform any necessary lifesaving measures. Monitor the
             casualty for development of conditions that may require you to perform necessary lifesaving measures.

text:
Fractures and Splinting




                                                WARNING
                Unless there is immediate life-threatening danger, such as a fire
                or an explosion, DO NOT move the casualty with a suspected
                back or neck injury. Improper movement may cause permanent
                paralysis or death.


   13-29. Locate the site of the suspected fracture by:
       • Asking the casualty—
           ▪ Where are you injured?
           ▪ Do they have any pain?
           ▪ Where is it tender?
           ▪ Can you move the extremity?

           Note. With the presence of an obvious deformity, do not make the casualty move the extremity.

       •     Look for an unnatural position of the extremity.
       •     Look for a bone sticking out (protruding).
   13-30. Prepare the casualty for splinting the suspected fracture.
       • Reassure the casualty. Tell them that you will be providing first aid for them, and that medical help
            is on the way.
       • Loosen any tight or binding clothing.
       • Remove all jewelry from the injured part and place it in the casualty’s pocket. Tell the casualty you
            are doing this because if the jewelry is not removed and swelling occurs later, they may not be able
            remove it and further bodily injury could result.
       • Boots should not be removed from the casualty unless they are needed to stabilize a neck injury, or
            there is actual bleeding from the foot.
   13-31. Gather splinting materials. If splinting materials (splints, padding, and cravats) are not available,
   gather improvised materials. If splinting materials are not available and the suspected fracture cannot be
   splinted, then swathes or a combination of swathes and slings can be used to immobilize the extremity.
   13-32. Pad the Splints. Pad the splints where they touch any bony part of the body, such as the elbow, wrist,
   knee, ankle, crotch, or armpit areas. Padding prevents excessive pressure on the area, which could lead to
   circulation problems.
   13-33. Check the circulation below the site of the injury.
       • Note any pale, white, or bluish-gray color of the skin, which may indicate impaired circulation.
       • Check the temperature of the injured extremity. Use your hand to compare the temperature of the
           injured side with the uninjured side. The body area below the injury may be colder to the touch
           indicating poor circulation.
       • Question the casualty about the presence of numbness, tightness, cold, or tingling sensations.

text:
Chapter 13




                                                   WARNING
                  Casualties with fractures of the extremities may show impaired
                  circulation, such as numbness, tingling, cold or pale to bluish
                  skin tone. These casualties should be evacuated to medical
                  personnel and treated as soon as possible. Prompt medical
                  treatment may prevent possible loss of the limb.




                                                   WARNING
                  If it is an open fracture and the bone is protruding from the skin,
                  DO NOT ATTEMPT TO PUSH THE BONE BACK UNDER THE SKIN.
                  Apply a field dressing over the wound to protect the area.


      13-34. Apply the splint in place by—
          • Splinting the fracture in the position found. DO NOT attempt to reposition or straighten the injury.
              If it is an open fracture, stop the bleeding and protect the wound.
          • Covering all wounds with field dressings before applying a splint. Remember to use the casualty’s
              field dressing, before using your own.
          • Placing one splint on each side of the fracture. Make sure that the splints reach, if possible, beyond
              the joints above and below the fracture.
          • Tying the splints by—
              ▪ Securing each splint in place above and below the fracture site with cravats, or improvised
                    material. Improvised materials, such as gauze bandage, strips of cloth, belts, or whatever other
                    materials you have, may be used.
              ▪ With minimal motion to the injured areas, place and tie the splints with the bandages.
              ▪ Push splint material through and under the natural body curvatures, and then gently position
                    splint material, and tie in place.
              ▪ Using square knots. Tie all knots on the splint away from the casualty (figure 13-3). DO NOT
                    tie knots directly over the suspected fracture site.




                          Figure 13-3. Square knots tied away from the casualty
      13-35. Check the splint for tightness—
          • CHECK to ensure that the bandages are tight enough to securely hold splinting materials in place,
              but not so tight that circulation is impaired.
          • RECHECK the circulation after application of the splint. Check the skin color and temperature. This
              is to ensure that the bandages holding the splint in place have not been tied too tightly. A fingertip
              check can be made by inserting the tip of the finger between the bandaged knot and the skin.
          • MAKE any necessary adjustments without allowing the splint to become ineffective.

Immobilizing a Spinal Column Fracture
369B




             13-48. It is often impossible to be sure if a casualty has a fractured spinal column. Be suspicious of any back
             injury, especially if the casualty has fallen or if their back has been sharply struck or bent. If a casualty has
             received such an injury and does not have feeling in their legs or cannot move them, you can be reasonably
             sure that they have a severe back injury which is managed as a fracture. A neck fracture or injury to the back
             should always be suspected, and it is often impossible to be sure if a casualty has a fractured spinal column.
             If the spine is fractured (figure 13-28 step A on page 137), bending it can cause the sharp bone fragments to
             bruise or cut the spinal cord and result in permanent paralysis or death. The spinal column must maintain
             normal spinal position at the lower back (lumbar region) to help remove pressure from the spinal cord.
             13-49. If the casualty is not to be transported until medical personnel arrive—
                 • Caution them not to move. Ask if they are in pain or, if they are unable to move any part of their
                      body.
                 • Leave them in the position in which they were found. DO NOT move any part of their body unless
                      they are in imminent danger.
                 • If the casualty is lying face up, slip a blanket or other supporting material under the arch of their
                      lower back to help support the spine in a normal position (figure 13-28 step B on page 137). Take
                      care not to place so much bulky padding under your casualty, as this will cause potential damage
                      and cause undue pressure on the spine.
                 • If the casualty is lying face down, DO NOT put anything under any part of their body.

          •     The number two Service member positions themself at the casualty’s head. Their responsibility is

Fractures and Splinting



Immobilizing a Neck Fracture
370B




          13-52. A fractured neck is extremely dangerous. Bone fragments may bruise or cut the spinal cord just as
          they might in a fractured back. If the casualty is not to be transported until medical personnel arrive—
              • Caution them not to move. Moving may cause permanent injury or death.
              • Leave the casualty in the position in which they are found. If their neck and head (cervical spine)
                  are in an abnormal position, immediately immobilize the neck and head.
              • Keep their head still, if the casualty is lying face up, raise their shoulders slightly, and slip a roll of
                  cloth that has the bulk of a bath towel under their neck (figure 13-30). The roll should be thick
                  enough to arch their neck only slightly, leaving the back of their head on the ground. DO NOT bend
                  their neck or head forward. DO NOT raise or twist their head.
              • Immobilize the casualty’s head (figure 13-31). Do this by padding heavy objects (such as rocks or
                  their boots filled with dirt, sand, gravel, or rock) and placing them on each side of their head. If it is
                  necessary to use boots, after filling them, tie the top tightly or stuff with pieces of cloth to secure
                  the contents.




          Figure 13-30. Casualty with a roll of cloth             Figure 13-31. Immobilization of the fractured
                     (bulk) under neck                                           neck with boots

          13-53. DO NOT move the casualty if they are lying face down. Immobilize the head and neck by padding
          heavy objects and placing them on each side of their head. DO NOT put a roll of cloth under the neck.
          13-54. DO NOT bend the neck or head, nor roll the casualty onto their back. If the casualty must be prepared
          for transportation before medical personnel arrive at least two persons are needed to move the casualty’s head
          and trunk in unison.
          13-55. Care is taken should a casualty have to be moved prior to medical personnel arrival. The casualty is
          prepared by—
              • A wide board is placed lengthwise beside the casualty. It should extend at least 4 inches beyond the
                  casualty’s head and feet (figure 13-32 step A on page 140). Avoid prolonged use, if possible.
              • If the casualty is lying face up, the number one Service member steadies the casualty’s head and
                  neck between their hands. At the same time, the number two Service member positions one foot and
                  one knee against the board to prevent it from slipping. They then grasp the casualty underneath their
                  shoulder and hip and gently slide the casualty onto the board (figure 13-32 step B on page 140).
              • If the casualty is lying face down, the number one member steadies the casualty’s head and neck
                  between their hands, while the number two Service member gently rolls the casualty over onto the
                  board (figure 13-32 step C on page 140).
              • The number one Service member continues to steady the casualty’s head and neck. The number two
                  Service member simultaneously raises the casualty’s shoulders slightly, places padding under their
                  neck, and immobilizes the casualty’s head. Any improvised supports are secured in position with a
                  cravat, gauze bandage, or strip of cloth extended across the casualty’s forehead and under the board
                  (figure 13-32 step D on page 140).
              • The board is lifted onto a litter or blanket in order to transport the casualty (figure 13-32 step E).

Chapter 14
             Expedient Techniques for other Secondary Injuries

OVERVIEW OF SECONDARY INJURIES
254B




          14-1. Because medical personnel will not always be readily available, nonmedical personnel must rely on
          themselves and other Service members’ knowledge and fundamentals of first aid for secondary injuries until
          medical assistance is gained and initiated. This section will provide additional first aid, non-TCCC,
          procedures that nonmedical personnel can use in a garrison environment, or in combat situations.

ABDOMINAL WOUNDS
25B




          14-2. The most serious abdominal wound is one in which an object penetrates the abdominal wall and pierces
          internal organs or large blood vessels. In these instances, bleeding may be severe, and death can occur rapidly.
          14-3. The first step in treating an abdominal wound is to position the casualty. Place and maintain the casualty
          on their back with their knees in an upright (flexed) position (figure 14-1). The knees-up position helps relieve
          pain, assists in the treatment of shock, prevents further exposure of the bowel (intestines) or abdominal
          organs, and helps relieve abdominal pressure by allowing the abdominal muscles to relax.




           Figure 14-1. The casualty positioned (lying) on their back with their knees (flexed) up
          14-4. Expose the wound by—
              • Removing the casualty's loose clothing to expose the wound. However, DO NOT attempt to remove
                  clothing that is stuck to the wound; removing it may cause further injury.
              • Gently pick up any organs that may be on the ground. Do this with a clean, dry dressing or with the
                  cleanest available material. Place the organs on top of the casualty's abdomen (figure 14-2).




                              Figure 14-2. Protruding organs placed near the wound

title: U.S. Army: Casualty Response, Tactical Combat Casualty Care, and First Aid (ATP 4-02.11)
text:
Chapter 14



              Note. DO NOT probe, clean, or try to remove any foreign object from the abdomen. DO NOT
              touch with bare hands any exposed organs. DO NOT push organs back inside the body.

      14-5. It may be necessary to wear improvised dressing (for example strips of cloth, a t-shirt, or the cleanest
      material available). Stabilize any protruding or impaled objects and apply a sterile abdominal dressing as
      follows:

              Note. Protruding abdominal organs should be kept moist to prevent the tissue from drying out. A
              moist sterile dressing should be applied if available.

          •     Using the sterile side of the dressing, or other clean material, place any protruding organs near the
                wound. (DO NOT try to push organs back inside the body.)
          •     Ensure that the dressing is large enough to cover the entire mass of protruding organs or area of the
                wound.
          •     If large enough to cover the affected area, place the sterile side of the plastic wrapper directly over
                the wound.
          •     Moisten the dressing with clean water prior to placing a dressing over the exposed organs.
          •     Place the dressing directly on top of the wound or plastic wrapper, if used.
          •     Tie the dressings loosely at the casualty’s side.
      14-6. If two dressings are needed to cover a large wound, repeat steps in paragraph 15-5. If necessary, loosely
      cover the dressing with a cravat, elastic bandage, or gauze bandage. Tie them on the side of the casualty
      opposite to that of the dressing ties.
      14-7. To avoid causing further injury to the casualty—
          • Do not touch any exposed organs.
          • Do not try to push any exposed organs back into the body.
          • Do not tie the dressing tails tightly or directly over the wound.
          • Do not give the casualty anything by mouth.

              Note. Continue to evaluate the casualty and provide necessary first aid.

      14-8. Prepare the casualty for evacuation as follows:
          • Place the casualty on their back (face up) with the knees flexed.
          • Keep the patient warm, cover with a blanket as needed.
          • If evacuation is delayed, check the casualty for shock every five minutes.
          • Seek medical aid.
          • Record the procedures applied on DD Form 1380.
      14-9. The first responder continues to evaluate the casualties and is prepared to perform basic first aid
      measures. Always check for both entry and exit wounds. If there are two wounds (entry and exit), treat the
      wound that appears more serious first (for example, the heavier bleeding, protruding organs, larger wound,
      and so forth). It may be necessary to improvise dressings for the second wound by using strips of cloth, a t-
      shirt, or the cleanest material available.
      14-10. Use the casualty’s dressing from the first aid kit, not your own. If the dressing is not large enough to
      cover the entire wound, the plastic wrapper from the dressing may be used to cover the wound first (placing
      the dressing on top). Open the plastic wrapper carefully without touching the inner surface. If necessary,
      other improvised dressings may be made from clothing, blankets, or the cleanest materials available.
      14-11. Hypothermia prevention measures are taken with abdominal injuries due to the risk of rapid heat loss
      from the exposed abdominal cavity or organs. Moisten the dressing with clean water prior to placing a
      dressing over the exposed organs and seeking medical assistance.

BANDAGING
256B




          14-12. Expedient bandaging techniques are of paramount importance for the U.S. military due to their ability
          to provide immediate and effective medical care in combat situations. In the fast-paced and unpredictable
          nature of military operations, Service members often face severe injuries that require immediate attention to
          stabilize the wounded and prevent further harm. Expedient bandaging techniques enable military personnel
          to apply life-saving measures to control bleeding and increase the chances of survival for injured personnel.
          These techniques not only buy valuable time until medical help arrives but also contribute to the overall
          mission readiness by ensuring that Service members can continue their duties with confidence and knowing
          that essential medical support is readily available when needed.
SHOULDER BANDAGE
123B




          14-13. To apply shoulder bandages attached to the field first aid dressing—
              • Take one bandage across the chest, the other across the back, and under the arm opposite the injured
                  shoulder.
              • Tie the ends with a square knot (figure 14-3 on page 144).
              • Ensure that the bandages are snug but not too tight, allowing for proper circulation and comfort for
                  the casualty.

      14-14. To apply a bandage to the shoulder or armpit—
          • Make an extended bandage by using two cravats or an elastic bandage (figure 14-4 step A on page
              145); place the end of the first cravat along the base of the second one (figure 14-4 step B on page
              145).
          • Fold the two bandages into a single extended bandage (figure 14-4 step C on page 145).
          • Fold the extended bandage into a single cravat (figure 14-4 step D on page 145). After folding,
              secure the thicker part (overlap) with tape or two or more safety pins (figure 14-4 step E on page
              145).
          • Place the middle of the cravat under the armpit so that the front end is longer than the back end and
              safety pins are on the outside (figure 14-4 step F on page 145).
          • Cross the ends on top of the shoulder (figure 14-4 step G on page 145).
          • Take one of the bandages, which ends across the back and under the arm on the opposite side and
              the other end across the chest. Tie the ends (figure 14-4 step H on page 145).
      14-15. Be sure to place sufficient wadding in the armpit. DO NOT tie the bandage too tightly. Avoid
      compressing the major blood vessels in the armpit.

text:
Chapter 15
               Casualty Monitoring and Evacuation Preparation

CASUALTY MONITORING
258B




          15-1. After the first responder and CLS have treated the casualty in CUF and TFC phase of TCCC they may
          be required to continue to monitor the casualty and prepare the casualty for evacuation. The first responder
          and CLS cannot treat a casualty and then forget about them. The casualty must be continually monitored and
          reassessed prior to the casualty’s evacuation. The continued monitoring utilizing the MARCH-PAWS
          sequence will allow the first responder and CLS to identify changes in the casualty’s condition and initiate
          those interventions necessary to prevent unnecessary death.
          15-2. Casualty monitoring follows the same MARCH-PAWS process and will guide the first responder and
          CLS through their reassessments. After the initial casualty assessment and any treatments that are performed,
          the casualty must be reassessed every 15 minutes, or if seriously wounded every five to 10 minutes. The
          reassessment should start by reexamining any massive bleeding issues or interventions, should proceed
          through the rest of the MARCH-PAWS sequence, and be repeated until that casualty is transferred to the care
          of medical personnel.
          15-3. The first responder or CLS should next evaluate any changes in respiratory status, look for signs or
          symptoms of shock, hypothermia, or head injuries. Also, monitor the casualty's respiratory rate, pulse, and
          level of consciousness. Assessing the casualty's respiratory status involves checking the rate and the quality
          of the respirations. By looking, listening, and feeling for breaths on the cheek, the respiratory rate can be
          determined (documented in the number of breaths per minute) and the respiratory effort (shallow breaths,
          difficulties moving air in and out, and loss of air movement on one side of the chest).
          15-4. If a casualty becomes unconscious or breathing rate drops below eight respirations within one minute,
          insert an NPA. The casualty must be reassessed for tension pneumothorax and treated as necessary by
          performing an NDC. The NDC must be reassessed to confirm that it was successful. Document the rate,
          respiratory effort, and time assessed on DD Form 1380. If the casualty's respiratory status begins to change,
          reassess their status using the same approach used in the tactical trauma assessment.
          15-5. The level of consciousness is best expressed by addressing the casualty's response using the AVPU
          method. Document any AVPU assessments or any changes in the casualty's status on the DD Form 1380.
          This documentation helps medical personnel better understand the casualty's situation.

                Note. If the casualty is not ALERT, indicating decreased mental status, the casualty should not
                have weapons or communications equipment.

          15-6. Assessing the casualty's circulation status is done by checking for pulses. Depending on the casualty
          and their injuries, the first responder and CLS can check the casualty's pulse at the carotid artery (neck) or
          radial artery (wrist). The first responder and CLS should use their index and middle fingers, NOT their thumb,
          to check pulses (figure 15-1 on page 152). Document pulse rates, locations, and time taken on the DD Form
          1380.

                Note. The absence of a radial pulse is an indication that the casualty is in shock.

text:
Chapter 15




                                        Figure 15-1. Technique to Check the Pulse
             15-7. When requesting MEDEVAC, several preparatory actions are crucial for ensuring the casualty's safety
             and stability during transport. These steps include:
                 • Securing the Casualty's Weapons and Equipment: It is vital to secure all weapons and equipment
                      according to the SOPs or mission requirements. Due to the potential inability of casualties to manage
                      their own equipment owing to injuries or altered mental status, it is essential to secure these items
                      to prevent accidents. If possible, weapons should not accompany the casualty during evacuation. If
                      securing the weapon is not feasible, ensure it is cleared and rendered safe.
                 • Selecting Appropriate Litter: Choose a litter that aligns with both the casualty’s specific needs and
                      the mission profile to facilitate a safe and efficient evacuation.
                 • Preparing Equipment for Evacuation: Organize and prepare any equipment that is needed to
                      accompany the casualty. This includes medical supplies or specialized gear necessary for their
                      condition.
                 • Anticipating Environmental Factors: Consider environmental challenges that might impact the
                      casualty’s stability during evacuation. This includes extreme noises, vibrations from the transport
                      vehicle, high winds from propeller wash, and exposure to cold temperatures due to altitude or the
                      environment.
                 • Developing a Mitigation Plan: Formulate a plan to address each potential environmental threat to
                      maintain the casualty's stability throughout the evacuation process.
             15-8. It is important to note that medical personnel receiving the casualty may not be familiar with the
             equipment or have the means to secure it. Thus, preparing adequately and ensuring everything is in order
             prior to evacuation is critical for the safety and care of the casualty.

PRE-EVACUATION PROCEDURES, COMMUNICATION, AND
259B




DOCUMENTATION
             15-9. Pre-evacuation procedures bridge both TFC and Tactical Evacuation Care. Immediate life-threatening
             hemorrhage control, followed by the prevention and treatment of other injuries and complications have all
             been completed before most pre-evacuation procedures are initiated. Although, some of the communication
             and documentation may be ongoing during the TFC phase.
COMMUNICATING WITH THE CASUALTY
129B




             15-10. When providing care, the first responder or CLS should always talk to the injured person. Getting hurt
             can cause a lot of worry and fear, on top of the stress from combat. It helps to speak openly with them about
             what injuries they have and what you're doing to help. Let them know that you're doing everything possible
             for them and assure them that they're in good hands. This kind of support can help lessen their anxiety.
             15-11. It's important to be truthful about the injuries but keep a hopeful tone when talking about rescue and
             treatment. Chatting with the injured person is not only comforting but also lets you check how they are feeling
             mentally. Explaining what you're doing as you provide care can boost both your own confidence and the
             injured person's trust in you.

text:
Casualty Monitoring and Evacuation Preparation



COMMUNICATING WITH LEADERS
130B




          15-12. Communicate with leaders as soon as possible and throughout casualty treatment. Leaders need to
          understand the impact of casualties on the mission. Communicate with medical providers about details of the
          casualty injuries. This includes 9-line communication and ongoing MIST reports. Communication is also
          important, as the injured casualty may affect the success of the mission or change the tactical landscape.
MEDICAL DOCUMENTATION
13B




          15-13. Medical documentation may be difficult to accomplish in tactical prehospital settings, but it is
          important to the casualty's subsequent care that every effort should be made to document the care provided
          by first responders and medics throughout the trauma care continuum from point of wounding and injury to
          definitive care at the hospital. A DD Form 1380 is provided in each first aid kit.
          15-14. Based on the principles of TCCC, this card provides an easy way to document initial lifesaving care
          provided at the point of wounding. The card also serves as a prompt to remind first responders and CLS of
          the assessment and treatment steps of the MARCH-PAWS sequence. DD Form 1380 is relatively self-
          explanatory once personnel have been trained on using the form.
          15-15. The MIST information about the casualty informs the MEDEVAC request and can be collected
          simultaneously with the other required information. The MIST report transmits medical information to the
          receiving combat medic, evacuation platform, and MTF to better prepare for specific inbound casualties. A
          MIST report conveys additional evacuation information that may be required by commanders.
          15-16. Transitioning casualty care to another medical team is best accomplished with an oral discussion of
          the casualty's status, along with the written documentation on the DD Form 1380. When an oral hand-off is
          not a viable option, the written information may be the only way receiving medical personnel will know what
          the provider has done to help the casualty and what the next steps should be to provide the best care going
          forward.
          15-17. The DD Form 1380 (figure 15-2 on page 154) should be completed on every casualty before handoff
          to another provider or evacuation to an MTF. DD Form 1380 will follow the patient and will be used until
          the patient arrives at a role of care where a DD Form 3019 (Resuscitation Record), can be used.

                Note 1. This document should remain with the casualty throughout the prehospital evacuation
                system and become part of the casualty’s medical record upon reaching an MTF. The data from
                the DD Form 1380 will also be uploaded into the DOD Trauma Registry maintained by the JTS.

                Note 2. Many commercially available casualty cards do not replicate all information requirements
                of the DD Form 1380. While the DD Form 1380 may be reproduced locally, it should be on
                waterproof paper or laminated with a means of attaching it to the casualty. It is best to have an
                indelible or permanent marker available for writing on the TCCC Card.

             15-19. First responders and CLS personnel are advised to fill out the DD Form 1380 to the best of their
             ability. DD Form 1380 is crucial as it records evidence of initial treatment and provides subsequent levels of
             medical care with essential information. This documentation is vital for medical personnel to assess and
             determine the appropriate continuation of care for the casualty. This process ensures that each step of medical
             intervention is informed and based on prior actions taken, facilitating a cohesive and effective treatment
             pathway.
MEDICAL EVACUATION REQUEST
132B




             15-20. Every Service member should be able to initiate a 9-line MEDEVAC request. The standard
             MEDEVAC request has nine lines. However, lines one through five are required before a MEDEVAC can
             be launched. Using a phonetic alphabet and following the unit's normal communications procedures, call in:
                  • Grid location.
                  • Radio frequency and call sign.
                  • Number of casualties by precedence.
                  • Equipment that needs to be brought by the evacuation team.
                  • Number of litter and ambulatory casualties.
             15-21. Before initiating a 9-line MEDEVAC request, collect all the information needed. When calling in, be
             sure to follow all appropriate communication protocols and guidance.
             15-22. Depending on operational, mission variables, and availability, evacuation options may involve
             MEDEVAC, CASEVAC, or a combination of the two. During CASEVAC, casualties are moved without
             medical regulating and do not possess a protected status under the Geneva Conventions. As such, CASEVAC
             platforms may be engaged by enemy forces. With MEDEVAC, patients may be regulated or unregulated and
             the ambulance is properly marked, MEDEVAC cannot be used for nonmedical missions without losing its
             protected status. The 9-line MEDEVAC request is communicated through the designated evacuation system
             or Patient Evacuation Coordination Cell, depending on orders and the tactical SOP.
             15-23. When a Service member requests a MEDEVAC, they are not directly coordinating with a medical
             provider but are explaining the requestor’s evacuation requirements with someone who coordinates the
             movement assets. Although they still require some general information about the status of the casualty, much
             of the information that they need to coordinate evacuation is not clinical and relates to logistical and
             operational issues.
             15-24. Communicate with medical providers on the evacuation asset if possible and relay the MIST report.
             Provide additional information as appropriate. For additional information on MEDEVAC request refer to
             ATP 4-02.2.

text:
Casualty Monitoring and Evacuation Preparation



EVACUATION EQUIPMENT AND CASUALTY PACKAGING
260B




          15-25. Essential evacuation equipment (for example, litters, packaging materials, and BVMs) should be
          prepared by other unit personnel while medical treatment continues and coordinating with the casualty
          treatment team to save time. For example, other unit members can prepare litters while treatment is being
          provided. Do not delay getting casualties onto litters. The first responder and CLS can better prevent
          hypothermia by getting casualties off the ground.
LITTERS
13B




          15-26. Casualty movement in TFC may be better accomplished using litter due to the tactical situation and
          the need to move casualties rapidly. The litter exists only to facilitate casualty movement, and the casualty
          can be placed in the best position that facilitates their care and comfort. Casualties do not have to be placed
          on their backs on a litter. It is easier to move them if they are already on the litter; however, they must be
          secured to the litter before movement. Litter is also usually better for moving a casualty long distance.
          15-27. All unit members should know how to open and set up litters and rehearse their use during pre-mission
          training. All unit members should know who will carry litter or where litter is located on vehicles.
          15-28. Selecting the proper litter is dependent on several different factors:
              • The evacuation platform.
              • The terrain at the location of pick-up.
              • The casualty’s injuries.
              • The availability of different types of litters.
          15-29. Two of the more common litters often used are the quad-folding litter and the lightweight flexible
          stretchers. Each of them has advantages and disadvantages and maybe the proper litter depends on the
          situation. For example, flexible litter can be moved using a one-person drag (terrain permitting) but are more
          difficult to carry longer distances than a quad-folding litter.
          15-30. Each unit will have litters that have been proven to support their mission profile, and it is important
          to be aware of the limitations and advantages of each litter at your disposal before being deployed in a
          situation where you will require them.
CASUALTY PACKAGING
134B




          15-31. When preparing a casualty for evacuation, the first responder or CLS need to anticipate the
          environmental factors that could prevent the casualty from remaining stable. Examples include extreme
          noises, vibrations, high winds from propeller washing, and exposure to cold environments from either altitude
          or low ambient temperatures. A plan should be developed to mitigate each of those potential threats when
          preparing for your casualty.
          15-32. All loose ends of bandages, medical equipment, and hypothermia prevention materials should be
          secured. The first responder or CLS should prevent dressings and other medical items from being blown
          around by the rotor wash or becoming entangled with other equipment.
          15-33. Loose materials can catch on anything from tree limbs to body-armor of litter bearers, to parts of the
          aircraft or vehicles. Any snag like this can cause delays in evacuation or even further injury to casualties or
          providers. Blankets and foil-based hypothermia materials are especially susceptible to being caught in the
          wind.
          15-34. Hypothermia prevention equipment should be tucked and secured beneath the casualty and litter
          straps. Loose edges can be caught up in wind or rotor wash or snagged on objects in the helicopter as the
          casualty is loaded aboard.
          15-35. The TQs should remain visible and not be hidden. The DD Form 1380 should be attached to the
          casualty.

Evacuation Considerations for Suspected Spinal Injuries
371B




             15-36. A spinal injury should be expected in certain situations, like fast-roping falls or being near a significant
             blast. In those cases, when tactically feasible, ensure the C-spine is immobilized and the casualty is kept
             straight during evacuation. Keep the litter type and evacuation platform in mind and ensure the evacuation
             ground or air vehicle can accommodate the selected litter.

Walking Wounded
372B




             15-37. Not all casualties require a litter for evacuation. For those casualties who are still ambulatory, provide
             instructions or assistance as needed. Depending on the nature of their injuries, they may be able to assist with
             carrying litters or providing security.
             15-38. It is best to guide disoriented or visually impaired casualties by having them place their hand on the
             shoulder of the casualty in front of them, or a nonmedical attendant as they move to the evacuation platform.
             Instruct them on repeatedly checking their own wounds and dressings to ensure that bleeding remains
             controlled throughout the evacuation process.

CASUALTY STAGING
261B




             15-39. A particular importance when moving more than one casualty is the process of staging the casualties.
             Based on the guidance from the MEDEVAC personnel, certain casualties have priority and may need to be
             loaded last, so that they are the first ones offloaded at the destination.
             15-40. If not given specific guidance, place the most serious casualty in a position where they are loaded last,
             and have casualties who may be less severely injured loaded before them. The first responder or CLS may
             also need to assist in marking the LZ, providing security, or assisting in marshalling the aircraft or litter-
             bearer teams.

EVACUATION CARE AFTER-ACTION REVIEW
26B




             15-41. It is critical that documentation of personnel, injury, and treatment be annotated using DD Form 1380
             and should be completed prior to any handoff of the casualty. If care cannot be documented using the DD
             Form 1380 at the point of care by the first responder or CLS, it should be documented using the TCCC after
             action review, found on the JTS website, as soon as possible (within 72 hours) after treatment. The
             nonmedical first responder or CLS should follow up with the supporting unit medical personnel to complete
             and submit the TCCC after action review.

text:
PART THREE
                                                      291B




           FIRST AID PROCEDURES FOR NON-TACTICAL
           294B




               COMBAT CASUALTY CARE INJURIES
          In the operational environment, Service members are exposed to risks and receive
          injuries beyond those caused by an operational event. First aid skills play a vital role
          in ensuring the safety and well-being of Service members. As personnel participate in
          outdoor activities and training, the potential for accidents or injuries increases. Having
          a solid foundation in first aid equips Service members with the necessary knowledge
          and abilities to respond swiftly and effectively in times of emergencies. Whether it's
          treating minor cuts and bruises, providing initial care for more serious injuries, or even
          saving lives, the importance of first aid skills cannot be overstated. By acquiring these
          skills, Service members not only become more responsible and capable individuals,
          but they also contribute to creating a safer environment for themselves and others.

                                                             Chapter 16
                                               Bites and Stings

OVERVIEW OF BITES AND STINGS
263B




          16-1. Bites and stings are common occurrences that can happen in almost every environment. From pesky
          mosquito bites to venomous snakebites, these encounters with creatures big and small can lead to a range of
          discomfort, pain, and even potential danger. Understanding the various types of bites and stings, their causes,
          and proper treatment is crucial for minimizing the associated risks and ensuring a swift recovery.
          16-2. Poison and venom are terms often used interchangeably, but they have distinct differences in their
          mode of delivery and the way they affect living organisms. A poison is a substance that is harmful or lethal
          when ingested, inhaled, or absorbed through the skin. It is typically produced by plants, animals, or
          microorganisms as a defensive mechanism. Poisonous substances can be found in various forms, such as
          toxins in certain plants, chemicals in household products, or even certain medications when taken in excessive
          amounts. The key characteristic of poison is that it needs to be ingested or absorbed into the body to cause
          harm.
          16-3. Venom is a specialized secretion that is actively injected into another organism. It is typically produced
          by certain animals, such as snakes, spiders, scorpions, and some insects. Venom is delivered through
          specialized organs, such as fangs, stingers, or spines, and is primarily used for hunting or self-defense. Unlike
          poison, venom is actively injected into the victim's bloodstream, tissues, or body cavities, often leading to
          localized or systemic effects, which can range from pain and swelling to paralysis or even death. The main
          distinction between poison and venom lies in their delivery method. Poison is harmful when ingested or
          absorbed, while venom is specifically injected into another organism through specialized organs.
          16-4. If bites and stings are not treated promptly and correctly, they may cause serious illness or death. The
          severity of a snakebite depends upon whether the snake is venomous or nonvenomous, the type of snake, the
          location of the bite, and the amount of venom injected. Bites from humans and other animals, such as dogs,
          cats, bats, raccoons, and rats, can cause severe bruises and infection and tears or lacerations of tissue.
          Awareness of the potential sources of injuries can reduce or prevent them from occurring. Knowledge and
          prompt application of first aid measures can lessen the severity of injuries from bites and stings and keep the
          Service member from becoming a serious casualty.

text:
Chapter 16



HUMAN OR ANIMAL BITES
264B




             16-5. First aid for human or animal bites aims to prevent infection and provide initial care for the wound. To
             perform first aid for a human or animal bite:
                 • Remove yourself from further harm. If dealing with an animal bite, ensure that you are no longer at
                      risk of being bitten again.
                 • Control bleeding. If the bite wound is bleeding, apply direct pressure with a clean cloth or sterile
                      gauze to stop or minimize the bleeding. Elevating the wound, if possible, can also help reduce
                      bleeding.
                 • Clean the wound. Rinse the bite wound thoroughly with clean water or saline solution to flush out
                      any dirt, bacteria, or saliva that may have entered the wound. Gently remove any debris from the
                      wound using mild soap and water.
                 • Apply an antiseptic. After cleaning, apply an antiseptic solution or ointment to the wound to help
                      reduce the risk of infection. Follow the instructions on the product label and ensure it is suitable for
                      use on open wounds.
                 • Cover the wound. Use a sterile dressing or clean bandage to cover the wound. This will protect it
                      from further contamination and promote healing. Change dressing regularly to maintain cleanliness.
                 • Seek medical attention. It is important to seek medical evaluation for all animal bites, especially
                      those from unfamiliar or wild animals, deep wounds, or those that become red, swollen, or
                      increasingly painful. A health care professional can assess the severity of the bite, prescribe
                      antibiotics if necessary, and administer tetanus prophylaxis if required.
             16-6. If someone gets bitten by an animal, whether known, unknown, wild, or domestic, the primary concern
             is rabies. Unless the animal is someone's pet and verified to be up to date on rabies, the individual who has
             been bitten must get the rabies post-exposure vaccine. Seemingly minor bites can lead to infection, so it is
             essential to consult a health care professional to determine the appropriate course of action and receive any
             necessary medical treatment.

                   Note. If unable to capture or kill the animal, provide medical personnel with any information that
                   will help identify it.

MARINE (SEA) ANIMALS
135B




             16-7. Except for sharks and barracuda, most marine animals will not deliberately attack. The most frequent
             injuries from marine animals are wounds by biting, stinging, or puncturing. Wounds inflicted by marine
             animals can be very painful but are rarely fatal.
             16-8. Wounds from sharks, barracuda, and crocodilian can involve major trauma because of bites and
             lacerations. Bites from large marine animals are potentially the most life-threatening of all injuries from
             marine animals. Major wounds from these animals can be treated by controlling the bleeding, preventing
             shock, giving basic life support, splinting the injury, and by securing prompt medical aid.
             16-9. Turtles, moray eels, and corals normally inflict minor wounds. Treat by cleansing the wound(s)
             thoroughly and by splinting if necessary.
             16-10. Jellyfish, anemones, and others marine animals inflict injury by means of stinging cells in their
             tentacles. Contact with the tentacles produces burning pain with a rash and small hemorrhages on the skin.
             Shock, muscular cramping, nausea, vomiting, and respiratory distress may also occur. Gently remove the
             clinging tentacles with a towel and wash or treat the area. Use diluted ammonia or alcohol, a meat tenderizer,
             and talcum powder. If symptoms become severe or persist, seek medical assistance.
             16-11. Spiny fish, urchins, stingrays, and cone shells inject their venom by puncturing the skin with their
             spines. General signs and symptoms include swelling, nausea, vomiting, generalized cramps, diarrhea,
             muscular paralysis, and shock. Deaths are rare. Treatment consists of soaking the wound(s) in hot water
             (when available) for 30 to 60 minutes. This inactivates the heat sensitive toxin. In addition, further first aid
             measures should be taken such as controlling bleeding or applying a dressing. This should be carried out as
             necessary.

                                                        CAUTION
                       Be careful not to scald the casualty with water that is too hot because
                       the pain of the wound will mask the normal reaction to heat.


SNAKE BITES
136B




          16-12. Snakebites can occur unexpectedly during outdoor activities or encounters with snakes in their natural
          habitats. Understanding how to identify snakes, knowing the proper steps to take after a snakebite, and having
          a grasp of basic first aid techniques can significantly increase the chances of a positive outcome in such
          situations. Snakes are categorized between nonvenomous and venomous snakes.
          16-13. Snakes can be categorized into various groups based on different characteristics. One common
          classification system categorizes snakes into four main categories of colubrid snakes, constrictor snakes, non-
          venomous snakes, and venomous snakes. These categories may overlap, and some snakes may possess traits
          from multiple categories. Understanding the different categories of snakes can aid in snake identification,
          assessing potential risks, and knowing how to respond appropriately in various situations.

Colubrid Snakes
37B




          16-14. Colubrid snakes represent the largest snake family and include a wide range of non-venomous species.
          These snakes have diverse habitats, sizes, and feeding habits. Common colubrid snakes include rat, king,
          gopher, and water snakes.

Constrictor Snakes
374B




          16-15. Constrictor snakes are non-venomous snakes that subdue their prey by coiling around them and
          squeezing until they can no longer breathe. Constrictors then swallow their prey whole. Well-known
          constrictor snakes include boas, pythons, and anacondas.

Non-venomous Snakes
375B




          16-16. Non-venomous snakes include snakes that lack venom glands or fangs and pose no direct threat to
          humans. Non-venomous snakes play an essential role in controlling rodent populations and maintaining
          ecological balance. Examples of non-venomous snakes are boas, pythons, corn, and garter snakes.
          16-17. There are approximately 130 different varieties of nonvenomous snakes in the U.S. They have oval-
          shaped heads and round eyes. Unlike venomous snakes, discussed below, nonvenomous snakes do not have
          fangs with which to inject venom. Figure 16-1 depicts the characteristics of a nonvenomous snake.

text:
Chapter 16



Venomous Snakes
376B




             16-18. Venomous snakes possess venom glands and specialized fangs to inject venom into their prey or as a
             defense mechanism. It is important to exercise caution and seek immediate medical attention in the event of
             a venomous snakebite.
             16-19. It is important to note that the distribution of venomous snakes may vary within states, and some
             species may be specific to certain regions. When spending time in areas known to have venomous snakes, it
             is crucial to be aware of the local species, understand their habitats and behavior, and take appropriate
             precautions to avoid encounters and bites.
             16-20. Venomous snakes in other parts of the world include sea snakes, the Fer-De-Lance, the Bushmaster,
             tropical rattlesnake in tropical Central America; the Malayan pit viper in the tropical Far East; the cobra in
             Africa and Asia; the mamba (or black mamba) in central and southern Africa; and the krait in India and
             Southeast Asia.

Categories of Venomous Snakes
421B




             16-21. Venomous snakes can be categorized into several groups based on their characteristics and taxonomic
             classification. The following are some common categories of venomous snakes:
                  • Vipers.
                  • Elapids.
                  • Rear-Fanged Snakes.
                  • Burrowing Asps.
                  • Sea Snakes.
             16-22. These categories provide a general overview of the different types of venomous snakes based on their
             taxonomic families and key characteristics. It's important to note that there may be variations within each
             category, and some venomous snakes may exhibit characteristics from multiple families.
             16-23. This family of snakes includes some of the most well-known venomous snakes. Vipers are
             characterized by their large, triangular heads, heat-sensing pits between their eyes and nostrils, and hinged
             fangs that can fold back when not in use. Examples include rattlesnakes, copperheads, and cottonmouths or
             water moccasins. See figure 16-2 for characteristics of a venomous pit viper and figure 16-3 on page 163
             provides examples of viper snakes.




                                 Figure 16-2. Characteristics of the venomous pit viper

   16-24. In the U.S, there are several species of venomous snakes. The following are some of the venomous
   snakes commonly found in different regions of the country:
       • Rattlesnakes: Rattlesnakes are a group of venomous snakes known for the rattling sound they
            produce by shaking their tails. Species such as the eastern and western diamondback, timber and
            Mojave rattlesnakes are found in various parts of the U.S.
       • Copperheads: Copperheads are venomous snakes with distinctive copper-colored heads. They are
            commonly found in the eastern and southeastern regions of the U.S.
       • Cottonmouths or Water Moccasins: Cottonmouths or Water Moccasins are venomous semi-aquatic
            snakes primarily found in the southeastern U.S. They are known for their aggressive behavior and
            are often encountered near bodies of water.
       • Coral Snakes: Coral snakes are venomous snakes with colorful bands of red, yellow, and black. The
            Eastern and Texas Coral Snakes are found in specific regions of the southern U.S.
       • Various Pit Vipers: Pit vipers include venomous snakes that possess heat-sensing pits between their
            eyes and nostrils. Along with rattlesnakes and copperheads, this category includes species such as
            the eastern and western Massasauga Rattlesnakes, and the Mojave Desert Sidewinder.
   16-25. The casualty’s condition provides the best information about the seriousness of the situation and how
   much time has passed since the bite occurred. Pit viper bites are characterized by severe burning pain.
   Discoloration and swelling around the fang marks usually begins within five to ten minutes after the bite. If
   only minimal swelling occurs within 30 minutes, the bite will almost certainly have been from a
   nonvenomous snake or possibly from a venomous snake, which did not inject venom. The venom destroys
   blood cells, causing a general discoloration of the skin. Blisters and numbness in the affected area follow this
   reaction. Other signs, which can occur, are weakness, rapid pulse, nausea, shortness of breath, vomiting, and
   shock.
   16-26. The venom of viper bites affects the circulatory system and destroys muscle. Severe pain, swelling
   and change in skin color usually develop within five to 10 minutes and slowly spreads. After several hours,
   the following signs and symptoms will occur:
        • Further swelling and changes in skin color.
        • Bleeding blisters.
        • Numbness of the affected area.
   16-27. Other signs and symptoms which may occur include:
       • Weaknesses.
       • Rapid pulse.
       • Nausea.
       • Vomiting.
       • Shortness of breath.
       • Sweating.
       • Shock.
