text:
Chapter 16



      16-28. Elapids are a family of venomous snakes known for their fixed front fangs and potent neurotoxic
      venom. They generally have slender bodies and smooth scales. Famous elapid snakes include cobras, coral
      snakes, kraits, and mambas. Corals (figure 16-4), cobras (figure 16-5), kraits, and mambas all belong to the
      same group even though they are found in different parts of the world. All four inject their venom through
      short, grooved fangs, leaving a characteristic bite pattern.




                       Figure 16-4. The Coral snake              Figure 16-5. The Cobra
                                 example                             snake example

      16-29. To identify a coral snake, a common phrase used in the U.S. is “Red or yellow, kill a fellow; red on
      black, venom lack.” This phrase refers to the color pattern on the snake's bands and serves as a mnemonic
      device to help distinguish coral snakes from non-venomous snakes with similar markings, such as milk or
      scarlet kingsnakes. Coral snakes have red bands touching yellow bands, while non-venomous snakes have
      red bands touching black bands. It's important to remember that this phrase is specific to the U.S. and may
      not apply to coral snake species found in other regions. When encountering any snake, it is advisable to
      maintain a safe distance and seek professional assistance if unsure of its venomous nature.
      16-30. The venom from corals, cobras, kraits, and mambas, which belong to the elapid family, notably affects
      the central nervous system, producing a distinct set of symptoms that diverge from those caused by pit vipers.
      Initially, these bites may result in only minimal pain and swelling, leading many individuals to underestimate
      the severity of the bite. Typically, the onset of neurological symptoms occurs within one to seven hours post-
      bite, including blurred vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, drowsiness, and an increase in salivation and
      sweating.
      16-31. If the bite is not addressed quickly with appropriate medical intervention, more severe symptoms can
      manifest, such as nausea, vomiting, respiratory difficulties, shock, and eventually more critical conditions
      like paralysis, convulsions, and coma. This progression underscores the necessity of recognizing the potential
      danger of elapid bites early and seeking immediate medical treatment to mitigate these serious outcomes.
      16-32. While most rear-fanged snakes are non-venomous, some species within this family possess venomous
      rear fangs. These fangs are located toward the back of the mouth and are used to subdue their prey. Rear-
      fanged venomous snakes include boomslangs, mangrove, and vine snakes.
      16-33. Burrowing asps are a family of venomous snakes primarily found in Africa and parts of the Middle
      East. They have small, fixed front fangs and are adapted for burrowing in sandy or loose soil. Examples
      include the stiletto snakes and mole vipers.
      16-34. Sea snakes are a group of venomous snakes that have adapted to life in aquatic environments. They
      have paddle-shaped tails and can be found in the coastal waters of the Indian and Pacific Oceans. Sea snakes
      have highly potent venom but are generally not aggressive towards humans.
      16-35. Sea snakes (figure 16-6 on page 165) are found in the warm water areas of the Pacific and Indian
      Oceans, along the coasts, and at the mouths of some larger rivers. Their venom is VERY venomous, but their
      fangs are only ¼ inch long.

text:
Bites and Stings




                                          Figure 16-6. The Sea snake example

Venomous Snakebite
42B




          16-36. Venomous snakes DO NOT always inject venom when they bite or strike a person. However, all
          snakes may carry tetanus (lockjaw); anyone bitten by a snake, whether venomous or nonvenomous, should
          immediately seek medical attention.
          16-37. Venom is injected from the venom sacs through grooved or hollowed fangs. Depending on the species,
          these fangs are either long or short. Pit vipers have long hollow fangs. These fangs are folded against the roof
          of the mouth and extend when the snake strikes. This allows them to strike quickly and then withdraw.
          Cobras, coral snakes, kraits, mambas, and sea snakes have short, grooved fangs. These snakes are less
          effective in their attempts to bite, since they must chew after striking to inject enough venom (poison) to be
          effective.
          16-38. In the event you are bitten, do not attempt to identify and or kill the snake. Freshly killed snakes can
          continue to bite due to reflexive action. Snake identification is not critical. Medical personnel will treat
          symptoms by geography and not someone’s best guess at a species.
          16-39. The venoms of different snakes cause different effects. Pit viper venom (hemotoxin [blood toxin])
          destroys tissue and blood cells. Cobras, adders, and coral snakes inject powerful venom (neurotoxin [nerve
          toxin]) which affects the central nervous system, causing respiratory paralysis. Water moccasins and sea
          snakes have venom that is both hemotoxic and neurotoxic.
FIRST AID FOR A SNAKEBITE
137B




          16-40. In the event of a snakebite, prompt first aid is crucial to minimizing the potential effects of the venom.
          To perform first aid for a snakebite:
              • Stay calm and call for medical assistance immediately. Provide medical personnel with information
                   about the snake, if possible, but do not attempt to capture or kill the snake as it may increase the risk
                   of further bites.
              • Keep the bitten Service member as still and calm as possible. Restrict movement and avoid
                   unnecessary exertion, as it can accelerate the spread of venom in the bloodstream.
              • Remove any constricting items, such as jewelry or tight clothing, from the affected area, as swelling
                   may occur.
              • Position the affected limb slightly below the level of the heart, if possible. This can help slow the
                   spread of venom.
              • Cleanse the wound gently with mild soap and water to reduce the risk of infection. Do not apply ice
                   or use a TQ, as they are not effective and can cause additional harm.
              • Apply a sterile bandage or dress over the bite, ensuring it is snug but not too tight. This can help
                   immobilize the area and reduce the spread of venom.
              • Encourage the person to remain calm and still, while waiting for medical help to arrive. Monitor
                   their vital signs, such as breathing and heart rate, and be prepared to administer CPR if necessary.

text:
Chapter 16



             16-41. The above steps are general guidelines and may vary depending on the snake species and the region.
             It is crucial to seek medical attention immediately after a snakebite, as they can provide appropriate anti-
             venom treatment and further evaluate the situation.


                                                             CAUTION
                          DO NOT attempt to cut open the bite or suck out the venom. If the
                          venom should seep through any damaged or lacerated tissues in your
                          mouth, you could immediately lose consciousness or even die.


             16-42. If accompanying the casualty on CASEVAC to an MTF, observe the casualty carefully for signs and
             symptoms of an allergic reaction. Continue to monitor the airway, breathing, circulation, vital signs (for first
             aid purposes; pulse, and respiration), and distal pulse of the bitten extremity, treating for shock, and
             conserving body heat.

INSECT (ARTHROPOD) BITES AND STINGS
265B




             16-43. An insect bite or sting can cause great pain, allergic reaction, inflammation, and infection. If not
             treated correctly, some bites or stings may cause serious illness or even death. When an allergic reaction is
             not involved, first aid is a simple process. In any case, medical personnel should examine the casualty at the
             earliest possible time. It is important to identify spiders, bees, or creatures that cause bites or sting, especially
             in cases of an allergic reaction.
             16-44. The insects found throughout the world that can produce a bite or sting are too numerous to mention
             in detail. Commonly encountered stinging or biting insects include the brown recluse spiders, black widow
             spiders, tarantulas, scorpions, urticating caterpillars, bees, wasps, centipedes, conenose beetles (kissing
             bugs), ants, and wheel bugs. Upon being reassigned, especially to overseas areas, take the time to become
             acquainted with the types of insects to avoid.
             16-45. Arthropods are segmented invertebrates with jointed antennae and legs. They include insects,
             arachnids, centipedes, and millipedes. See figure 16-7 for examples of venomous arthropods.




                                              Figure 16-7. Venomous Arthropods
             16-46. Of all deaths due to venomous stings or bites in a year, most are caused by arthropods. Most injuries
             resulting from venomous arthropods can be prevented by doing the following:
                 • If you are allergic to certain stings or bites, be prepared with the proper medication.
                 • Ask the local inhabitants about the local venomous and harmful arthropods.
                 • Avoid touching unfamiliar arthropods or allowing them to touch you.
                 • Watch where you put your hands and feet.
                 • Before using it, check places where harmful arthropods may hide.
                      ▪ Closets, wall spaces, doorways, and eaves.
                      ▪ Outdoor privies and latrine boxes.

text:
Bites and Stings



                   ▪ Bed clothing, beds, and sleeping bags.
                   ▪ Shoes, boots, and clothing.
                   ▪ Logs, felled trees, and leaves.
                   ▪ Rocks, boards, and debris.
              •    Avoid beehives, ant and wasp nests, and spider webs.
              •    Wear foot protection (shoes, boots, and sandals) always.
              •    Hang up clothes.
              •    Practice good sanitation by removing debris, trash, and board piles.
              •    Avoid wearing deodorants, colognes, perfumes, or cosmetics with fragrances.
INSECTS
138B




          16-47. An insect is a small invertebrate animal characterized by having a segmented body, three pairs of legs,
          and often one or two pairs of wings. Insects are a diverse group, with over a million known species, and they
          play important roles in ecosystems as pollinators, decomposers, and prey for other organisms.
          16-48. First aid treatment for insect bites can vary depending on the type of insect and the individual's
          reaction. The general first aid steps for treating insect bites are:
              • Remove the stinger (if applicable): In the case of stinging insects like bees or wasps, it's important
                    to remove the stinger as quickly as possible to prevent further venom injection. Gently scrape it off
                    the skin using a blunt edge like a credit card or your fingernail. Avoid squeezing the venom sac, as
                    it may release more venom.
              • Wash the bite area: Clean the bite site with mild soap and water to reduce the risk of infection. Be
                    gentle and avoid excessive scrubbing.
              • Apply a cold compress: To alleviate pain, reduce swelling, and minimize itching, apply a cold
                    compress or an ice pack wrapped in a cloth to the bite area. Do this for 10-15 minutes at a time,
                    several times a day.
              • Use over-the-counter remedies: Over-the-counter topical creams, ointments, or sprays containing
                    ingredients such as hydrocortisone, calamine lotion, or antihistamines can help relieve itching and
                    inflammation. Follow the instructions and precautions on the product packaging.
              • Take oral antihistamines: If itching or swelling persists, you can take over-the-counter oral
                    antihistamine to help reduce allergic reactions and relieve symptoms. Consult a pharmacist or health
                    care professional for appropriate dosage and recommendations.
              • Avoid scratching: Although it may be tempting, refrain from scratching the insect bite to prevent
                    further irritation, infection, or the development of a secondary skin condition.
              • Monitor for severe reactions: In rare cases, insect bites can cause severe allergic reactions, known
                    as anaphylaxis. If you experience symptoms such as difficulty breathing, dizziness, swelling of the
                    face or throat, or a widespread rash, seek immediate medical attention.
          16-49. If the insect type is unknown or if the Service member is experiencing severe or worsening symptoms,
          it is best to consult a health care professional for proper evaluation and guidance.
ARACHNIDS
139B




          16-50. An arachnid is a class of joint-legged invertebrate animals that include spiders, scorpions, ticks, and
          mites. Arachnids are part of the phylum Arthropoda, which also includes insects, crustaceans, and millipedes.
          16-51. Arachnids are characterized by having two main body segments: the cephalothorax (a fused head and
          thorax region) and the abdomen. They typically have four pairs of legs attached to the cephalothorax and
          possess specialized mouthparts called chelicerae, which are used for feeding and defense. Most arachnids
          also have specialized structures like spinnerets for producing silk (used by spiders for web-building) and a
          pair of pedipalps that may serve various functions depending on the species.
          16-52. While spiders are perhaps the most well-known arachnids, other arachnids exhibit unique features.
          Scorpions have large pincers and a long tail ending in a venomous stinger. Ticks and mites are tiny arachnids
          that often parasitize animals, including humans, and can transmit diseases. Some arachnids, such as daddy
          longlegs and sun spiders, have distinct body shapes and behaviors.

             16-53. Arachnids play diverse roles in ecosystems. Spiders, for example, are predators of insects and help
             control their populations. Arachnids have adapted to various habitats worldwide, from deserts to forests to
             aquatic environments. Arachnids are a diverse group of invertebrates that exhibit a wide range of adaptations,
             behaviors, and ecological roles within the animal kingdom.
SPIDERS
140B




             16-54. Among the many species of spiders found around the world, a few are known for their potentially
             dangerous bites. The most well-known dangerous spider species are the:
                 • Brazilian Wandering Spider.
                 • Sydney Funnel-web Spider.
                 • Black Widow Spider.
                 • Brown Recluse Spider.
             16-55. The Brazilian Wandering Spider is found in South and Central America and is known for its highly
             venomous bite. It is considered one of the most venomous spiders in the world. Their venom can cause severe
             pain, priapism (prolonged erection), and, in rare cases, can be life-threatening.
             16-56. The Sydney Funnel-web Spider is found in Australia, the Sydney Funnel-web Spider is highly
             venomous and can be aggressive when threatened. Their venom is potent and can cause severe symptoms,
             including muscle spasm, difficulty breathing, and in rare cases, it can be fatal. Prompt medical attention is
             crucial if bitten.
             16-57. The Black Widow Spider is found in various parts of the world. Females have a distinctive black body
             with a red hourglass-shaped mark on the abdomen. Their venom contains neurotoxins that can cause intense
             pain, muscle cramps, nausea, and in severe cases, can affect the nervous system. While bites are rarely fatal,
             medical attention is still recommended.
             16-58. The Brown Recluse Spider is found primarily in the U.S. Their bites can cause tissue necrosis (cell
             death), leading to an ulcerous wound that may require medical attention. Other symptoms can include pain,
             itching, and systemic effects.
             16-59. While these spiders are considered dangerous, actual bites and severe reactions are relatively rare.
             Most spiders are not aggressive and will only bite in self-defense. If bitten by a spider and experiencing
             severe symptoms, seek immediate medical attention.
             16-60. Specific risks associated with spider bites can vary depending on a Service member’s health,
             sensitivity, and potential allergies. Therefore, it is always advisable to exercise caution around spiders and
             seek professional medical advice if a bite occurs.
SCORPION
14B




             16-61. The most dangerous scorpions are typically found in regions with warm climates, particularly in arid
             or desert areas. Some locations known for housing dangerous scorpion species are:
                 • North Africa.
                 • Middle East.
                 • Mexico.
                 • Brazil.
                 • India.
             16-62. Countries in North Africa, such as Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, and Egypt, are home to highly
             venomous scorpion species. These species include the Deathstalker scorpion and the Androc tonus australis.
             16-63. Several countries in the Middle East have venomous scorpions, including Saudi Arabia, Iran, Iraq,
             Jordan, and Yemen. The Deathstalker scorpion is found in this region, along with other dangerous species
             such as the Arabian Fat-tailed scorpion and the Palestine Yellow scorpion.
             16-64. Mexico is known for its diverse scorpion fauna, and it is home to several highly venomous species.
             The Bark scorpion is found in various parts of the country, including the notorious Arizona Bark scorpion,
             which is also found in the southwestern U.S.

          16-65. In Brazil, the Brazilian Yellow scorpion is considered one of the most venomous scorpions. It is
          primarily found in southeastern and southern regions of the country.
          16-66. India is home to several dangerous scorpion species. The Indian Red scorpion and the Indian Black
          scorpion are found to live in this region.
          16-67. While these regions have known populations of dangerous scorpions, encounters with venomous
          scorpions and severe envenomation are relatively rare. However, it is always advisable to exercise caution
          and take necessary precautions when in scorpion-prone areas. Figure 16-8 provides an example of a scorpion.




                                                   Figure 16-8. Scorpion
CENTIPEDES
142B




          16-68. A centipede is a type of arthropod characterized by elongated, multi-segmented creatures with
          numerous pairs of legs, ranging from tens to hundreds depending on the species. Centipedes are found in
          various habitats worldwide, including forests, deserts, and tropical regions.
          16-69. While most centipedes are not considered dangerous to humans, some larger species possess
          venomous pincers or fangs located on their first pair of legs. When threatened or provoked, they can deliver
          a painful sting or bite. The severity of the reaction to a centipede sting can vary depending on the species and
          the individual's sensitivity to the venom. Centipede bites are painful but not life-threatening. If a Service
          member is stung by a centipede, first aid steps to take are:
               • Stay calm and move away from the centipede to avoid further stings.
               • Wash the affected area gently with soap and water to clean the wound and reduce the risk of
                   infection.
               • Apply a cold compress or ice pack wrapped in a cloth to the sting site. This can help alleviate pain
                   and reduce swelling.
               • Take over-the-counter pain relievers, such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen, to manage pain if
                   necessary. Follow the instructions and recommended dosage.
               • Keep the sting site clean and dry and avoid scratching or irritating the area to prevent infection.
          16-70. If there are signs of an allergic reaction, such as difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or
          widespread hives, seek immediate medical attention.
MILLIPEDES
143B




          16-71. Millipedes, belonging to the class Diplopoda, are arthropods distinguished by their elongated,
          segmented bodies with two pairs of legs per body segment, excluding the first few segments. These creatures
          are commonly found in moist environments such as forests, gardens, and areas with decaying vegetation.
          16-72. Unlike centipedes, millipedes lack venomous pincers or fangs and are generally harmless to humans.
          However, they possess defensive mechanisms that can release toxins or irritating chemicals, which may cause
          mild reactions in some individuals, particularly those with sensitive skin.
          16-73. If a Service member encounters a millipede and experiences irritation or a sting, the recommended
          first aid steps include:

                 •    Washing the affected area gently with soap and water to cleanse the site and remove any secretions
                      from the millipede.
                 •    Applying a cold compress or an ice pack wrapped in a cloth to reduce swelling and alleviate
                      discomfort at the sting site.

             16-74. In cases where there is a severe allergic reaction, characterized by symptoms such as difficulty
             breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or widespread hives, it is crucial to seek immediate medical attention.
             While millipede stings are typically mild and self-limiting, if symptoms persist, worsen, or if there are
             concerns about an individual’s reaction, consulting a healthcare professional for further advice and treatment
             is advisable.
FIRE ANTS
14B




             16-75. Fire ants are a type of stinging ant that are native to South America but have spread to various parts
             of the world, including the southern U.S, Southeast Asia, and Australia. Fire ants are known for their
             aggressive behavior and painful stings.
             16-76. When a fire ant stings, it injects venom into the skin, resulting in a sharp, burning sensation and the
             formation of a raised, reddish bump. Multiple ants may attack simultaneously, leading to multiple stings. If
             stung by a fire ant, the first aid steps are to:
                 • Move away from the area where the ants are present to avoid further stings.
                 • Remove any clothing or jewelry that may have ants trapped in them, as they can continue to sting.
                 • Gently wash the affected area with soap and water to clean the site.
                 • Apply a cold compress or ice pack wrapped in a cloth to the sting site. This can help reduce pain
                      and swelling.
                 • Over-the-counter pain relievers, such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen, can be taken to help manage
                      pain if necessary. Follow the instructions and recommended dosage.
                 • Avoid scratching the sting site to prevent infection. If itching is severe, over-the-counter
                      antihistamines or hydrocortisone creams may be used under the guidance of a health care
                      professional.
                 • Monitor the individual for signs of an allergic reaction, such as difficulty breathing, swelling of the
                      face or throat, or widespread hives. If these symptoms occur, seek immediate medical attention.
             16-77. Fire ant stings can be particularly problematic for individuals who are allergic or hypersensitive to ant
             venom. In such cases, immediate medical attention should be sought. These first aid steps are general
             guidelines, and the severity of the reaction may vary from person to person. If there are concerns about the
             Service member’s health or if the symptoms worsen or persist, consult a health care professional for
             appropriate advice and treatment.
TICKS
145B




             16-78. A tick is a small arachnid parasite that feeds on the blood of animals, including humans. Ticks are
             found in various environments, such as forests, grasslands, and shrubby areas. They latch onto their hosts
             and can transmit diseases through their bites.
             16-79. When a tick bites, it burrows its mouth parts into the skin to feed on blood. If you discover a tick
             attached to your skin, it's important to remove it promptly and take the following first aid steps:
                  • Prepare for tick removal: Use fine-tipped tweezers to grasp the tick as close to the skin's surface as
                      possible. Avoid squeezing or crushing the tick's body.
                  • Remove the tick: Gently and steadily pull the tick upward with even pressure. Do not twist or jerk
                      it. The goal is to remove the entire tick, including its mouthparts. Dispose of the tick by placing it
                      in a sealed bag or container or by submerging it in alcohol.
                  • Clean the bite area: Thoroughly clean the bite area with soap and water or an antiseptic solution to
                      reduce the risk of infection.

   16-82. The signs and symptoms of a tick bite can vary depending on factors such as the type of tick, the
   individual's sensitivity to the tick's saliva, and the presence of any tick-borne diseases. The common signs
   and symptoms associated with tick bites are:
       • Redness and swelling: After a tick bite, it is common to experience localized redness and swelling
            at the site of the bite. This is a normal reaction to the tick's saliva.
       • Itching or irritation: The bite site may be itchy or irritated, like a mosquito bite. Avoid scratching to
            reduce the risk of infection.
       • Tick remnants: If a tick is not promptly and properly removed, parts of the tick's body, such as its
            mouthparts, may remain embedded in the skin. This can lead to ongoing irritation and a risk of
            infection.
       • Rash: In some cases, a small red spot or rash may develop around the tick bite. This can expand
            over time and may resemble a target-like pattern. It is important to note that not all tick bites result
            in a rash.
       • Flu-like symptoms: Tick-borne diseases such as Lyme disease, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, or
            babesiosis can cause flu-like symptoms. These may include fever, fatigue, headache, muscle aches,
            joint pain, and swollen lymph nodes. However, these symptoms usually develop days or weeks after
            the tick bite.
       • Allergic reaction: In rare cases, individuals may have an allergic reaction to tick bites, resulting in
            more severe symptoms such as difficulty breathing, swelling, hives, or anaphylaxis. Immediate
            medical attention is necessary in such cases.
   16-83. Not all tick bites lead to the transmission of diseases, and most tick bites are harmless. If a Service
   member experiences any concerning symptoms or if you live in an area where tick-borne diseases are
   prevalent, seek medical attention for proper evaluation, diagnosis, and appropriate treatment.

                           Climatic and Environmental Injuries

OVERVIEW OF CLIMATIC INJURIES
26B




         17-1. Climatic injuries, also known as weather-related injuries, occur when people's health is negatively
         affected by extreme weather conditions. These injuries can range from heat-related illnesses to cold-related
         conditions, and they are often a result of prolonged exposure to harsh environmental elements. Climate plays
         a significant role in determining the risks individuals face, with hot climates posing dangers of heat
         exhaustion and heatstroke, while cold climates can lead to frostbite and hypothermia. Understanding the
         signs, symptoms, and prevention strategies for these climatic injuries is essential in ensuring our well-being
         and staying safe in different weather conditions.
         17-2. Specialized clothing and equipment (such as cold weather gear) for a specific environment should be
         obtained and used properly. For information on the prevention of heat and cold injuries, refer to TC 4-02.3,
         Field Hygiene and Sanitation.
         17-3. Personal factors can significantly influence health and well-being in a climatic environment. Some
         personal factors that play a role are:
             • Physical Health and Fitness: A person's physical health and fitness levels affect how they cope with
                  different climatic conditions. Individuals with good overall physical health, including
                  cardiovascular fitness, strength, and endurance, are generally more resilient to extreme
                  temperatures, humidity, and other climate-related challenges.
             • Adaptability: Personal adaptability and the ability to adjust to changing climatic conditions can
                  impact well-being. Some people are naturally more adaptable to different climates, while others may
                  struggle with the challenges posed by extreme temperatures, high humidity, or other climatic factors.
             • Sensitivity and Allergies: Some individuals may be more sensitive to specific climate-related
                  factors, such as pollen, air pollution, or mold, which can trigger allergies or respiratory issues.
                  Understanding personal sensitivities and taking necessary precautions can help maintain health and
                  well-being in a climatic environment.
             • Mental Resilience: Mental resilience plays a vital role in dealing with challenging climatic
                  conditions. People with strong coping mechanisms, stress management skills, and the ability to
                  maintain a positive mindset are better equipped to handle adverse weather conditions, such as
                  extreme heatwaves or cold snaps.
             • Knowledge and Awareness: Being well-informed about the climatic environment and understanding
                  how it can impact health is crucial. Knowing the risks associated with specific climate-related
                  factors, such as heatstroke or frostbite, and taking appropriate preventive measures can help protect
                  health and well-being.
             • Lifestyle Choices: Personal lifestyle choices, including clothing preferences, outdoor activities, and
                  exposure to natural elements, can affect health in a climatic environment. Wearing appropriate
                  clothing for protection against extreme temperatures, staying hydrated, and engaging in activities
                  that are suitable for the climate, contribute to well-being.
             • Pre-existing Health Conditions: Individuals with pre-existing health conditions may be more
                  vulnerable to the effects of certain climatic conditions. For example, individuals with respiratory
                  conditions like asthma may experience worsening symptoms in highly polluted or allergen-rich
                  climates. Managing pre-existing health conditions effectively becomes crucial for maintaining well-
                  being in a climatic environment.
             • Access to Resources: Personal access to resources, such as reliable shelter, heating or cooling
                  systems, and clean water, can impact health and well-being in different climates. Having access to
                  appropriate resources to adapt to climatic conditions can significantly improve overall well-being.
         17-4. Personal factors interact with other environmental and social factors, such as the availability of
         infrastructure, socioeconomic conditions, and cultural norms. Understanding these personal factors and their

                                                           WARNING
                         Service members should use extreme caution when starting fad
                         diets or taking over-the-counter herbal supplements. Death and
                         severe injury may occur in individuals using dietary or herbal
                         supplements without medical monitoring.
                         A trained health care provider should supervise weight loss and
                         the use of weight loss supplements.


HEAT INJURIES
267B




             17-5. Heat injury prevention is of utmost importance in the military, where Service members face intense
             physical challenges and operate in diverse climatic conditions. When the body gets overheated, it can lead to
             serious health risks and impair a Service member’s ability to perform their duties effectively. Heat-related
             injuries, such as heat exhaustion and heat stroke, can be prevented through various measures, including
             wearing appropriate clothing, taking regular rest breaks, acclimatization and fluid replacement. By
             prioritizing heat injury prevention, Leaders ensure the well-being and operational readiness of their
             personnel, allowing them to fulfill their responsibilities and accomplish their missions with strength and
             resilience.
             17-6. Exertional heat illness refers to a spectrum of heat-related conditions that occur when the body's core
             temperature rises excessively during physical activity or exercise. It is primarily caused by prolonged exertion
             in hot and humid environments, leading to an imbalance between heat production and heat dissipation.
             Exertional heat illness encompasses various conditions ranging from mild heat exhaustion to severe heat
             stroke, which is a medical emergency. Symptoms of heat injuries may include:
                  • Fatigue.
                  • Dizziness.
                  • Headache.
                  • Nausea.
                  • Excessive sweating.
                  • Rapid heartbeat.
                  • Confusion.
                  • Loss of consciousness in severe cases.
             17-7. Prompt recognition and treatment of exertional heat illness are essential to prevent complications and
             potentially life-threatening consequences. Effective prevention strategies, such as acclimatization,
             appropriate clothing, fluid replacement, and regular rest breaks, are crucial in minimizing the risk of
             exertional heat illness. For more information on heat illness refer to TB MED 507 and TC 4-02.3.
             17-8. While there is a range of adverse effects that can result from the body overheating, the two major kinds
             of heat illnesses that are referred to as heat casualties are heat exhaustion (can be mild or more severe) or
             heat stroke. Heat stroke is the most severe form of heat illness and possibly fatal.

                   Note. For more information on heat illness prevention, refer to the Defense Centers for Public
                   Health – Aberdeen website.

HEAT EXHAUSTION
146B




             17-9. Heat exhaustion is a heat-related condition that occurs when the body becomes overheated due to
             prolonged exposure to high temperatures and inadequate fluid replacement. It is considered a milder form of
             heat illness compared to heat stroke. Signs and symptoms of heat exhaustion may include:
                  • Heavy sweating.

              •    Weaknesses and fatigue.
              •    Dizziness or lightheadedness.
              •    Headache.
              •    Nausea or vomiting.
              •    Pale, cool, or clammy skin.
              •    Rapid and shallow breathing.
              •    Elevated heart rate.
              •    Muscle cramps.
              •    Feeling faint or fainting.
          17-10. If a Service member is suspected to have heat exhaustion, immediate first aid treatment should be
          provided. The first aid steps to treat heat exhaustion are:
              • Move the Service member to a cooler environment: Get them out of the heat and into a shaded or
                   air-conditioned area.
              • Encourage rest and rehydration: Have the Service member lie down and elevate their legs slightly.
                   Provide them with cool water and or an electrolyte-containing sports drink to sip on. Avoid alcohol
                   or caffeine.
              • Cool the Service member's body: Loosen or remove any tight or unnecessary clothing. Apply a cool,
                   wet cloth or towels to their skin, especially on the neck, face, and armpits. Use a fan or create air
                   movement to aid in evaporation.
              • Monitor their condition: Stay with the Service member and observe their symptoms. If they do not
                   improve within 30 minutes or their condition worsens, seek medical assistance immediately.
          17-11. Heat exhaustion can progress to heat stroke, a life-threatening condition. If the person's symptoms
          worsen, they become disoriented, confused, or lose consciousness, immediately call for medical assistance.
          17-12. Prevention is key in avoiding heat exhaustion. Practice proper fluid replacement, especially when
          engaging in physical activity or spending time in hot environments. Wear lightweight and loose-fitting
          clothing, use sunscreen, and take regular breaks in cool areas to avoid prolonged exposure to heat.
          17-13. Heat exhaustion is often preceded by heat cramps, muscle cramps of the arms, legs, or abdomen. Heat
          cramps and heat exhaustion often act as indicators. These conditions need to be identified and treated before
          they get to an extreme case of heat stroke. Catch these conditions early, as the casualty needs rest, water,
          shade, evaluation, and possible medical care.
HEAT STROKE
147B




          17-14. Heat stroke is a severe and potentially life-threatening illness characterized by a rapid increase in body
          temperature. It occurs when the body's cooling mechanisms fail to regulate internal heat, often because of
          prolonged exposure to high temperatures or physical exertion in hot environments. Heat stroke is a medical
          emergency that requires immediate intervention. The signs and symptoms of heat stroke may include:
              • Altered mental state or confusion.
              • Headache, dizziness, or fainting.
              • Nausea or vomiting.
              • Difficulty breathing.
              • Hot, dry skin (lack of sweating).
              • High body temperature (typically above 104°Fahrenheit or 40°Celsius).
              • Rapid and strong heartbeat.
              • Seizures.
          17-15. If someone is suspected of having heat stroke, it is crucial to seek emergency medical help
          immediately. While waiting for medical professionals to arrive, follow these first aid steps:
              • Move the person to a cooler location: Get them out of the heat and into a shaded or air-conditioned
                   area as quickly as possible.
              • Call for emergency assistance: Dial 911 or the appropriate local emergency number to request
                   immediate medical help to include MEDEVAC.

text:
Chapter 17



                 •     Cool the person rapidly: Reduce their body temperature as quickly as possible. You can immerse
                       the person in a tub of cold water, use ice cooling sheets or apply cold water to their body using wet
                       towels or sponges. Fan the person while misting them with cool water to enhance cooling.
                 •     Monitor their vital signs: Keep a close eye on the person's breathing, pulse, and level of
                       consciousness. If they stop breathing and you can no longer find a pulse, begin CPR if you are
                       trained to do so.
             17-16. It's important to note that heat stroke is a severe condition, and professional medical treatment is
             essential. Rapid cooling of the body is crucial in preventing potential organ damage and reducing the risk of
             complications.
             17-17. To prevent heat stroke, it is important to avoid excessive physical exertion in hot environments, wear
             lightweight and breathable clothing, and take regular breaks in cool areas. Understanding the signs and
             symptoms of heat stroke and promptly seeking medical help can save lives.

                     Note. The same person should observe the Service member during cooling and evacuation to spot
                     symptom changes.

HYPONATREMIA (WATER INTOXICATION)
148B




             17-18. Hyponatremia (water intoxication) is a condition characterized by abnormally low levels of sodium
             in the blood. Sodium plays a crucial role in maintaining the body's fluid balance and proper nerve and muscle
             function. When sodium levels become significantly diluted, usually due to excessive water intake or
             inadequate sodium intake, hyponatremia can occur. The signs and symptoms of hyponatremia can vary
             depending on the severity of the condition. Common manifestations include:
                  • Nausea and vomiting.
                  • Headache.
                  • Confusion or altered mental state.
                  • Fatigue and weakness.
                  • Seizures.
                  • Muscle cramps or spasms.
                  • Loss of appetite.
                  • Swelling in the hands, feet, or legs.
                  • Low blood pressure.
                  • Coma (in severe cases).
             17-19. If someone is suspected to have hyponatremia, it is important to seek medical attention. In the
             meantime, you can provide the following first aid measures:
                 • Assess the person's condition: Check for any signs of severe symptoms such as seizures, loss of
                      consciousness, or difficulty breathing. If any of these are present, call emergency services
                      immediately.
                 • Move the person to a cool, shaded area: Ensure they are away from direct sunlight or heat sources.
                 • Encourage fluid intake: If the person is conscious and able to swallow, give them small sips of a
                      beverage containing electrolytes, such as a sports drink. This can help restore sodium levels.
                 • Do not give more water. Providing additional water will make the casualty more hyponatremic.
                 • If awake, allow the Service member to consume salty foods or snacks.
                 • Monitor the person's vital signs: Keep an eye on their breathing, heart rate, and level of
                      consciousness. If their condition worsens, be prepared to administer CPR if necessary.
             17-20. Hyponatremia can be mistaken for heat stroke, and the treatment is very different. Hyponatremia is a
             medical emergency that requires professional diagnosis and treatment. It is important to address the
             underlying cause and restore sodium levels under the guidance of a health care professional.

                     Note. This condition most often occurs during initial entry training; however, it may occur anytime
                     when overhydration is encountered.

Climatic and Environmental Injuries



COLD WEATHER INJURIES
268B




          17-21. Preventing cold weather injuries is a vital aspect of military training and operations in cold climates.
          When Service members face extreme cold conditions, they are at risk of various cold weather injuries, such
          as frostbite and hypothermia, which can significantly impact their ability to fulfill their duties effectively.
          Cold weather injury prevention measures are essential to ensure the well-being and operational readiness of
          military personnel. By implementing strategies such as proper clothing layering, maintaining adequate
          hydration, practicing cold weather survival techniques, and promoting awareness of cold weather risks, the
          military prioritizes the safety and health of its Service members. By emphasizing cold weather injury
          prevention, the military ensures that its personnel can endure the challenging cold environments and
          accomplish their missions with strength, resilience, and readiness.
          17-22. Cold weather injuries encompass various conditions that occur due to exposure to extreme cold
          temperatures. The main cold weather injuries are:
              • Frostbite.
              • Hypothermia.
              • Trench Foot.
              • Nonfreezing injuries (such as chilblains and snow blindness).
          17-23. These injuries are often caused by a combination of factors. Prolonged exposure to cold temperatures,
          inadequate protection against the cold, wet clothing, wind chill. Other contributing factors include poor
          nutrition, dehydration, fatigue, and certain medical conditions can increase the susceptibility to cold weather
          injuries. Proper preparation, adequate clothing, layering, regular breaks to warm up, maintain hydration, and
          practicing good cold weather safety measures can help reduce the risk of cold weather injuries. For more
          information on heat illness prevention, refer to the Defense Centers for Public Health–Aberdeen (Cold
          Weather Casualties and Injuries) website. For additional information on cold weather injuries refer to TC 4-
          02.3.
FROSTBITE
149B




          17-24. Frostbite is a cold weather injury that occurs when tissues freeze due to prolonged exposure to extreme
          cold temperatures. It typically affects extremities, such as the fingers, toes, ears, and nose, but can also occur
          in other exposed areas of the body. The signs and symptoms of frostbite may vary depending on the severity,
          and they can include:
               • Cold, pale, or bluish skin.
               • Numbness or a loss of sensation in the affected area.
               • Tingling or a “pins and needles” sensation.
               • Hard or waxy appearance of the skin.
               • Swelling or blistering (in severe cases).
               • Pain or a burning sensation (as the affected area rewarms).
               • Blackened or gangrenous tissue (in severe, untreated cases).
          17-25. If someone is suspected of having frostbite, it is important to provide immediate first aid and seek
          medical attention. Take the following first aid steps:
              • Move to a warm environment: Get the person out of the cold and into a warm area as soon as possible
                   to prevent further damage.
              • Remove wet or constrictive clothing: Take off any wet clothing or accessories that could contribute
                   to heat loss or restrict blood flow to the affected area.
              • Gradually rewarm the affected area: Immerse the frostbit area in warm (not hot) water or use warm
                   compresses. Avoid using direct heat sources like fires or heating pads, as the person may not be able
                   to sense heat properly and could burn the skin.
              • Avoid rubbing or massaging the area: Vigorous rubbing can further damage the tissues. Let the
                   affected area rewarm naturally.
              • Protect and elevate the affected area: Once the frostbitten area has thawed, cover it with a sterile
                   dressing or clean cloth. Keep the area elevated to reduce swelling, if possible.

Chapter 17



                 •     Offer pain relief if needed: Over-the-counter pain relievers like ibuprofen can help alleviate pain
                       and reduce inflammation. However, consult a health care professional before administering any
                       medication.
                 •     Seek medical attention: Frostbite requires medical evaluation and treatment. Even if the frostbite
                       appears mild, professional medical care is essential to assess the extent of the injury and prevent
                       complications.
             17-26. Frostbite can cause long-term damage, including tissue loss and nerve damage. Prompt and
             appropriate treatment is crucial for minimizing complications and maximizing recovery.
             17-27. Frostbite accounts for the largest number of cold weather injuries each year and occurs when tissue is
             exposed to temperatures that are usually below 32°Fahrenheit depending upon wind chill factor, length of
             exposure, and adequacy of protection.
             17-28. Frostbite can occur suddenly due to contact with cold metal or super-cooled liquids such as alcohol,
             fuel, or antifreeze or can develop over time due to prolonged cold exposure. Frostbite is most common in
             exposed skin such as the nose, ears, cheeks, but can also occur in the hands and feet due to reduced blood
             flow.

                     Note. The onset is signaled by a sudden blanching of the skin of the nose, ears, cheeks, fingers, or
                     toes followed by a momentary tingling sensation. Frostbite is indicated when the face, hands, or
                     feet stop hurting.

HYPOTHERMIA
150B




             17-29. Hypothermia is a concern regarding TCCC and the body’s ability to form clots is impaired. This
             condition can cause a tendency toward prolonged or excessive bleeding, which may occur spontaneously or
             following an injury. Hypothermia is a potentially life-threatening condition that occurs when the body's core
             temperature drops significantly below normal.
             17-30. The risks differ with environmental hypothermia. Victims of moderate to severe environmental
             hypothermia are known to have a risk of an irregular heartbeat associated with “afterdrop.” Afterdrop is the
             continued fall of deep body temperatures during rewarming after hypothermia. Afterdrop is thought to
             endanger the heart by further cooling from cold blood presumed to be returning to the body’s center or core.
             17-31. Environmental hypothermic casualties should be monitored and gently handled as afterdrop is not
             always observed. The goals for overall casualty treatment (such as hemorrhage control and resuscitation in
             TCCC versus warming measures along with gentle handling in environmental hypothermia) should be
             understood, trained, and rehearsed. For further discussion on hypothermia see Chapter 8.
TRENCH FOOT
15B




             17-32. Trench foot, also known as immersion foot, is a non-freezing cold injury that occurs when the feet are
             exposed to prolonged damp and cold conditions. It can lead to tissue damage and infection. Contributing
             factors include wet and cold environments, inadequate foot hygiene, prolonged periods of immobility, and
             improper footwear.
             17-33. Trench foot is often associated with Soldiers during World War I who endured long periods in wet
             trenches. Trench foot can occur in any situation where the feet are exposed to excessive moisture and cold
             temperatures. The signs and symptoms of trench foot include:
                  • Redness and swelling of the feet.
                  • Numbness or tingling sensation.
                  • Itching or a burning sensation.
                  • Pain or discomfort.
                  • Blisters or open sores.
                  • Coldness and paleness of the skin.
                  • Foul odor.
             17-34. If someone is suspected to have trench feet, the following first aid steps can be taken:

              •    Move them to a warm and dry environment: Get the person out of wet and cold conditions as soon
                   as possible to prevent further damage.
              •    Remove wet footwear and socks: Take off wet footwear and socks to allow the feet to dry. Avoid
                   rubbing or massaging the feet, as it can further damage the skin.
              •    Elevate the feet: Raise the feet slightly to help reduce swelling and improve circulation.
              •    Clean and dry the feet: Gently wash the feet with warm water (not hot) and mild soap. Pat the feet
                   dry with a clean towel, avoiding excessive friction.
              •    Apply clean, dry socks: Once the feet are dry, put on clean, dry socks to help insulate and protect
                   the feet. Avoid using tight or constrictive socks.
              •    Avoid direct heat sources: Do not use direct heat sources like fires, heaters, or heating pads to warm
                   the feet. The affected feet may be numb, and exposure to high heat can cause burns.
              •    Seek medical attention: It is important to seek medical evaluation and treatment for trench feet.
                   Health care professionals can provide appropriate care, clean, and dress any blisters or open sores,
                   and monitor any signs of infection.
          17-35. Prevention is key in avoiding trench feet. Keep the feet dry, wear appropriate footwear that is
          waterproof and well-insulated, change wet socks and shoes promptly, and take breaks to allow the feet to dry
          and warm up. Proper foot hygiene and regular inspection of the feet can help identify any early signs of
          trench foot and prevent its progression.
NONFREEZING INJURIES
152B




          17-36. Exposure to temperatures from 32°Fahrenheit to 60°Fahrenheit may cause nonfreezing cold injuries
          of skin, fingers, toes, ears, and facial parts. Exposure of skin to cold metal; super cold fuel, petroleum, oil,
          and lubricants; wind chill; and the wear of tight, circulation-restricting clothing (particularly boots).
          17-37. Riding in open vehicles, exposure to propeller or rotor-generated wind, running or skiing, and altitude
          exposure where there is little tree cover can all contribute to greater wind chill.
          17-38. Nonfreezing cold injuries are chilblain and snow blindness. Trench foot occurs when tissues are
          exposed to temperatures from 32°Fahrenheit to 60°Fahrenheit for prolonged periods of time (>12 hours),
          whereas chilblains, which is a more superficial injury, can occur after repeated prolonged exposure of bare
          skin to low temperatures from 60°Fahrenheit down to 32°Fahrenheit. Snow blindness is caused by
          unprotected exposure to UV rays. Snow blindness can be prevented using appropriate eye protection
          (sunglasses). Snow blindness can be painful as it gets closer to three to five hours later.

Chilblains
37B




          17-39. Chilblains, also known as pernio, is a nonfreezing cold weather injury that can occur after one to five
          hours in cold, wet conditions at temperatures from about 50°Fahrenheit down to 32°Fahrenheit. Chilblains
          are a localized inflammatory response of the skin that occurs due to prolonged exposure to cold and damp
          conditions.
          17-40. The most affected areas are the fingernail-side of the fingers, but the ears, face, and other exposed
          skin are also areas of occurrence. There are no lasting effects from chilblain. They are more common in
          colder climates and during the winter season. The signs and symptoms of chilblains include:
              • Redness and inflammation of the affected area.
              • Itching or a burning sensation.
              • Swelling and tenderness.
              • Skin discoloration (bluish or purplish appearance).
              • Formation of small, fluid-filled blisters.
              • Dry or cracked skin.
              • Pain or discomfort, especially when exposed to warmth after being cold.
          17-41. If someone is experiencing chilblains, the following first aid procedures can be performed:
              • Move to a warm environment: Get the person indoors or to a warmer area to prevent further exposure
                   to cold temperatures.

Chapter 17



                 •    Gradually rewarm the affected areas: Avoid sudden temperature changes or direct heat sources like
                      heaters or fires, as this can worsen the condition. Instead, gently warm the affected areas by placing
                      them near warm body parts (such as under the armpits) or by using warm water. The water should
                      be comfortably warm, not hot.
                 •    Protect and cover the affected areas: Once the affected areas have been warmed, keep them protected
                      from further exposure to cold. Cover them with warm clothing, gloves, or socks to help insulate and
                      maintain a stable temperature.
                 •    Avoid scratching or rubbing the affected areas: Itching can be intense, but scratching or rubbing can
                      further damage the skin and increase the risk of infection. Encourage the person to resist the urge to
                      scratch.
                 •    Apply soothing lotions or creams: If recommended by a health care professional, apply mild lotions
                      or creams to alleviate itching and provide relief. Avoid using excessive amounts or substances that
                      may irritate the skin.
                 •    Seek medical advice if needed: If symptoms worsen, if blisters or open sores develop, or if signs of
                      infection (such as increased redness, swelling, or discharge) are present, it is important to seek
                      medical attention for proper evaluation and treatment.
             17-42. Preventing chilblains is essential. It can be achieved by keeping the extremities warm and dry, wearing
             appropriate protective clothing and footwear, avoiding prolonged exposure to cold and damp environments,
             and gradually acclimating the body to temperature changes. Regularly checking the skin for any signs of
             chilblains can help identify and address the condition early on.

Snow Blindness
378B




             17-43. Snow blindness, also known as photokeratitis or UV keratitis, is a condition that occurs when the eyes
             are exposed to excessive UV radiation, typically from sunlight reflected off snow or ice. It can also happen
             when exposed to other intense light sources, such as welding arcs or tanning beds. Snow blindness is
             essentially a temporary sunburn of the cornea, the clear front surface of the eye. The signs and symptoms of
             snow blindness include:
                  • Eye pain or a sensation of grittiness.
                  • Redness and inflammation of the eyes.
                  • Watery eyes and excessive tearing.
                  • Blurred vision or sensitivity to light.
                  • Feeling as if there is something in the eye.
                  • Headache.
                  • Temporary vision loss in severe cases.
             17-44. If someone is experiencing snow blindness, the following first aid treatment can be administered:
                 • Move to a dark and sheltered area: Get the person indoors or to a shaded area to protect the eyes
                      from further exposure to bright light.
                 • Rest the eyes: Keep the eyes closed or minimize eye movements to reduce discomfort and prevent
                      further irritation.
                 • Avoid rubbing the eyes: Rubbing the eyes can exacerbate the condition and potentially cause
                      additional damage.
                 • Apply cold compresses: Place a cold, damp cloth or cool pack over closed eyes to help reduce
                      inflammation and alleviate pain. Avoid using ice directly on the skin.
                 • Use artificial tears: Over-the-counter artificial tear drops can be used to provide relief and moisture
                      to the eyes. Follow the instructions on the packaging or consult a health care professional for
                      appropriate usage.
                 • Wear protective eyewear: If the person needs to be in a bright environment, ensure they wear
                      sunglasses that offer 100 percent UV protection. Wrap-around sunglasses or goggles with side
                      shields provide the best protection.
                 • Seek medical attention: It is advisable to seek medical advice if the symptoms persist, worsen, or if
                      vision loss occurs. A health care professional can examine the eyes and provide appropriate
                      treatment and guidance.

          17-45. Prevention is crucial in avoiding snow blindness. To protect the eyes from excessive UV radiation,
          wear sunglasses or goggles that provide 100 percent UV protection, especially in snowy or high-altitude
          environments. Additionally, using wide-brimmed hats or visors can help shield the eyes from indirect

MOUNTAINOUS TERRAIN INJURIES
269B




          17-46. Approximately 27 percent of the earth’s land surface is considered mountainous terrain. These areas
          are characterized by rugged landscapes, elevated peaks, and varying degrees of slope. Mountains play a
          crucial role in shaping the Earth’s geography, influencing climate patterns, and providing habitat for diverse
          ecosystems.
          17-47. Service members operating in mountainous terrain should be well-prepared, have the necessary skills,
          and carry a first aid kit to address potential injuries and emergencies. Additionally, understanding the terrain,
          weather conditions, and having proper equipment can contribute to safer operations in mountainous terrain.
          17-48. Mountainous terrain poses various challenges and risks, and injuries can range from minor to severe.
          Common injuries in mountainous terrain include:
              • Sprains and Strains. Uneven and rocky surfaces can lead to twisted ankles or muscle strains.
              • Fractures. Falls or accidents may result in broken bones, particularly in extremities.
              • Cuts and Abrasions. Sharp rocks and uneven surfaces can cause cuts and scrapes.
              • Altitude Sickness. At higher elevations, individuals may experience symptoms like headache,
                  nausea, and dizziness due to reduced oxygen levels.
              • Hypothermia. Cold temperatures, especially at higher altitudes, can lead to a drop in body
                  temperature.
              • Dehydration. Strenuous activity, combined with lower humidity and potential difficulty accessing
                  water sources, can lead to dehydration.
              • Exhaustion. Hiking or climbing in mountainous terrain can be physically demanding, leading to
                  fatigue and exhaustion.
              • Frostbite. Exposure to cold conditions, especially at high altitudes, can result in frostbite, where skin
                  and tissues freeze.
              • Avalanche and Rockfall Injuries. In certain mountainous regions, avalanches or rockfalls can pose
                  significant dangers, causing trauma and injuries.
              • Wildlife Encounters. Depending on the location, encounters with wildlife can lead to injuries.
          17-49. Many of the above injury types and treatments have been discussed throughout this publication,
          however operating in mountainous terrain can be challenging, but it's crucial to be aware of the potential
          risks, including altered mental status, high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE), and high-altitude cerebral
          edema (HACE).
ALTITUDE EMERGENCIES
153B




          17-50. Changes in consciousness, confusion, or disorientation can occur due to factors like altitude sickness,
          dehydration, or exhaustion. Recognizing and responding to an altered mental status promptly is essential for
          ensuring the well-being of Service members. Some general first aid measures for Service members
          experiencing altered mental status in mountainous terrain include:
              • Move to Lower Altitude: If the altered mental status is due to altitude sickness, move the Service
                  member to a lower altitude immediately. Descending to lower elevations allows the body to
                  acclimatize and receive more oxygen, potentially alleviating symptoms.
              • Rest and Hydration: Ensure the Service member rests and stays hydrated. Dehydration and fatigue
                  can contribute to an altered mental status, so providing water and allowing for adequate rest are
                  important.
              • Monitor Breathing: Keep a close eye on the Service member's breathing. Shallow or irregular
                  breathing may indicate respiratory distress. If breathing difficulties persist, promptly seek medical
                  assistance.
              • Check for Signs of Hypoxia: Assess for signs of hypoxia, which occurs when the body doesn't
                  receive enough oxygen. Look for bluish discoloration of the lips or fingertips. If observed, it may
                  indicate a more severe oxygen deficiency, requiring immediate medical attention.

                 •    Keep Warm: If the altered mental status is due to cold temperatures, provide warmth by using
                      blankets, jackets, or other insulating materials. Preventing hypothermia is crucial.
                 •    Monitor for Improvement or Worsening: Keep a close watch on the Service members’ condition. If
                      there is no improvement or if the symptoms worsen, seek medical assistance as soon as possible.
                 •    Administer Oxygen (if available): If you have access to supplemental oxygen and the person is
                      experiencing severe symptoms, administering oxygen can be beneficial. However, this may require
                      specific training and equipment.
                 •    Evacuation if Necessary: In severe cases or if the person's condition doesn't improve, consider
                      evacuating them to a medical facility at a lower altitude. This may involve calling for professional
                      rescue or using available means of transportation.
             17-51. First aid of an altered mental status is a temporary measure, and medical assistance should be sought
             for any significant or worsening symptoms. If in doubt or if the altered mental status persists, it is essential
             to prioritize the Service member's safety and seek timely medical help.
HIGH-ALTITUDE PULMONARY EDEMA
154B




             17-52. High-Altitude Pulmonary Edema is a serious condition that can occur at higher elevations, typically
             above 2,500 meters (8,200 feet). It involves the accumulation of fluid fluids in the lungs and can be life-
             threatening. Some general first aid measures for Service members experiencing HAPE in mountainous terrain
             include:
                  • Immediate Descent. The most critical first aid measure for HAPE is an immediate descent to lower
                      altitudes. Every effort should be made to get the affected individual to a lower elevation as quickly
                      as possible, as this is the most effective way to alleviate symptoms.
                  • Rest and Oxygen. Ensure the person rests and provide supplemental oxygen if available. Oxygen
                      therapy can help improve oxygen levels in the blood and alleviate breathing difficulties.
                  • Keep Warm. Maintain the person's warmth by using blankets and insulating layers. Cold
                      temperatures can exacerbate symptoms, so preventing hypothermia is important.
                  • Stay Hydrated. Encourage the individual to drink fluids to stay hydrated. Dehydration can worsen
                      the condition, so maintaining adequate fluid intake is essential.
                  • Monitor Breathing. Keep a close watch on the person's breathing. If there are signs of severe
                      respiratory distress, such as blue lips or fingertips, it may indicate a critical situation, and
                      professional medical help should be sought immediately.
                  • Administer Medications (if available). In some cases, medications such as nifedipine or sildenafil
                      may be used to help manage HAPE symptoms. The medical professional should determine the
                      availability and use of these medications.
                  • Evacuation. Seek evacuation to the MTF at a lower altitude as soon as possible. Evacuation may
                      involve contacting medical personnel and requesting evacuation to a lower elevation where more
                      definitive medical care can be provided.
             17-53. HAPE is a medical emergency, and prompt action is crucial. While these first aid measures can
             provide initial assistance, professional medical help should be sought without delay. If you suspect someone
             has HAPE, it's essential to prioritize their safety and act swiftly to get them to a lower altitude and seek
             immediate medical attention.
HIGH-ALTITUDE CEREBRAL EDEMA
15B




             17-54. High-Altitude Cerebral Edema is a severe and life-threatening condition that can occur at high
             elevations, typically above 3,000 meters (9,800 feet). It involves swelling of the brain and can lead to
             neurological symptoms. Some general first aid measures for Service members experiencing HACE in
             mountainous terrain include:
                 • Immediate Descent. The most critical first aid measure for HACE is an immediate and rapid descent
                      to lower altitudes. Descending to a lower elevation is essential to reduce the impact of high altitude
                      on the brain.
                 • Rest and Oxygen. Ensure the affected person rests and provide supplemental oxygen if available.
                      Oxygen therapy can help improve oxygen levels in the blood and alleviate neurological symptoms.

Chapter 18
                                                Sickle Cell Trait

OVERVIEW OF SICKLE CELL TRAIT
270B




          18-1. Sickle cell trait (SCT) is an inherited genetic condition in which a person carries one copy of the sickle
          cell gene and one normal hemoglobin gene. It is different from sickle cell disease (SCD), which occurs when
          a person inherits two copies of the sickle cell gene. The SCT is usually asymptomatic and generally does not
          cause health problems. However, under certain conditions, such as extreme physical exertion, high altitudes,
          or dehydration, individuals with SCT may experience complications.
          18-2. SCD is a genetic disorder that affects the red blood cells, which are responsible for carrying oxygen
          throughout the body. It is caused by a mutation in the gene responsible for producing hemoglobin, a protein
          that enables red blood cells to carry oxygen. In individuals with SCD, the hemoglobin gene mutation leads
          to the production of abnormal hemoglobin, known as hemoglobin S. This abnormal hemoglobin causes red
          blood cells to become rigid and take on a sickle or crescent shape instead of their normal disc shape. These
          sickle-shaped cells can get stuck in small blood vessels, leading to various complications.
          18-3. For more information on SCT and SCD, refer to the National Institute of Health website. Service
          members with SCT can typically participate fully in any physical activity. Under certain circumstances
          Service members with SCT may suffer negative effects such as muscle weakness, pain, and collapse. This
          collapse is termed exercise collapse associated with sickle cell trait (ECAST).
          18-4. ECAST refers to a specific syndrome that can occur in individuals with SCT during or immediately
          after strenuous exercise. It is characterized by symptoms such as dizziness, weakness, fatigue, and in rare
          cases, collapse, or loss of consciousness. The ECAST can occur due to a mismatch between oxygen supply
          and demand in the muscles during intense physical activity.
          18-5. The ECAST is a relatively rare occurrence, and most individuals with SCT can engage in regular
          physical activities without any issues. However, to minimize the risk of complications, individuals with SCT
          are advised to take precautions during exercise, such as staying well-hydrated, avoiding excessive heat or
          cold exposure, and gradually increasing the intensity and duration of physical activity. It is also recommended
          to consult with a health care professional for personalized guidance and address any concerns related to
          exercise.
          18-6. The ECAST, as a cause of collapse in Service members, is considered because the relative risk of death
          is significantly higher in-Service members with SCT than those without. Early recognition and proper
          treatment of ECAST can increase survival and decrease complications. For more information on ECAST,
          refer to the American Medical Society for Sports Medicine website.
RISK FACTORS
156B




          18-7. While the exact causes of ECAST are not fully understood, there are several risk factors that can
          contribute to its occurrence. These include:
              • Strenuous exercise: Engaging in high-intensity or prolonged physical activity can increase the risk
                   of ECAST.
              • Dehydration: Inadequate fluid intake or excessive fluid loss through sweating can contribute to the
                   risk of ECAST.
              • Heat and humidity: Exercising in hot and humid environments can further exacerbate the risk of
                   ECAST.
          18-8. Preexisting medical conditions and environmental factors that may increase the likelihood of an
          ECAST episode include:
              • Poor Hydration.
              • Exercise-induced asthma.
              • Dietary supplements contain stimulants.
              • Excessive heat exposure.
