                 •    High altitude.
                 •    High humidity.
                 •    Inadequate rest between intense exercise periods (for example, prolonged wind sprints).
                 •    Intense exercise for an extended period.
                 •    Pre-exercise fatigue due to illness.
                 •    Returning from prolonged leave after little physical activity.
                 •    Inadequate acclimatization to environment.
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
157B




             18-9. Service members experiencing ECAST may have—
                 • Dizziness or lightheadedness.
                 • Weakness or fatigue.
                 • Nausea or vomiting.
                 • Shortness of breath.
                 • Muscle pain or cramping.
                 • Paleness or cyanosis (bluish discoloration) of the skin.
                 • Collapse or loss of consciousness (rare cases).
                 • Increased pain and weakness in the muscles, especially the large muscles of the legs, buttock(s), and
                      low back.
                 • Muscle tenderness.
                 • Slumping to the ground.
                 • Rapid breathing.
                 • Slightly elevated body temperature (usually less than 103° Fahrenheit).
             18-10. Some of the differences between the signs and symptoms of ECAST and other causes of exercise
             related collapse include:
                    ⚫   Service members with ECAST will have soft, weak muscles while Service members with muscle
                        cramps will have firm, tight muscles.
                    ⚫   Service members with cardiac issues experiencing an ECAST event may not be able to speak or
                        think normally.
                    ⚫   Service members with ECAST will have a slightly elevated body temperature while Service
                        members experiencing exertional heat stroke will have a core body temperature above 104°
                        Fahrenheit.
                    ⚫   Service members with ECAST will usually be able to speak and think normally, while Service
                        members suffering from heat illness may appear to be confused.
             18-11. If someone experiences symptoms of ECAST, the following first aid measures can be taken:
                 • Stop the activity: Immediately cease any physical exertion and allow the person to rest.
                 • Move to a cool and shaded area: Transfer the individual to a cooler environment to minimize heat
                      stress.
                 • Rehydrate: Encourage the person to drink fluids to rehydrate, preferably water or sports drinks.
                 • Elevate the legs: If the person is conscious and able to do so, elevate their legs to improve blood
                      flow and circulation.
                 • Monitor vital signs: Keep an eye on the person's breathing, heart rate, and level of consciousness.
                      Seek medical assistance if the symptoms worsen or persist.
PREVENTIVE MEASURES
158B




             18-12. It is crucial to note that ECAST is a relatively rare occurrence, and most individuals with SCT can
             engage in regular physical activities without complications. However, taking preventive measures, such as
             staying well-hydrated, avoiding excessive heat exposure, and gradually increasing exercise intensity can help
             reduce the risk of ECAST. If an individual with SCT experiences recurrent or severe episodes of ECAST, it
             is recommended to consult with a health care professional who specializes in SCD for further evaluation and
             personalized guidance.

Sickle Cell Trait



          18-13. Early identification of SCT in Service members is needed to prevent ECAST this is done with a blood
          test. Defense Health Agency Procedural Instruction (DHA-PI) 6025.14, Active Duty Service member (ADSM)
          Erythrocyte Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) Deficiency and Sickle Cell Trait Screening;
          DODI 6465.01, Erythrocyte Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase Deficiency, (G6PD) and Sickle Cell Trait
          Screening Programs; and All Army Activities 094/2020, Implementation of Army Sickle Cell Trait Screening
          of All Soldiers establish the Department of Defense’s, Defense Health Agency’s, and the Army’s procedures
          to implement erythrocyte G6PD deficiency and SCT screening at—
                • Entry to the Military Services (at appointment, enlistment, or induction).
                • Pre-deployment.
                • Other points as indicated for validation of results.
          18-14. Safe exercise practices that decrease the risk of ECAST include:
              • Participate in exercise and conditioning activities year-round to maintain physical fitness.
              • Gradually increase exercise intensity when starting a training regimen or returning to training after
                  an absence, such as illness, injury, or extended leave.
              • Take adequate recovery time between repetitive sprints or drills (for example, wind sprints or
                  intervals).
              • Acclimate to the altitude or temperature at which training will occur.
              • Exercise for shorter periods and with less intensity during hot or humid conditions.
              • Hydrate before, during, and after exercise.
              • Understand the signs and symptoms of ECAST. If any symptoms arise, report immediately to the
                  Holistic Health and Fitness staff, unit leaders, or health care personnel.

DUTIES AND RESPONSIBILITIES
271B




          18-15. Preventing ECAST is a primary and critical responsibility within the military, given the demanding
          physical exertion and operational requirements faced by Service members. ECAST can have severe
          consequences on both the health and operational readiness of military personnel. Recognizing the
          significance of these risks, the military assumes a proactive stance in fulfilling its responsibilities. This
          commitment involves the identification of command, personal, medical and first responder responsibilities.
COMMAND RESPONSIBILITIES
159B




          18-16. Commanders ensure that—
              • Every Service member in their command has been screened for SCT.
              • Every Service member with a positive SCT screening is issued and wears a red medical warning tag
                  and receives a formal counseling from a unit or MTF, and health care provider to discuss their SCT-
                  positive result.
              • Service members receive educational information and counseling that includes:
                  ▪ Erythrocyte G6PD and SCT deficiency diagnosis, causes, complications, treatment, and
                       strategies to mitigate symptoms.
                  ▪ Materials and resources that enable the Service member to self-identify symptoms experienced
                       during exercise and know when to seek immediate medical attention.
              • Service members without record of an SCT screening is referred to a lab for screening unless the
                  Service member can provide documentation of a prior screening. The date and results of the SCT
                  screening are annotated in the Army Medical Protection System and recorded in the Service
                  member’s electronic medical record.
              • Unit or MTF health care providers—
                  ▪ Train all unit medical personnel to recognize the signs of ECAST.
                  ▪ Train unit medical personnel and leaders on actions to take during an ECAST event.
                  ▪ Conduct an initial patient evaluation, provide treatment, and determine whether to call for
                       urgent MEDEVAC, or immediately transport the individual to the nearest MTF.
              • Discrete means of identifying SCT positive Service members are developed and added to the unit
                  tactical SOP. Identification is like those used to identify Service members who have sustained cold
                  and or heat related injuries.

text:
Chapter 18



SERVICE MEMBER RESPONSIBILITIES
160B




             18-17. Service members with a positive SCT screen are responsible for—
                 • Obtaining and wearing their red medical warning tags and unit SOP directed markings.
                 • Seeking formal counseling includes educational materials and resources to aid in their ability to self-
                     identify symptoms experienced during exercise and know when to seek immediate medical
                     attention.
                 • Gradually increasing exercise intensity when starting a training regimen or returning to training after
                     an absence, such as an illness or leave.
                 • Taking adequate time to recover between repetitive sprints or drills (for example, wind sprints or
                     intervals).
             18-18. Appropriate casualty response measures for suspected ECAST are to—
                 • Identify if the casualty has SCT (looking for a red identification tag or unit specific marking).
                 • Check the casualty’s pulse, breathing, and mental status.
                 • Remove the casualty from the environment.
                 • Cool the casualty (as indicated by weather conditions).
                 • Notify nearest medical personnel to assess the casualty for a suspected ECAST event.
                 • Call for urgent MEDEVAC or immediately transport the casualty to the nearest MTF.
                 • Notify the receiving MTF that the Service member is suspected of experiencing an ECAST.

                   Note. Trained medical personnel should consider fluid and oxygen resuscitation.

             18-19. Before returning to duty, Service members who have collapsed during exercise showed signs or
             symptoms of ECAST will (if not already completed) be tested for SCT. Tests for other diseases such as
             diabetes, electrolyte abnormalities, muscle damage, and heart and lung conditions may also be needed.
             18-20. Service members will meet with a unit or MTF health care provider to discuss:
                 • The signs and symptoms of ECAST.
                 • Family history.
                 • Environmental factors.
                 • Dietary supplements and medications that increase the risk of collapse.
                 • The importance of good hydration.
                 • The possibility of future ECAST episodes when exercising strenuously in high heat and humidity.
             18-21. Service members must have no symptoms at rest and normal lab values before resuming exercise or
             training. The training must resume slowly and under a doctor’s supervision.
FIRST RESPONDER, STRETCHER BEARER, MEDIC, CORPSMAN, AND LEADER TRAINING
16B




             18-22. The unit or MTF healthcare providers are tasked with training both first responders and medical
             personnel, such as combat medics or corpsmen, in the vital competencies of recognizing signs of ECAST.
             This training encompasses conducting rapid initial evaluations, providing immediate treatment, and making
             critical decisions regarding the need for urgent MEDEVAC or direct transport of the casualty to the nearest
             MTF.
             18-23. Additionally, these healthcare providers also extend their training to unit leaders, equipping them with
             the necessary skills to identify the initial indicators of ECAST. This preparation is crucial for leaders to make
             informed decisions about whether to initiate an urgent MEDEVAC or to expedite the transportation of the
             affected individual to the closest medical facility, ensuring prompt and effective care.

Chapter 19
            First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and
                             Nuclear Environment

GENERAL INFORMATION FOR FIRST AID IN A CHEMICAL,
27B




BIOLOGICAL, RADIOLOGICAL, AND NUCLEAR ENVIRONMENT
          19-1. Planning for large-scale combat operations must account for possible operations in a CBRN
          environment and allied response options. The threat of CBRN hazards can rapidly degrade unit effectiveness
          by forcing troops to wear protective clothing and by creating confusion and fear. Through training in CBRN
          protective and preventive procedures and first aid, units can maintain the desired level of combat
          effectiveness to meet mission requirements.
          19-2. Because of the differences in presentation for CBRN casualties, specific triage and treatment
          recommendations along with evacuation priority considerations are addressed in the CPGs located on the
          deployed medicine website.
          19-3. CBRN exposure is an enemy attack, and security will be the first priority to be coordinated. Triage for
          a CBRN event follows established triage principles, including doing the best for most people. Because of the
          complexity of combining CBRN and trauma casualties, it may be beneficial to assign experienced medical
          personnel to triage. Triage occurs for decontamination, for medical treatment, and for evacuation. Although
          assigning casualties to ambulatory vs. non-ambulatory decontamination lanes is a method of sorting, the
          optimal triage for decontamination determines who can tolerate delays in decontamination.
          19-4. Decontamination triage may be based on extent of exposure and not on initial symptoms, as symptoms
          may be delayed. Those with greater exposure may benefit from rapid decontamination to increase their
          survivability and thus reduce the future burden on medical resources. Once decontaminated, patients are
          triaged according to medical priority. Decontamination is a medical intervention (it minimizes or eliminates
          the conversion of an external dose to an internal dose). Any casualty within an area suspected to contain a
          liquid chemical agent is automatically medically triaged as immediate until immediate decontamination has
          been accomplished. The casualty is then re-triaged. Except for blister agent casualties, those exposed only to
          vapor can tolerate delays in decontamination or may not even require thorough decontamination.
          19-5. It is important to frequently reassess patients. Because many CBRN hazards have delayed symptoms,
          a casualty initially assessed to be minimal may become immediate as the hazard presents itself and process
          of decontamination can significantly change the casualty status. Additionally, actions during
          decontamination can significantly change the casualty status. It is critically important to monitor
          hypothermia, disruption of previously controlled bleeding, and other changes in casualty status that would
          change triage priority.
CLASSIFICATION OF CHEMICAL AND BIOLOGICAL AGENTS
162B




          19-6. Chemical agents are classified based on their properties, effects, and intended use. There are different
          classification systems depending on the context, such as their use in warfare, industry, or transportation. One
          widely used classification system for chemical agents is based on their potential harm to human health and
          the environment. Common chemical agent categories are:
               • Adversary use: Persistent agents intended to cause casualties for more than 24 hours or restrict
                    terrain. Nonpersistent agents that can lose their ability to cause casualties after 10-15 minutes.
               • Hazard classification: Explosiveness (Class 1), flammability (Classes 3,4), toxicity (Class 6).
               • Physiological action: Nerve, blood, blister, choking, and incapacitating.
               • Physical state: solid, liquid, or vapor.
          19-7. Different regulatory bodies and organizations may have their own specific classification systems and
          criteria for chemical agents, depending on the context and intended use. These classifications help in

text:
Chapter 19



             identifying and managing potential hazards, ensuring appropriate handling, storage, transportation, and
             emergency response measures are in place.
             19-8. Biological agents, also known as bioagents or biological hazards, are classified based on their potential
             to cause harm to living organisms, including humans. They can be categorized in various ways, considering
             factors such as their origin, mode of transmission, pathogenicity, and potential for use as weapons. Common
             classification systems for biological agents are:
                  • Risk Group Classification: Biological agents can be classified into different risk groups based on
                       their level of pathogenicity and the risk they pose to human health. This classification system is
                       commonly used in research laboratories and health care settings. The risk groups range from Risk
                       Group 1 (low individual and community risk) to Risk Group 4 (high individual and community
                       risk). The classification is determined by considering factors such as infectivity, severity of disease,
                       available preventive measures, and efficacy of treatment.
                  • Biosafety Level Classification: This classification system is primarily used in laboratory settings to
                       ensure appropriate containment measures and safety protocols are followed when handling
                       biological agents. It categorizes agents into different biosafety levels based on their risk to laboratory
                       personnel and the environment. The biosafety levels range from biosafety levels 1 (lowest level of
                       risk) to biosafety levels 4 (highest level of risk). The classification is determined by factors such as
                       pathogenicity, ease of transmission, and availability of effective preventive measures and
                       treatments.
                  • The U.S. Centers for Disease Control (also known as CDC) and Prevention Category A, B, and C
                       Classification: Developed by the Centers for Disease Control, is focused on potential bioterrorism
                       agents. Biological agents are classified into three categories:
                       ▪ Category A: Agents that pose the highest risk to national security and public health. They have
                            the potential for widespread dissemination, high mortality rates, and significant public panic.
                            Examples include anthrax, smallpox, and Ebola virus.
                       ▪ Category B: Agents that are moderately easy to disseminate and cause moderate morbidity and
                            low mortality rates. Examples include Q fever, Brucellosis, and ricin toxin.
                       ▪ Category C: Agents that have the potential for emerging threats and can be engineered for mass
                            dissemination. Examples include Nipah virus, hantavirus, and emerging strains of influenza.
             19-9. These classification systems help in identifying and managing biological hazards, implementing
             appropriate biosafety and biosecurity measures, developing effective response plans, and conducting research
             and surveillance activities. They are essential tools in ensuring the safe handling, containment, and prevention
             of the spread of biological agents. The classification of biological warfare (also known as BW) agents can
             vary slightly depending on the organization or country using the classification system. These classifications
             help guide efforts in preparedness, response planning, research, surveillance, and the development of
             countermeasures against potential biological warfare threats.


                                                            WARNING
                          Swallowing water or food contaminated with some chemical
                          agents (i.e. nerve, blisters), and with some biological agents can
                          be fatal.


CONDITIONS FOR MASKING WITHOUT ORDER OR ALARM
163B




             19-10. Once an attack with a chemical or biological agent is detected or suspected, you must STOP
             BREATHING and mask immediately. DO NOT WAIT to receive an order or alarm if you observe any of
             these indicators:
                 • Artillery missiles, rockets, unmanned ariel vehicles or other delivery systems that produce vapors,
                      smoke, mists, and aerial sprays, near your position.
                 • Smoking or vaporing from an unknown source is present or approaching.
                 • A suspicious odor, liquid, or solid is present.
                 • You are entering an area known or suspected of being contaminated.

First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment



              •     Casualties from an area where chemical or biological agents have reportedly been used enter your
                    area.
              •     You have one or more of the following symptoms:
                    ▪ An unexplained runny nose.
                    ▪ A sudden unexplained headache.
                    ▪ A feeling of choking or tightness in the chest or throat.
                    ▪ Dimness of vision.
                    ▪ Irritation of the eyes.
                    ▪ Difficulty in or increased rate of breathing without obvious reasons.
                    ▪ Sudden feeling of depression.
                    ▪ Dread, anxiety, or restlessness.
                    ▪ Dizziness or light-headedness.
                    ▪ Slurred speech.
              •     Unexplained laughter or unusual behavior is noted in others.
              •     Numerous unexplained ill personnel.
              •     Service members collapsing without evident cause.
              •     Animals or birds exhibiting unusual behavior or suddenly dying.
          19-11. For further information on individual protective measures, masking procedures, and other tasks
          related to surviving and operating in a CBRN environment, refer to ATP 3-11.32, ATP 4-02.7, ATP 4-02.84,
          and ATP 4-02.85.

FIRST AID IN A CHEMICAL ENVIRONMENT
273B




          19-12. Assessment and management of CBRN casualties is complex because it involves not only life-
          threatening symptoms (some of them have rapid onset) but also the threat of contamination of first
          responders. An added source of complexity is the combination of CBRN and penetrating trauma injuries.
          This complexity requires a stepwise approach that first rules in or rules out CBRN injuries so first responders
          can protect themselves before rendering aid. The next step integrates assessment and management of both
          CBRN and traumatic injuries, prioritizing the management of life-threats first. Chemical agents may be
          inhaled or ingested. Chemical agents are ingested when food or water contaminated by the agent is consumed
          or absorbed when the agent is exposed to the skin or eyes.
          19-13. Service member’s field protective mask and chemical protective clothing provide good protection
          from most chemical agents. The Skin Decontamination Kits are used to remove liquid chemical agents from
          exposed skin. The Individual Equipment Decontamination Kit is used to decontaminate personal equipment.
          Medications contained in the antidote treatment – nerve agent, auto-injector (ATNAA) kit help to counteract
          nerve agent poisoning. The effects of the antidote can be enhanced by taking pyridostigmine bromide tablets
          prior to being exposed to the nerve agent.
          19-14. The field protective mask gives protection against biological and chemical warfare agents as well as
          radiological fallout. Service members should be able to do their field protective masks in nine seconds or less
          without the hood, and within 15 seconds with the hood.
          19-15. The steps to donning a field protective mask in response to a chemical attack are to: stop breathing,
          put on (don) the mask, seal it properly, clear, and check it; resume breathing, give the alarm, and continue
          the mission. Keep your mask on until the “all clear” signal has been given.

                  Note. Keep your protective mask on until the area is no longer hazardous, and you are told to
                  unmask.

          19-16. If you begin to experience symptoms of nerve agent poisoning, immediately give yourself one
          ATNAA.

text:
Chapter 19




                                                           CAUTION
                         Do not inject a nerve agent antidote until you are sure you need it.


             19-17. If your eyes and face become contaminated, you must immediately begin decontamination. You
             should try to get under cover before beginning immediate decontamination, but do not delay immediate
             decontamination to search for overhead cover. You need shelter to prevent further contamination while
             performing decontamination procedures on your face. If no overhead cover is available, put your poncho
             over your head before beginning the decontamination process. Then, you put on the remaining protective
             clothing. If vomiting occurs, the mask should be lifted momentarily and drained—with your eyes closed and
             while holding your breath—then replace, clear, and seal.
             19-18. Decontaminate your skin, immediately, and clothing and equipment as soon as the mission permits.
             19-19. You may come upon an unconscious chemical agent casualty who requires first aid. You should be
             able to successfully—
                  • Mask the unconscious casualty if they are unmasked.
                  • Inject them, if necessary, with all their auto injectors.
                  • Decontaminate their skin.
                  • Seek medical assistance.
CHEMICAL BIOLOGICAL RADIOLOGICAL NUCLEAR CASUALTY ASSESSMENT
164B




             19-20. Just as trauma casualties present differently (blunt, trauma, GSW, blasts, etc.), CBRN casualties also
             have varied presentations. CBRN casualties can be categorized by circumstances of exposure and presence
             or absence of trauma and CBRN effects. The acronym CRESS (Consciousness, Respirations, Eyes,
             Secretions, Skin) is employed to improve rapid identification of the type of chemical agent exposure.
                 • C - Consciousness (unconscious, seizures, depressed consciousness, agitation).
                 • R - Respirations (present or absent, labored, increased or decreased).
                 • E - Eyes (constricted, dilated, normal).
                 • S - Secretions (dry, normal, increased).
                 • S - Skin (diaphoretic, dry, hot, cyanosis).

                   Note. After using the CRESS algorithm to rule out or rule in a CBRN injury, and first responders
                   doing PPE if present, the integrated assessment and management of TCCC and CBRN injuries
                   can proceed. Additionally, NATO STANAG 2358 and Joint Trauma System Clinical Practice
                   Guide contain additional details, figures, and tables.

             19-21. The acronym (MARCHE)2 which stands for (mask, antidotes, rapid spot decontamination,
             countermeasures, hypothermia prevention, extraction or evacuation) integrates the established TCCC
             MARCH algorithm with CBRN considerations. Combining these two approaches gives the acronym
             (MARCHE)2 or “MARCHE-squared.” Like TCCC, (MARCHE)2 can be broken into phases of care from
             highest threat (care under fire or active CBRN threat), to intermediate threat (tactical field care or warm zone
             casualty management), to lowest threat (PFC and or evacuation or care of decontaminated casualties in cold
             zone).
                 • M - Massive Hemorrhage.
                 • A - Airway.
                 • R - Respirations.
                 • C - Circulation.
                 • H - Hypothermia.
                 • M - Mask.
                 • A - Antidotes.
                 • R - Rapid spot decontamination.
                 • C - Countermeasures.

NERVE AGENTS

          19-23. Nerve agents are among the deadliest chemical agents. They can be delivered by artillery shell, mortar
          shell, rocket, aircraft bomb, spray, or land mine. In general, nerve agents are colorless, odorless, and tasteless.
          There are multiple signs and symptoms of nerve agent poisoning, which can vary from mild to severe.
          19-24. Nerve agents enter the body by inhalation, ingestion, and through the skin. Depending on the route of
          entry and the amount, nerve agents can produce injury or death within minutes. Nerve agents can achieve
          their effects with small amounts. Nerve Agent Pyridostigmine Pretreatment (NAPP) provides an effective
          pre-treatment for all Soldiers before exposure to nerve agents.

          medications contained in the ATNAA.

                   Figure 19-1. Nerve Agent Pyridostigmine Pretreatment Tablet Set
      19-26. To be effective the NAPP Tablet Set must be taken within eight hours prior to exposure to nerve
      agents. Since the specific time of exposure is difficult to predict, units should assess the threat and direct
      Soldiers to initiate NAPP before they could be exposed. The NAPP consists of a blister pack containing 21
      tablets to be taken over seven days. Each tablet contains 30mg pyridostigmine bromide. If a dose is missed,
      do not make it up. Do not take two tablets at one time because of a missed dose; merely start again with one
      tablet every eight hours. Taking more than one tablet at a time DOES NOT provide additional protection-in
      fact, it may be more hazardous if there is exposure to a nerve agent.
      19-27. Service members are initially issued one NAPP when the chemical biological protective ensemble is
      expected to be donned. You are responsible for carrying out the NAPP and safeguarding it against loss.
      Service members will secure the blister pack in the sleeve or breast pocket of the chemical biological
      protective ensemble (or in another part of the ensemble, as directed by local SOP).
      19-28. When the order to take pyridostigmine pretreatment is given, it should be taken as directed even if the
      protective mask is worn.

            Note. Commanders must follow protocols for pyridostigmine bromide issuance and use.



                                                   WARNING
                  Pyridostigmine bromide is for pre-exposure prophylaxis only. Do
                  not give to any patient who has been exposed to, presents, or has
                  symptoms of organophosphate nerve agent poisoning.


      19-29. Although no detrimental effects are expected at the recommended dosage, depending on the length of
      time and the amount of medication taken as well as individual physiological variations, some individuals
      may have contraindications for taking pyridostigmine bromide, while others may experience adverse
      reactions.
      19-30. Signs and symptoms of overdose, adverse reactions, or side effects are:
          • Abdominal cramps.
          • Nausea and vomiting.
          • Diarrhea.

             19-36. If nerve agents are used, mission permitting, watch for persons needing nerve agent antidotes and
             immediately follow procedures. When you have the signs and symptoms of nerve agent poisoning, you
             should immediately put on the protective mask and then inject yourself with one set of the ATNAA. First aid
             for nerve agent poisoning consists of administering the ATNAA, CANA, or AAS.

Convulsant Antidote for Nerve Agent and Advanced Anticonvulsant System
423B




             19-37. Two anticonvulsant autoinjectors are available to control actively seizing patients. CANA (figure 19-
             2 on page 197) is the drug diazepam. AAS (figure 19-3 on page 197) is the drug midazolam. CANA and
             AAS are not intended for self-administration.
             19-38. Diazepam or midazolam should be administered with the three ATNAA kits when the casualty's
             condition warrants the use of three ATNAA kits at the same time. Use either the CANA or the AAS to control
             an actively seizing patient. Do not administer both for the same series of three ATNAA kits.

             particularly important as it promotes the decontamination reaction by actively desorbing, retaining, and
             sequestering the chemical agent, while the active ingredient (Dekon 139) chemically reacts with, and rapidly
             neutralizes the vesicant chemical or the organophosphorus nerve agent. This reaction starts immediately, and

Combat Lifesaver Assistance for Nerve Agent Poisoning
384B




             19-50. The CLS must check to verify if the individual has received three sets of ATNAAs. If not, the CLS
             performs first aid as described for buddy aid above. If the individual has received the three sets of, ATNAA,
             the CLS may administer additional injections at approximately 15-minute intervals until atropinization is
             achieved (that is a heart rate above 90 beats per minute, reduced bronchial secretions, and reduced
             salivations). Administer additional atropines at intervals of 30 minutes to four hours to maintain
             atropinization or until the casualty is placed under the care of medical personnel. Check the heart rate by
             lifting the casualty’s mask hood and feeling for a pulse at the carotid artery. Request medical assistance as
             soon as the tactical situation permits.
             19-51. The CLS should administer additional CANA or AAS to casualties suffering from convulsions.
             Administer a second, and if needed, a third CANA or AAS at 5-to-10-minute intervals for a maximum of
             three injections (30mg diazepam or 30mg midazolam). Follow the steps and procedures described in
             paragraph 19-49 on page 201 for administering the CANA or AAS. DO NOT give more than two additional
             injections for a total of three (one self-aid plus two by the CLS).
BLISTER AGENTS
167B




             19-52. Blister agents (vesicants) include mustard, nitrogen mustards, lewisite, and other arsenicals, mixtures
             of mustards and arsenicals, and phosgene oxime. Blister agents may act on the eyes, mucous membranes,
             lungs, and skin. They burn and blister the skin or any other body parts they contact. Even relatively low doses
             may cause serious injury. Blister agents damage the respiratory tract (nose, sinuses, and windpipe) when
             inhaled and cause vomiting and diarrhea when absorbed. Lewisite and phosgene oxime cause immediate pain
             on contact. However, mustard agents are deceptive as there is little or no pain at the time of exposure. In
             some cases, signs of injury may not appear for several hours after exposure.

text:
First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment



Protective Measures for Blister Agent Poisoning
385B




          19-53. Your protective mask with hood and protective over garment provides protection against blister
          agents. If it is known or suspected that blister agents are being used, STOP BREATHING, put on your mask
          and your protective over garment.


                                                       CAUTION
                       Large drops of liquid vesicants on the protective over garment
                       ensemble may penetrate it if allowed to stand for an extended period.
                       Remove large drops as soon as possible.


Signs and Symptoms of Blister Agent Poisoning
386B




          19-54. Immediate and intense pain upon contact with L, LH (lewisite and mustard) mixture, and phosgene
          oxime. No initial pain upon contact with mustard.
          19-55. Inflammation and blisters (burns) resulting in tissue destruction. The severity of a chemical burn is
          directly related to the concentration of the agent and the duration of contact with the skin. The longer the
          agent is in contact with the tissue, the more serious the injury will be.
          19-56. Vomiting and diarrhea. Exposure to high concentrations of vesicants may cause vomiting or diarrhea.
          19-57. The blister agent vapors absorbed during ordinary field exposure will probably not cause enough
          internal body (systemic) damage to result in death. However, death may occur from prolonged exposure to
          high concentrations of vapor or from extensive liquid contamination over wide areas of the skin, particularly
          when decontamination is neglected or delayed.

First Aid Measures for Blister Agent Poisoning
387B




          19-58. Use your RSDL to decontaminate your skin and use water to flush contaminated eyes.
          Decontamination of vesicants must be done immediately (within one minute is best).
          19-59. If blisters form, cover them loosely with a field dressing and secure the dressing.


                                                       CAUTION
                       Blisters are burns. DO NOT attempt to decontaminate the skin where
                       blisters have formed, as the agent has already been absorbed.


          19-60. If you receive blisters over a wide area of the body, you are considered seriously burned. Seek medical
          assistance immediately.
          19-61. If vomiting occurs, the mask should be lifted momentarily and drained. Make sure, while doing this,
          the eyes are closed, and the breath is held. As soon as it is complete, replace, clear, and seal the mask.
          19-62. Remember, if vomiting or diarrhea occurs after having been exposed to blister agents, seek medical
          assistance immediately.
CHOKING AGENTS (LUNG-DAMAGING AGENTS)
168B




          19-63. Chemical agents that attack lung tissue, primarily causing fluid buildup (pulmonary edema), are
          classified as choking agents (lung-damaging agents). This group includes phosgene, diphosgene (known as
          DP), chlorine (known as Cl), and chloropicrin (known as PS). Of these four agents, phosgene is the most
          dangerous and is more likely to be employed by the enemy in future conflict. Your protective mask gives
          adequate protection against choking agents.

Chapter 19



Signs and Symptoms for Choking Agents
38B




             19-64. During and immediately after exposure to choking agents (depending on agent concentration and
             length of exposure), you may experience some or all the following signs and symptoms:
                 • Tears (lacrimation).
                 • Coughing.
                 • Choking.
                 • Tightness of chest.
                 • Nausea and vomiting.
                 • Headaches.

Self-Aid for Choking Agents
389B




             19-65. The protective mask should be put on immediately when any of the conditions described above exist.
             Another indication of a phosgene attack is an odor like newly mown hay; however, DO NOT rely upon odor
             as indication of a chemical attack.
             19-66. If some phosgene is inhaled, normal combat duties should be continued unless there is difficulty in
             breathing, nausea, vomiting, or more than the usual shortness of breath during exertion. If any of the above
             symptoms occur and the mission permits, remain at quiet rest until MEDEVAC is accomplished.

Death from Choking Agents
390B




             19-67. With ordinary field exposure to choking agents, death will probably not occur. However, prolonged
             exposure to high concentrations of the vapor and neglect, or delay in masking can be fatal.

Cyanogen (Blood) Agents
391B




             19-68. Cyanogen agents interfere with proper oxygen utilization in the body. Hydrogen cyanide (AC) and
             cyanogen chloride are the primary agents in this group.

Protective Measures for Cyanogen Agents
392B




             19-69. The protective mask with a fresh filter gives adequate protection against field concentrations of
             cyanogen agent vapor. Protective over garments, as well as the mask, are needed when exposed to liquid AC
             hydrogen cyanide.

Signs and Symptoms for Cyanogen Agents
39B




             19-70. During and immediately after exposure to cyanogen agents (depending on agent concentration and
             length of exposure), you may experience some or all the following signs and symptoms:
                 • Tearing (lacrimation).
                 • Eye, nose, and throat irritation.
                 • Sudden stimulation of breathing (unable to hold breath).
                 • Nausea.
                 • Coughing.
                 • Tightness of chest.
                 • Headache.
                 • Light-headedness (dizziness).
                 • Unconsciousness.

First Aid for Cyanogen Agents
394B




             19-71. Hydrogen cyanide. During any chemical attack, if you get a sudden stimulation to breathe or detect
             an odor like bitter almonds, PUT ON YOUR MASK IMMEDIATELY. Speed is essential since this agent
             acts so rapidly that within a few seconds its effects will make it impossible for Service members to put on
             their mask by themselves. Stop breathing until the mask is on. This may be very difficult since the agent
             strongly stimulates respiration.

text:
First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment



          19-72. Cyanogen chloride. Put your mask on immediately if you experience any irritation of the eyes, nose,
          or throat. The nearest Service member should mask Service members who are unable to mask themselves.


                                                       CAUTION
                       Before attempting to help anyone else, make sure you appropriately
                       mask yourself first.


Medical Assistance for Cyanogen Agents
395B




          19-73. If exposure to blood agents is suspected, immediate medical assistance is needed. Medical assistance
          for cyanogen agents is crucial because cyanogen is a highly toxic compound that poses significant health
          risks to humans. Cyanogen is a colorless gas that can be lethal when inhaled or when it encounters the skin
          or eyes.
INCAPACITATING AGENTS
169B




          19-74. An incapacitating agent is a chemical agent that produces temporary, disabling conditions, which
          persist for hours to days after exposure. Unlike riot control agents, which usually are momentary or fleeting
          in action, incapacitating agents have a persistent effect. It is likely that smoke-producing munitions or
          aerosols will disseminate such agents, thus making breathing their means of entry into the body. The
          protective mask is, therefore, essential.
          19-75. There are no specific first aid measures to relieve the symptoms of incapacitating agents. Supportive
          first aid and physical restraint may be indicated. If the casualty is stuporous or comatose, be sure that
          respiration is unobstructed; then turn them on their side in case vomiting should occur. Complete cleansing
          of the skin with soap and water, this should be done as soon as possible; or RSDL can be used if washing is
          impossible. Remove weapons and other potentially harmful items from Service members who are suspected
          of having these symptoms. Harmful items include cigarettes, matches, medications, and small items that
          might be swallowed accidentally. Delirious (confused) persons have been known to attempt to eat items
          bearing only a superficial resemblance to food.
          19-76. Incapacitating agents (anticholinergic drugs BZ type) may produce alarming dryness and coating of
          the lips and tongue; however, there is usually no danger of immediate dehydration. Fluids should be given
          sparingly, if at all, because of the danger of vomiting and because of the likelihood of temporary urinary
          retention due to paralysis of bladder muscles.
          19-77. Immediate and vigorous cooling of the casualties is indicated if the body temperature is elevated and
          mucous membranes are dry, (as for heatstroke). The casualty can be cooled by spraying them with cool water
          and fanning; applying alcohol-soaked cloths and air circulation; and providing maximum exposure to air in
          a shaded area, along with maximum air circulation. Such cases are usually a result of anticholinergic
          poisoning.


                                                       CAUTION
                                          DO NOT use ice for cooling the skin.


          19-78. Rapid evacuation should be accomplished since medical treatment with the appropriate medication
          may be lifesaving. Reassurance and a firm, but friendly, attitude by individuals providing first aid will be
          beneficial if the casualty appears to comprehend what is being said. Conversation is a waste of time if the
          Service member is incoherent or cannot understand what is being said. In such cases, the less said, the better
          it is. These casualties will benefit more from prompt and vigorous restraint and evacuation to an MTF.

text:
Chapter 19



INCENDIARIES
170B




             19-79. Incendiaries can be grouped as white phosphorus (WP), thickened gasoline, metal, and oil and metal.
             You must learn to protect yourself against these incendiaries.

White Phosphorus
396B




             19-80. WP is primarily used as a smoke-producing agent but also serves an incendiary role for igniting field
             expedients and combustible materials. The burns caused by WP are typically multiple, deep, and vary in size.
             Once WP particles contact the skin or clothing, they will continue to burn until deprived of air, and they tend
             to adhere to any surface they contact, requiring physical removal.
             19-81. In the event that WP particles ignite clothing, it's crucial to remove the contaminated clothing quickly
             to prevent the WP from burning through to the skin. If WP particles directly strike the skin, the immediate
             response should be to smother the flames using water, a wet cloth, or mud. It is important to note that since
             WP is soluble in oil, one should not use grease or oily substances to extinguish the flames as these can
             exacerbate the burning.
             19-82. To prevent further combustion, keep the WP particles covered with wet material to exclude air.
             Removal of WP particles from the skin should be done cautiously using a wet cloth to brush them away and
             a knife, bayonet, stick, or other available tools to pick them out.
             19-83. Once immediate first aid measures are taken, it is vital to seek medical assistance as soon as the
             mission allows us to address any burns or injuries caused by WP exposure properly.

Thickened Fuel Mixtures (Napalm)
397B




             19-84. Thickened fuel mixtures (napalm) tend to cling to clothing and body surfaces, thereby producing
             prolonged exposure and severe burns. The first aid for these burns is the same as for other heat burns. The
             heat and irritating gases given off by these combustible mixtures may cause lung damage, which must be
             treated by medical personnel.

Metal Incendiaries
398B




             19-85. Metal incendiaries pose special problems. Thermite particles on the skin should be immediately
             cooled with water and then removed. The first aid for these burns is the same as for other heat burns. Particles
             of magnesium on the skin burn quickly and deeply. Like other metal incendiaries, they must be removed.
             Ordinarily, medical personnel should do the complete removal of these particles as soon as possible.
             Immediate medical treatment is required.

Oil and Metal Incendiaries
39B




             19-86. Oil and metal incendiaries, upon contact with skin and clothing, produce effects similar to those
             caused by white phosphorus. These substances can cause severe burns that require immediate and proper first
             aid attention to prevent further damage and promote healing. For detailed guidance on administering first aid
             for burns resulting from exposure to incendiaries like oil and metal, see Chapter 12. This chapter provides
             comprehensive instructions on the steps to take in treating burns, including how to manage the injury before
             professional medical help is available.

FIRST AID IN A BIOLOGICAL ENVIRONMENT
274B




             19-87. Biological hazards can provide important advantages to adversaries who use them because of factors
             such as—
                 • Clandestine employment.
                 • Delayed onset of symptoms.
                 • Detection, identification, and verification difficulties.
                 • Agent persistence.
                 • Communicability.

text:
First Aid in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Environment



          19-88. Biological attacks can result in combat ineffectiveness by introducing disease-causing organisms such
          as bacteria or viruses into the force through aerosol release; food and water contamination; vectors such as
          ticks, fleas, mosquitoes, or body fluids from infected animals or humans. The occurrence of the signs and
          symptoms from a biological hazard may appear in a few minutes to several hours or days to weeks depending
          on the biological hazard, the Service member’s susceptibility, and the amount of biological hazard that is
          inhaled, ingested, or deposited on the skin. Many biological warfare agents present the same signs and
          symptoms as the flu or common cold such as fever, cough, runny nose, and tiredness.
          19-89. First aid or medical treatment is initiated after a disease is identified, depending on the seriousness of
          the disease. First aid measures are concerned with observable symptoms of the disease such as diarrhea or
          vomiting. For certain biological warfare hazards, Service members may be directed to take doxycycline or
          ciprofloxacin from the initial issue medical CBRN defense materiel.
TOXINS
17B




          19-90. Toxins have reportedly been used in past conflicts. Witnesses and survivors have described the
          employment of the T-2 mycotoxin as toxic rain (or yellow rain) because it was reported to have been released
          from aircraft as a yellow powder or liquid that covered ground, structures, vegetation, and people.

Signs and Symptoms of Toxin Poisoning
40B




          19-91. The occurrence of the symptoms from toxins may appear in a period of a few minutes to several hours
          depending on the toxin, the Service member’s susceptibility, and the amount of toxin that is inhaled, ingested,
          or deposited on the skin. Symptoms from toxins usually involve the central nervous system but are often
          preceded by less prominent symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, cramps, stomach irritation, and
          burning sensation. Typical neurological symptoms often develop rapidly in severe cases; for example, visual
          disturbances, inability to swallow, speech difficulty, lack of muscle coordination, and sensory abnormalities
          (numbness of the mouth, throat, or extremities). Yellow rain (mycotoxins) also may have hemorrhagic
          symptoms, which could include any or all of the following:
               • Dizziness.
               • Severe itching or tingling of the skin.
               • Formation of multiple, small, or hard blisters.
               • Coughing up blood.
               • Shock (which could result in death).

Self-Aid of Toxin Poisoning
401B




          19-92. Upon recognition of an attack employing toxins, you must immediately take the following actions:
              • Stop breathing, put on your protective mask with hood, and then resume breathing. Next, put on
                  your protective ensemble.
              • Should itching of the face become severe or unbearable, quickly—
                  ▪ Loosen the cap in your canteen or valve on your water source.
                  ▪ Take and hold a deep breath and lift your mask.
                  ▪ While holding your breath, close your eyes and flush your face with generous amounts of water.


                                                        CAUTION
                       DO NOT rub or scratch your eyes. Try not to let the water run onto
                       your clothing or protective over garment.

                   ▪    Put your protective mask back on, seat it properly, clear it, and check it for a seal; then resume
                        breathing.
                   ▪    Decontaminate your skin by bathing with soap and water as soon as the mission permits.
                   ▪    Change clothing and decontaminate your protective mask using soap and water. Replace the
                        filters if directed.

text:
Chapter 20
                        Combat and Operational Stress Control

OVERVIEW OF COMBAT AND OPERATIONAL STRESS CONTROL
276B




          20-1. Psychological first aid is just as crucial as physical first aid and is a familiar concept to many. Think
          back to when a simple comforting gesture from a parent soothed you as a child, or how supportive
          conversation with a friend helped you navigate through disappointment or grief. These actions are natural
          responses to emotional distress, similar to how we instinctively want to help someone who is physically hurt.
          20-2. Just as we use bandages to cover wounds, we use supportive words and actions to help heal emotional
          wounds. Psychological first aid involves assisting those who are emotionally distressed, whether due to
          physical injuries, illness, or overwhelming stress. Signs of emotional distress, like overexcitement, severe
          fear, excessive worry, deep depression, or anger, can sometimes be less visible than physical injuries but are
          equally important to address.
          20-3. These emotional reactions are indicators that stress is impacting someone's ability to cope effectively.
          When these symptoms become more pronounced, the need for psychological support becomes more urgent.
          Knowing how to offer this support is essential, as it can significantly aid in someone's recovery process, just
          as much as treating a physical ailment.

PSYCHOLOGICAL FIRST AID
27B




          20-4. You must know how to give psychological first aid to be able to help yourself, your team members,
          and your unit to keep performing the mission. Psychological first aid measures are simple and easy to
          understand. Your decision of what to do depends upon your ability to observe the Service member and
          understand their needs. Making the best use of resources requires ingenuity on your part. A stress reaction
          resulting in poor judgment can cause injury or even death to yourself or others on the battlefield. It can be
          even more dangerous if other personnel are affected by the judgment of an emotionally upset Service
          member. If it is detected early enough, the affected Service member stands a good chance of remaining in
          their unit as an effective member. If it is not detected early and if the Service member becomes more
          emotionally upset, they may become a threat to themselves and to others.
SITUATIONS REQUIRING PSYCHOLOGICAL FIRST AID
172B




          20-5. Psychological first aid (buddy aid) is most needed at the first sign that a Service member cannot perform
          the mission because of emotional distress. Stress is inevitable in combat, in hostage and terrorist situations,
          and in civilian disasters such as floods, hurricanes, or industrial accidents. Most emotional reactions to such
          situations are temporary, and the Service member can still carry on with encouragement. Painful or disruptive
          symptoms may last for minutes, hours, or days. However, if the stress symptoms are seriously disabling, they
          may be psychologically contagious and endanger not only the emotionally upset Service member but also
          the entire unit.
          20-6. Sometimes people continue to function well during a disastrous event, but suffer from emotional scars,
          which impair their job performance or quality of life later. Painful memories and dreams may recur for
          months and years and still be considered a normal reaction. However, an individual needs treatment if the
          memories are so painful that the person must avoid all situations which arouse them, becomes socially
          withdrawn, show symptoms of anxiety, depression, or substance abuse. Experience with police, firefighters,
          emergency medical technicians, and others who deal with disasters have proved that the routine application
          of psychological first aid to all the participants, including those who have functioned well, greatly reduces
          the likelihood of future serious post-traumatic stress disorder(s).

text:
Chapter 20



INTERRELATIONSHIP OF PSYCHOLOGICAL AND PHYSICAL FIRST AID
173B




             20-7. Psychological first aid should go together with physical first aid. The discovery of a physical injury or
             cause for an inability to function does not rule out the possibility of a psychological injury
             (or vice versa). The person suffering from pain, shock, fear of serious injury, or fear of death does not respond
             well to joking, indifference, or fearful-tearful attention. Fear and anxiety may take as high a toll of on the
             Service member's strength as does the loss of blood.
GOALS OF PSYCHOLOGICAL FIRST AID
174B




             20-8. Psychological First Aid is aimed at supporting Service members in managing immediate stress
             reactions effectively, ensuring both the well-being of the individual and the operational readiness of the unit.
             The primary goals of Psychological First Aid are multifaceted, focusing on immediate mental health support,
             safety, and a swift return to duty.
             20-9. The first and foremost goal of Psychological First Aid is to provide empathetic support to Service
             members experiencing stress reactions. By offering a supportive presence, responders can help individuals
             navigate their emotional responses effectively. This involves active listening, acknowledging their feelings
             without judgment, and providing reassurance. This supportive approach is crucial in helping Service
             members feel understood and less isolated in their experiences.
             20-10. Another critical aim of Psychological First Aid is to prevent and control behaviors that could be
             harmful to the individual or others. This includes identifying signs of distress that might lead to harmful
             actions and implementing strategies to mitigate these risks. The ability to intervene early and effectively can
             prevent the escalation of stress reactions into more serious mental health issues, thereby maintaining the
             safety and cohesion of the unit.
             20-11. Finally, Psychological First Aid seeks to return the Service member to duty as efficiently as possible
             after addressing their immediate psychological needs. This goal underscores the importance of resilience and
             rapid recovery within military operations, ensuring that personnel are mentally fit to resume their roles.
             Facilitating a quick return to duty not only helps maintain unit effectiveness but also promotes a sense of
             normalcy and purpose for the individual, which can be therapeutic in overcoming stress reactions.
RESPECT FOR OTHERS’ FEELINGS
175B




             20-12. Accept the Service member you are trying to help without censorship or ridicule. Respect their right
             to their own feelings. Even though your feelings, beliefs, and behavior are different, do not blame or make
             light of them for the way they feel or act. Your purpose is to help them in this tough situation, not to be their
             critic. A person does not want to be upset and worried. When they seek help, they need and expect
             consideration of their fears, not abrupt dismissal, or ridicule.
             20-13. Realize that people are the products of a wide variety of factors. All people do not react the same way
             to the same situations. Everyone has complex needs and motivations, both conscious and unconscious, that
             are uniquely their own. Often the one thing that finally causes the person to become overloaded by a stressful
             situation is not the stressor itself, but some other problem.
EMOTIONAL AND PHYSICAL DISABILITY
176B




             20-14. Accept emotional disability as being just as real as physical disability. If a Service member’s ankle
             is seriously sprained in a fall, no one expects them to run right away. A Service member’s emotions may be
             temporarily strained by the overwhelming stress of battle or another traumatic incident. Do not demand that
             they pull themselves together immediately and carry on without a break. Some individuals can pull
             themselves together immediately, but others cannot. The Service member whose emotional stability has been
             disrupted has a disability just as real as the Service member who has sprained their ankle. There is an
             unfortunate tendency in many people to regard as real only what they can see, such as a wound or bleeding.
             Some people tend to assume that damage involving a person’s mind and emotions is just imagined, they are
             not sick or injured, and that they could overcome their trouble by using their will power.
             20-15. The phrases “it is all in your head”, “snap out of it”, and “get control of yourself” are often used by
             people who believe they are being helpful. These terms are expressions of hostility because they show lack

text:
Combat and Operational Stress Control



          of understanding. They only emphasize weakness and inadequacy. The above stated phrases are of no use in
          psychological first aid.
          20-16. Every physically injured person has some emotional reaction to the fact that they are injured. It is
          normal for an injured person to feel upset. The more severe the injury, the more insecure and fearful they
          become, especially if the injury is to a body part that is highly valued. For example, an injury to the eyes or
          the genitals, even though relatively minor, is likely to be extremely upsetting. An injury to some other part
          of the body may be especially disturbing to an individual for their own reason. For example, an injury to the
          hand may be a terrifying blow to a surgeon, or an injury to the eye of a pilot.
          20-17. An injured Service member can sometimes feel less secure, more anxious, and more afraid not only
          because of what has happened to them but also what they imagine may happen because of their injury. This
          fear and insecurity may cause them to be irritable, uncooperative, or unreasonable. As you help the Service
          member, always keep in mind that such behavior has little or nothing to do with you personally. They need
          your patience, reassurance, encouragement, and support.

COMBAT AND OPERATIONAL STRESS REACTION
278B




          20-18. Stress reaction is a temporary emotional disorder or inability to function, experienced by a previously
          normal Service member as a reaction to the overwhelming or cumulative stress of combat. Stress reaction
          gets better with reassurance, rest, physical replenishment, and activities that restore confidence. All Service
          members are likely to feel stressed under conditions of intense or prolonged stress. They may even become
          stress reaction casualties and are unable to perform their mission for hours or days. Other combat and
          operational stress reactions may result in negative behavior, but are not termed stress reaction, as they need
          treatment that is more intensive. These negative combat and operational stress reactions may result in
          misconduct and stress behaviors such as drug and alcohol abuse, criminal acts, looting, desertion, and self-
          inflicted wounds. These harmful combat and operational stress reactions can often be prevented by good
          psychological first aid. Service members who commit misconduct stress behaviors may require disciplinary
          action rather than medical treatment.
REACTIONS TO STRESS
17B




          20-19. Most Service members react to stressful incidents after the situation has passed. Service members feel
          some fear. This fear may be greater than they have experienced at any other time, or they may be more aware
          of their fear. In such a situation, they should not be surprised if they feel shaky or become sweaty, nauseated,
          or confused. These reactions are normal and are not a cause for concern. However, some reactions, either
          short- or long-term, will cause problems if left unchecked.

Emotional Reactions
403B




          20-20. The most obvious combat and operational stress reaction is inefficient performance. This can be
          demonstrated by—
              • Slow thinking (or reaction time).
              • Difficulty recognizing priorities and seeing what needs to be done.
              • Difficulty getting started.
              • Indecisiveness and having trouble focusing.
              • Tendency to do familiar tasks and be preoccupied with familiar details. (This can reach the point in
                  which the person is very passive, sitting or wandering, and not knowing what to do).
          20-21. A less common reaction may be uncontrolled emotional outbursts; this can be demonstrated by crying,
          screaming, or laughing. Some Service members will react in the opposite way. They can show signs of being
          very withdrawn, silent, and try to isolate themselves from everyone. These Service members should be
          encouraged to remain with their assigned unit. Uncontrolled reactions may appear by themselves or in any
          combination. The person may be crying uncontrollably one minute and then laughing the next. In this state,
          the person is restless and cannot keep still. They may run about, apparently without purpose. Inside, they feel
          a great rage or fear and their physical acts may show this. In their anger, they may indiscriminately strike out
          at others.

text:
Chapter 20



Loss of Adaptability
40B




             20-22. In a desperate attempt to get away from the danger, which has overwhelmed them, a Service member
             may panic and become confused. Their mental ability may be so impaired they cannot think clearly or even
             follow simple commands. Their judgment may be faulty, and they may not be aware of their actions, such as
             standing up in their fighting position during an attack.
             20-23. In other cases, overwhelming stress may produce symptoms that are often associated with head
             injuries. For example, the Service member may appear dazed or be found wandering around aimlessly. They
             may appear confused and disoriented and may seem to have a complete or partial loss of memory. In such
             cases, especially when no eyewitnesses can provide evidence that the Service member has NOT suffered a
             head injury, it is necessary for them to be rapidly evacuated. DO NOT allow the Service members to expose
             themselves to further personal danger until the cause of the problem has been determined.

Sleep Disturbance and Repetition of Dreams
405B




             20-24. A person who has been overwhelmed by stress, often has difficulty sleeping. The Service member
             may experience nightmares related to the stressors. Remember that nightmares, in themselves, are not
             considered abnormal when they occur soon after a period of intensive stress. As time passes, the nightmares
             usually become less frequent and less intense. In extreme cases, a Service member, even when awake, may
             think repeatedly of the incident, feel as though it is happening again, and act out parts of their stress
             repeatedly.
             20-25. For some individuals, this repetitious re-experiencing of the stressful event may be necessary for
             eventual recovery; therefore, it should not be discouraged or viewed as abnormal. For the person re-
             experiencing the event, such reaction may be disruptive. The Service member needs to be encouraged to
             ventilate about the incident. Ventilation is a technique where the Service member is given the opportunity to
             talk extensively and often repetitiously about the experience.

Severe Stress or Stress Reaction
406B




             20-26. You do not need specialized training to recognize severe stress or stress reaction that will cause
             problems for the Service member, the unit, or the mission. Reactions that are less severe, however, are more
             difficult to detect. To determine whether a person needs help, you must observe them to see whether they are
             doing something meaningful, performing their duties, taking care of themselves, behaving in an unusual
             fashion, or acting out of character.
APPLICATION OF PSYCHOLOGICAL FIRST AID
178B




             20-27. The emotionally disturbed Service member has built a barrier against fear. They do this for their own
             protection, although they are probably not aware that they are doing it. If they find that they do not have to
             be afraid and that there are normal, understandable things about them, they will feel safer in dropping this
             barrier. Persistent efforts to make them realize that you want to understand them will be reassuring, especially
             if you remain calm. Nothing can cause an emotionally disturbed person to become even more fearful than
             feeling that others are afraid of them. Try to remain calm. Familiar things, such as a cup of coffee, the use of
             their name, attention to a minor wound, being given a simple job to do, or the sight of familiar people and
             activities, will add to their ability to overcome their fear. They may not respond well if you get excited, angry,
             or abrupt.

Ventilation
407B




             20-28. After the Service member becomes calmer, they are likely to have dreams about the stressful event.
             They also may think about it when they are awake or even repeat their personal reaction to the event. One
             benefit of this natural pattern is that it helps them master the stress by going over it just as one master the
             initial fear of parachuting from an aircraft by doing it repeatedly. Eventually, it is difficult to remember how
             frightening the event was initially. In giving first aid to the emotionally disturbed Service members, you
             should let them follow this natural pattern. Encourage them to talk. Be a good listener. Let them tell you, in
             their own words, what happened. If home front problems or worries have contributed to stress, it will help
             them to talk about these problems. Your patient listening will prove to the Service member that you are

text:
Combat and Operational Stress Control



          interested in them, and by describing their personal problem, they can work at mastering their fear. If they
          become overwhelmed, suggest a cup of coffee or a break. Whatever you do, assure them that you will listen
          again as soon as they are ready. Try to help put the Service member's perception of what happened back into
          realistic perspective; but DO NOT argue about it.

Activity
408B




          20-29. A person who is emotionally disturbed as the result of a combat action is a casualty of anxiety and
          fear. The person may feel as though they are disabled because they have become temporarily overwhelmed
          by their anxiety. A good way to control fear is through activity. For example, almost all Service members
          experience a considerable sense of anxiety and fear while they are poised, awaiting the opening of a big
          offensive; but this is normally relieved, and they feel better once they begin to move into action. They take
          pride in effective performance and pleasure in knowing that they are a good Service member, perhaps being
          completely unaware that overcoming their initial fear was their first major accomplishment.
          20-30. Useful activity can be very beneficial to Service members who are emotionally disturbed and not
          physically incapacitated. After you help a Service member get over their initial fear, help them to regain some
          self-confidence. Help them realize their job continues by finding them something useful to do. Encourage
          them to be active. Get them to help load trucks, clean up debris, or dig fighting positions. If possible, get
          them back to their usual duty. Seek out their strong points and help them apply these attributes. Avoid having
          them just sit around. You may have to provide directions by telling them what to do and where to do it. The
          instructions should be clear, simple, and should be repeated. A person who has panicked is likely to argue.
          Respect their feelings, but point out more immediate, obtainable, and demanding needs. Channel their
          excessive energy and, above all, DO NOT argue. If you cannot get them to become interested in doing
          profitable work, it may be necessary to enlist aid in controlling their over-activity before it results in more
          panic. Prevent the spread of such infectious feelings by restraining and segregating if necessary.
          20-31. Involvement in an activity helps the Service member in three ways; they—
              • Place their thoughts on something more productive.
              • Have an outlet for their excessive tensions.
              • Prove to them that they can do something useful.

Rest
409B




          20-32. There are times, particularly in combat, when physical exhaustion is a principal cause for emotional
          reactions. A unit sleep plan should be established and implemented. When possible, Service members should
          be given a safe and relatively comfortable area in which to sleep. Examples would be an area away from
          heavy traffic, noise, congestion, a place that is clean, dry, and protected from environmental conditions. The
          more uninterrupted sleep a Service member gets the better they will be able to function in the tactical
          environment.

Hygiene
410B




          20-33. Field hygiene is an important ingredient in a Service member's morale. A Service member who is
          lacking personal hygiene will not function as well as others who have had the opportunity to bathe and put
          on clean, dry clothing. During combat, unit leaders should stress the importance of personal hygiene. Good
          personal hygiene not only improves morale, but it is also a preventive measure against disease and disease
          and nonbattle injury.

Group Activity
41B




          20-34. You have probably already noticed that a person who works, faces danger, and handles serious
          problems better if they are a member of a closely-knit group. Each Service member in the team supports the
          other team members. Esprit de corps is built because the Service members have the same interests, goals, and
          mission. As a result, they are more productive; and are less worried because everyone is involved. This is
          one of the most effective tools you have in your psychological first aid bag. Getting the Service member back
          into the team or squad activities will re-establish their sense of belonging and security. This will go far toward
          making them a useful member of the unit.
